chapters.title: Chapter 1
chapters.html:
Marmoreal Palace was only standing due to a mixture of spite and golden threads.

The rest of Okhema’s city centre was much the same. Gold threads bound around broken pillars and sealed the cracks of building rafters. Various floors shimmered with gold, gaps in the ground woven together into something liquid that had since dried into concrete.

Irontomb had been defeated but not without cost.

The city was as much of a ruin as the actual ruins torn asunder by the black tide. It would need to be rebuilt and fast. Aglaea’s golden threads could keep things in place long enough for further evacuation from the more structurally unstable regions of Okhema but she couldn’t rebuild a city with her powers alone.

…Phainon probably could have done it.

With millions of Mnestia’s coreflames squirreled away in his chest, he probably could’ve done it all on his own. Was it rude of him to have not taken the initiative and strung up his own set of threads? It was difficult to know. Honestly, it was still a little difficult to think.

Tracking all of the damage for an entire city, identifying the structural damage and then subsequently fixing the damages in whichever way was most reliable would be far too difficult on the best of days. An hour ago, Phainon had torn himself - with much agony - free from the scepter’s core. It was not exactly the best of days.

For now, he settled on what he could manage: He reinforced any trembling threads at risk of snapping with his own. When Aglaea shot a sharp look in his direction, he flashed her a tired smile and a thumbs up, as if he weren’t currently dead on his feet.

He was still focusing on reinforcing her threads when the conversation began. It was a debrief of the past 24 hours as much as it was to be a meeting to discuss immediate plans for Okhema’s future.

Hopefully, whatever workload got placed on his shoulders wouldn’t be so time sensitive that he couldn’t take a short nap first. Titans, there was nothing Phainon wanted more than to lie down and sleep. It was a statistical wonder that he was still conscious.

Conscious, maybe. Tracking the conversation? Not at all.

He’d need to ask for a summary from the trailblazer later. Currently she stood beside Cyrene and was explaining her part as the deliverer of this latest cycle. Phainon caught some words - something about the cycles, something about Lygus’ administrative access being revoked. He even heard his own name mentioned a couple of times.

Like now. Stelle was probably explaining something about Irontomb or whatever, so of course his name was coming up a bunch of times. He took hold of fraying gold wrapped around a crumbling pillar and reinforced it with a net of finely spun strings.

…Wait. She was still saying his name. It was louder than before, his name spoken with more persistence.

Phainon’s gaze flicked back to the group. A dozen pairs of eyes were all focused on him.

“Huh?”

“Are you still there with us, partner?” Stelle asked. Phainon tilted his head and blinked at her. She added, “You weren’t responding when we called your name.”

The smile he offered was deeply tired and overly forced. He couldn’t add enough emotion into his voice for it to be anything but dull and exhausted. “Sorry. What did I miss?”

“Everyone wants to know a bit more about the cycles you lived through,” Stelle said, with a wan smile.

Phainon felt something jolt in his chest. Could’ve been the coreflames. Could’ve been grief. He said, “Uh… Right now?”

“Not too much. Just—you know…”

“We’d like to know how many times you went through them,” Aglaea interrupted. “The trailblazer has mentioned that there have been many but she has not mentioned any specific number.”

Threads slipped through his hands. He wasn’t sure whether it was his thoughts stuttering or Mnestia’s physical, tangible strings. The building wasn’t immediately crumbling apart so it was probably just his thoughts.

“Oh,” he said. There wasn’t really any reason not to tell them. Sure, they’d probably be angry that it took him millions of cycles to bring any real change to Amphoreus, but surely they wouldn’t be too angry if he reiterated that the idea had been to draw out the cycles for as long as possible to buy them all time for Stelle’s arrival to Amphoreus. “Uh, well. Thirty three—”

He felt the snap just in time for the pillar to come crashing into the pool. The sound of falling stone drowned out the rest of his words: “—million, five hundred and fifty thousand, three hundred and thirty-six.”

Phainon whipped around as the rest of the pillar fell. Oh, so he had let go of some of his strings after all. Aglaea’s had snapped under the sudden weight.

Stupid. He should’ve been able to do better. Shame flooded his chest, burning as hot as any coreflame. Immediately his gaze was flickering for signs of any other trembling threads.

There were only a few. It was easy enough to encase them in a protective barrier.

When he returned his attention to the meeting, they were still staring at him. Tribbie’s eyes were rapidly filling with worried tears. Hyacine held little Ica close in her arms, hugging the pegasus for comfort.

“You had to go through that thirty-three times?” Tribbie asked. Her voice wobbled with unshed tears.

Ash caught in his throat. He’d definitely said million but the falling pillar must’ve drowned that part out.

Were thirty-three cycles really worth crying about? The number was shockingly low. Even a thousand cycles passed in a blink of an eye, compared to millions. Tribbie really shouldn’t be wasting tears over a number so small.

…It wasn’t just the little priestess who looked upset, though. It was all of his fellow heirs.

It was Aglaea, whose lips pressed together in a thin line, brows faintly furrowed. It was Mydei who was now glaring at the ground like it had wronged him. Castorice too, looked upset, like she wanted to hug him and never let go.

All for such a miniscule number.

And then it registered: If they reacted this way over the idea of thirty-three cycles, they were going to lose their shit when they learned the true number was far, far higher.

Phainon did the only thing possible in such a situation.

He panicked.

The first new feeling, past relief, exhaustion and rage, across millions of cycles hit him and it was pure, bone-chilling panic.

“Uh,” he said, because clearly his eloquence had abandoned him during one of the cycles, “yes?”

Behind Aglaea’s shoulder, the trailblazer stared at him. Not with shock— though her surprise was evident—but with a frown that clearly asked where he found the audacity to spin such a lie.

Phainon was a big fan of digging his own grave so he ignored her frown and said, “I lived through thirty three—” - million- “—cycles.”

The meeting continued, except now, Stelle was staring at him as if she were minutes away from having an aneurysm. Considering the fact that he was the cause of this sudden breakdown, Phainon did his best to avoid looking her way. Every time she managed to catch his eye, she began mouthing things at him that his brain was too tired to decipher.

All he’d managed to decipher thus far was ‘what the fuck’, which he could whole-heartedly understand the sentiment behind. Phainon too, wasn’t entirely sure what the fuck he’d just done. Nor could he answer why the fuck. Objectively, he already knew this was a disaster waiting to happen. And yet he did nothing to clear the misunderstanding.

Further conversation was had. Bits and pieces of information from the recent cycles were explained - things that the other heirs remembered. At one point, the Flame Reaver was brought up and Phainon waved the topic away by saying he’d killed him and that the reaver would no longer be a concern.

At that, Stelle let out a choked noise which had not gone ignored.

“Is something wrong, trailblazer?” Aglaea asked.

Stelle, without looking away from him, answered, “Nope. Nothing.”

Her voice was so tight that Phainon doubted anyone truly believed her. The only reason they weren’t asking was because the day had been long enough and their exhaustion had reached bone. Even Aglaea, who normally wouldn’t have given up on the question without some sort of minor interrogation, seemed happy to leave the questioning for later. The goldweaver would most likely pick the questioning back up when they’d gotten some rest and the buildings around them were no longer in the process of physically falling apart.

Once their meeting ended, Stelle burst forward. Her hand wrapped around his wrist like a bruise, forceful and heavy as she stared up at him with what was, most probably, the fakest smile he’d ever seen.

“Hey Partner?” She said, in a tone that made him want to hide his face in his hands. “It’s been a while. Let’s catch up.”

It was clear he was in some sort of trouble. Stelle dragged him away from the hero's baths, down the —surprisingly still functional— elevator and into one of the now abandoned public changing rooms. Through it all, her grip remained harsh, each footstep quick as she dragged him along.

Phainon did his best to keep up even if his body was beginning to feel like lead.

She did not speak again until she’d confirmed they were alone, at which point she let go of his wrist and pinched the bridge of her nose. It was an altogether odd look on her; She looked less like she was actually exasperated and more like she was mimicking Dan Heng in an attempt to let him know that he was an idiot.

“First off,” she said, dropping her hand back to her side. “I’m really glad you’re not dead. It was really cool watching you burst out of Irontomb like a baby chicken. Good shit. Ten out of ten.”

Ah, yes, Phainon thought, he’d missed the odd way in which she spoke. Even if said oddness included being likened to a bird.

His lips quirked upwards. There was a cold satisfaction in his chest that came with helping destroy a Lord Ravager that he didn’t think was going to go away anytime soon.

“It was very cathartic,” Phainon said.

“I can imagine,” Stelle said, with a small smile. Then it faded back into the indignant glare from before. “But enough about all of that. You, mister, what the fuck was that?”

He didn’t have the energy to grimace. Instead, he sighed and said, “Does it matter if they think the number is lower than it truly is?”

For a moment, she simply stared at him.

Then Stelle nodded in such a jerked manner that it was a surprise she did not give herself whiplash.

“You know,” Stelle said, her words altogether dumbfounded by what Phainon could only guess was his audacity. “I’ve heard people say you get wiser the older you get. Considering you’re probably older than the literal universe multiple times over, I’d have thought you wouldn’t be so stupid.”

Alright, well, that wasn’t necessarily fair.

“Well—”

“But maybe being wise isn’t like that at all, maybe it’s just this one repeating wave and at some point you regress and fall back into being a fool. What was that word again? Ah right, yeah, it’s a bell curve of stupidity. Maybe this is a bell curve and you, Phainon, are currently in the negatives because what the actual fuck, why would you even think the number doesn’t matter at all?”

It was kind of impressive actually, how she managed to get all the words out in seemingly very few breaths. She’d only taken two breaths the entire time. Maybe she’d been given tips by Anaxa, who was typically just as effective at drawing out each breath when lecturing others.

When he didn’t say anything, Stelle put a hand on his shoulder and said, “Phainon.”

“Stelle,” Phainon said.

“I want to study your stupidity like a bug.”

Yeah, Phainon wasn’t really sure what that meant. All he knew was that he was very tired and Stelle was displeased about his understatement. Typically when Stelle thought something was a stupid idea, it meant that it was very stupid indeed.

“I didn’t set out with the intent to lie,” Phainon said, slowly. “It just happened. I panicked.”

“I totally get that,” she said, and began nodding. “Totally. But you’re definitely going to have to un-panic yourself and tell them the truth. You’re not allowed to be the dog in the room that’s on fire, okay? It’s not fine and neither of us have enough fire extinguishers for this kind of thing.”

They fell into a silence where they both simply… nodded at each other. As if to emphasise that yes, they were totally hearing one another but they didn’t quite know what came next.

Probably fair - he and Stelle had never really been people that others pointed to and thought: ‘Hey, they’ve totally got their shit together’.

The silence began to bleed.

“...Is that… one of your meme references that I don’t understand?” Phainon asked.

Stelle’s hand tightened around his shoulder. Somewhat pained she said, “Yes it’s one of my memes that you don’t understand. I’ll show you it later. Right now, you need to fix this.”

Phainon sighed. Then, gently, he lifted Stelle’s hand from his shoulder and took a small step back.

“I’ll—Fine.” The words were dragged from his throat, utterly reluctant. “I’ll tell them the truth. Just… Let’s deal with rebuilding things first, alright? Okhema comes before all of this. But I will tell them eventually.”

Stelle narrowed her eyes at him. “You won’t try to wriggle out of this if I leave you to tell them yourself?”

“I won’t,” Phainon said. He wasn’t sure whether he was being truthful or whether it was a lie.

She watched him quietly, as if trying to determine the same thing. Either he was too hard to read or she saw something resembling sincerity in his eyes because eventually, Stelle dropped her shoulders and let out a long sigh. “Fine. But tell them soon, okay? Keeping secrets sucks.”

Four days later, at the behest of the genius Herta, the Astral Express bid them a temporary goodbye, taking with them the remains of the scepter Irontomb in a set of cargo containers. Phainon joined the other heirs in waving goodbye to the express crew and did his best to avoid the warning look Stelle sent his way.

“Whoa,” Tribbie said, by his side, “little grey is really glaring at you. Did you guys fight?”

Phainon, who was in the middle of wriggling his way out of telling the truth just as Stelle had feared he would, shook his head. He said, “We didn’t. That’s not a glare—I think she’s just a little tired.”

Tribbie hummed. She said, “We all are, I think.”

Ha, yeah, that was an understatement. It’d been days and Phainon still found it difficult to put one foot in front of the other without being flooded with exhaustion. If he were being honest, he probably should’ve gone to Hyacine about it by now but… Well, what was one more secret?

Everything would be fine.

Chapter Notes

i didn't expect such a response from people on my silly little au idea. but boi am i pleased that people enjoy this as much as i do. the next chapter will not be nearly as quick, so please don't expect super speedy updates. i am but a single mint, and i like playing with my doc of multiple aus rather than focusing on just one at a time.

Once the Astral Express departed Amphoreus and the train had warped from visible sight, Phainon took to the streets with an enthusiasm that felt antithetical to the exhaustion humming through his bones. The roaming was not without purpose - his official task was to patrol the currently occupied areas of Okhema and reinforce any weak spots in Aglaea’s matrix of golden string.

Unofficially, Phainon had taken it upon himself to do much more than that. It wasn’t enough to wade through rubble and debris that he - as an unwilling part of Irontomb - had created and look for trembling threads. He had to help fix the destruction he’d wrought. He needed to do more.

Fixing Okhema wasn’t just part of his duty as the Chrysos Heir of Worldbearing.

It was penance.

And either way, it wasn’t like physical labour was particularly hard. Even with his body as unwilling as it was, Phainon was capable of aiding the rebuilding effort. His limbs might have moved like he were sludging through mud but that wasn’t really anything new.

His current patrol led him to Kephale Plaza. Fallen boulders had crushed the flower beds. The mural of Kephale was in so many fragments that even the Tribios Triplets did not have enough power to restore it. Water flooded the eastern quarter of the plaza - the fountain had been smashed and now leaked like a bleeding wound.

Phainon’s gaze flicked for signs of gold and found that there weren’t many threads left behind. Most of the surrounding infrastructure had been demolished in the fight and thus there was minimal risk of further destruction.

Currently, the plaza was filled with citizens and chimeras alike, all working in unison to remove the worst of the debris. Chimera teams chipped away at larger pieces of fallen stone and human labourers relocated the smaller stone pieces into the awaiting carriages waiting outside the fallen gates.

They were making progress. Slow progress, but progress nonetheless.

Phainon joined them without a word. He took a large chunk of stone with ease from an older man in a fraying chiton and dropped it in a half filled carriage. When a chimera got caught at the top of a fallen pillar, trembling at the suddenly perceived height, he climbed up and brought the creature safely to the ground.

The people needed to get to the debris in the flooded area of the plaza? Phainon utilised the many coreflames of Phagousa and Georios and remoulded the earth beneath them so the flooded water had somewhere to flow.

It wasn’t exactly smart to go using the millions of coreflames in his chest when they’d slowly been killing him for just as many years, but the burn in his chest wasn’t hot enough to liquefy his organs. Arguably, he’d be alright with short time uses. Probably.

He continued.

His foot caught on a broken piece of mural as he returned from lugging a large crumbling of broken pillar out of the plaza’s gates. Dropping into a crouch, Phainon reached for sharpened edges. The chunk wasn’t overly big and yet, it was easy to place it in his mind’s eye. The tip of a finger and the gold of flowing ichor.

Phainon was looking at a piece of what had once been mural Kephale’s hand. Kephale, the worldbearer, Their hand stained in blood. It reminded him of a particular aeon. It reminded him of himself.

Around him, ripples of red glitched in and out of the world. The plaza emptied around him. Fire licked at his skin and the debris was stained a mixture of red and gold.

His spine stiffened. Phainon’s gaze narrowed on a limp hand caught beneath stone. The fire around him had begun to fill the cracks of his skin. Phainon’s jaw clenched—

“Lord Phainon—?”

—And the limp hand wasn’t a hand at all. It was just a small chimera. Its fur was deep gold with splotches of red on its tail.

The voice belonged to the older man with the fraying chiton. He’d stopped beside Phainon, not quite concerned but getting there. When Phainon’s gaze flicked up to meet him, he offered a small smile.

“Is everything alright, Lord Phainon?”

Phainon didn’t want to look at the chimera lest it turn back into blood and ichor, so instead he offered a tired smile of his own and stood. He said, “Everything is fine.”

Because it was.

It had to be.

“I’ll be moving on now to patrol the other areas,” he said. “If anything becomes too heavy for you all, leave it aside for me and I’ll come back for it later. Please don’t strain yourselves.”

He curled his fingers around the broken piece of mural only to find that it was no longer there. Instead there was only dust and the lingering tingle of destruction against his fingers.

…Strange. He hadn’t meant to render it dust.

And yet, he was glad that it was gone. This was better, actually. Now he’d never need to look at that stupid, fucking mural ever again. Endless millenia and finally— finally— Okhema would see its plaza change. The urge to let the rest of the mural crumble between his finger tips was almost too much to resist.

He tilted his hand so the dust drifted from his hand. Then, he brushed lingering remains away on his trouser leg. All through it all, he kept circling around a singular thought: He’d have to come back and find the other pieces later.

“They won’t be too upset over one mural, surely,” Phainon murmured to himself, as he continued past the plaza and deeper into the city.

“There you are!” Cyrene shouted later that day, when he’d settled into helping at a residential district east of the Marmoreal Palace. Her footsteps were skittering things - clearly she’d broken into a run the second she’d caught sight of him.

The wonderful thing about finally reaching Era Nova was that Cyrene was back.

The terrifying thing about it was that —like the Trailblazer— she knew everything he had done.

Phainon hadn’t exactly set out to avoid her but he’d not really gone out of his way to seek her out either. Which was pretty cruel of him, probably. He’d managed to justify it in his head by saying he’d not really been seeking anyone out recently and that he’d get around to it eventually.

But really, that wasn’t true at all. Things were just awkward. It got pretty hard to look your best friend in the eye when you’d spent more time over the eons killing her than speaking to her. He knew how best to bury her broken body, to set her into the ground so she could settle into peaceful slumber but he didn’t really know how to talk to her. Not that he’d tried yet. He would - eventually. But well… Okhema needed rebuilding, so of course he was busy.

Pulling scraps of broken wood from a building covered in shimmering gold, Phainon glanced at Cyrene over his shoulder. She’d come to a stop beside him, hands planted on her knees and body pitched forward as if doing so would help her inhale more air.

It wouldn’t but saying as such wouldn’t help. She’d probably just roll her eyes.

Phainon snapped the wood into smaller pieces - it was already too corroded to be of any use past firewood - and tossed it into a pile of firewood. Then, he waited for her to catch her breath.

When her breathing had evened out, Cyrene stood as tall as she could - which wasn’t very tall at all - and gave him a once over. Whatever she saw mustn’t have met her self imposed standards because she grimaced and said, “Wow. You look awful.”

“Thanks,” Phainon said dryly.

Not that he was surprised. He’d been helping out with the cleanup of debris, what was she expecting from him? He’d been covered in a layer of soot since the entry hour passed its second quint. Grime coated his skin like a film and dust had dyed his hair grey. It wasn’t a big deal - everyone else helping clean up was in a similar state.

Cyrene placed a hand on her hip and shook her head. She said, “I don’t mean it in a messy sense. You’re really pale. Are you feeling okay?”

He opened his mouth but she continued before he could speak.

“Bad question, I already know you’re going to say you’re fine.” Her voice lowered into a hum as she considered how to rephrase it. Then: “When did you last take a break?”

Phainon squinted at her. That really depended on how you decided to define ‘break’. Did sleep count? Even if it did… well. The answer still didn’t shine very favourably on him.

“I don’t exactly have a clock on me,” Phainon said, slowly. “So I couldn’t say.”

Tilting her head, Cyrene hummed. She said, “Is that supposed to make me worry less or more?”

“Ideally,” Phainon sighed, “you wouldn’t be worrying at all.”

At that, Cyrene laughed. Like he’d told some kind of joke. She was a terrible person. He’d never missed someone as much as he’d missed her. Even stood in front of him she felt like a ghost.

“After all those cycles,” she said, shaking her head fondly, “and you’re still the same Phainon I know and love. Which means, I know for certain you’ve not stopped at all today.”

The same Phainon, huh? What a joke.

Still, he couldn’t deny the fact that she’d clocked his lack of rest immediately. Since he couldn’t deny it, he fell silent and turned back to the golden ruins. Proceeded to retrieve wood and strip it to pieces.

Maybe if he didn’t acknowledge the need for a break, she’d leave him alone.

Yeah, that obviously wasn’t going to work.

This was Cyrene he was talking about. She was as stubborn as they came. But—was she? He couldn’t remember any instances of that stubbornness and yet that thought was so clear in his mind. When he thought of her, all he could conjure was blood and half-drawn breaths.

He drowned out her voice and cracked wood into splinters. Whenever they pierced his skin, Phainon let flame engulf them, small pieces of ash scattering across the ground in his wake.

“Hey!” A hand grabbed hold of his sleeve and yanked. When he turned, surprised, Cyrene’s eyes were wide. Her typical smile was gone, replaced with concern. Around them, the sun seemed dimmer than it had been before yet the sky was clear and there were no clouds in sight. “Don’t make me blackmail you into listening to me. I will, you know.”

“Blackmail?”

Cyrene nodded emphatically. “Maybe I’ll tell everyone that you’ve actually lived through fifty-four cycles instead of thirty-three. Or—oh, maybe I’ll tell them it was a hundred!”

“Why wouldn’t you just threaten to tell them about the full thirty-three million?” Phainon asked.

Clasping her hands behind her back, Cyrene took her time to think. Then, rather reluctantly, she admitted, “I don’t really want to tell them that our plan took that many cycles either.”

Somewhat vindicated, Phainon’s eyes widened. He would have thought that she’d have openly taken Stelle’s side in this, demanding that the truth be offered up without hesitation.

“Don’t get me wrong,” Cyrene continued, as if reading his thoughts. “The truth will come out eventually, it always does. But… I don’t know. The idea of admitting that I spent so long alone, stuck outside of the cycles… It sucks. I get why you said what you did.”

Phainon straightened. He said, “You… don’t think keeping it secret is a bad idea?”

Cyrene laughed. It was a kind of laugh that scraped at her ribs, deep and amused. She said, “It’s one hundred percent a terrible idea, Phai. I understand why you’re keeping quiet but I don’t agree with it. I just—I dunno. I’ll stay quiet until you tell them. If that’s what you want.”

The likelihood that he would ever tell the truth about the cycles got infinitesimally smaller the more time passed. It was probably best not to admit that though. Cyrene was only minorly on his side in all of this - while she hadn’t openly called him an idiot for it, like Stelle had, she was probably thinking it.

“I’d appreciate that,” he said, slowly.

“Co-conspirators, then?” Cyrene asked. Her eyelids crinkled as she smiled. Phainon had forgotten she had dimples but there they were, tiny crescents etched into her cheeks.

“...Alright,” Phainon said.

She grabbed hold of his hand as if to shake on the deal. Her fingers were so cold that Phainon flinched away from the touch. It was like a flame touching liquid nitrogen. The sensation was utterly foreign and unpleasant.

Cyrene must’ve felt it too, only in reverse, yet she ignored it and locked their fingers together. She said, “Perfect. Our first mission as co-conspirators is to take a break. Alright?”

…Oh.

He’d been duped.

“I’m fine,” Phainon said.

“Nuh-uh,” Cyrene said. She wasn’t as strong as he was but she had the advantage of extra energy. When she yanked on his arm, Phainon’s balance tipped out from beneath him and he was forced to stumble after her, lest he trip over his own feet. “This classes as official conspirator business. You’ve got to go along with it.”

“There’s too much that needs to be done,” he tried, weakly.

“Excuse rejected,” Cyrene said, somewhat gleefully. “I’m thinking… you need to get rid of all that grime. And either way, a bath will be relaxing. You look way too tense.”

Absolutely not.

“I’ve got to patrol, Aglaea said—”

“Aglaea said that we shouldn’t overwork ourselves.” Cyrene interrupted. “That we need to take breaks so that we don’t burn out while rebuilding. Relaxation is necessary - your excuse is rejected once again.”

“You can’t just keep rejecting my excuses.”

“So you admit they’re excuses?” Cyrene grinned and playfully stuck out her tongue. Phainon was too tired to argue back against her—all he could manage was another deep sigh.

And without giving him an inch lest he take a mile, she pulled on his arm again and began marching him to the nearest bath house.

Chapter End Notes

next chapter: a break is had and a sky clinician (and her pegasus familiar) says hello.

chapters.title: Chapter 3
chapters.html:
Chapter Notes

for my birthday, my best friend made me a phainon figurine and you guys, since i opened that present yesterday i've been looking at him like a woeful little maiden. damn. what a guy. i love him so much.

The baths outside of Marmoreal Palace were much smaller. Where the baths inside the palace had always been used socially - cycling through events and welcoming large parties from all over Amphoreus - those outside the palace existed solely for utility.

The bath house they headed to was a tiny thing. A small and empty reception area that lead to two changing rooms. On the other side of the changing rooms, there were three baths - two segregated by gender, the third unisex.

Obviously, they went with the third. It was empty considering the hour - most people were still focusing on the rebuilding effort and as such wouldn’t show themselves until the Parting hour. The water was tinged green where light reflected off viridian tiles.

Towel wrapped around his waist, Phainon met Cyrene by the water’s edge.

“If the water gets too hot—”

“It won’t,” Cyrene interrupted. Her hair had been pulled into a messy bun - only a few strands of pink fell free. Phainon’s fingers twitched with the urge to make it neater, like he used to when they’d been children in Aedes Elysiae. “If you warm it up, then I’ll cool it down.”

Could she truly do that? There was very little one could do to counteract four hundred million coreflames. The blaze was too much to fight. His was the kind of fire that you had to step back and let burn itself out.

“You’re doubting me, huh?” She asked, seeing through him to the skepticism lurking behind his eyes. “Well, let me prove it to you.”

She stepped into the pool.

The water around her ankles rippled and began to crystallise into sludging ice. The deeper she settled into the bath, the more it froze around her.

Cyrene turned back to him with a grin and said, “I don’t know if I’d call this a gift from the Remembrance, but if it’ll help us balance each other, I’ll take it. Whatever I freeze, you can melt. And if you raise the temperature too high, I’ll do what I can to bring it down.”

His fingers still felt strange from when she’d grabbed hold of his hand previously - now, at least, he knew what had caused it.

Alright then, maybe he wouldn’t worry too much about the water’s temperature. As long as he kept a tight control over the coreflames, Cyrene could clearly counteract the heat that managed to snake its way free. He dipped his toes into the water and flinched away from the ice.

From where she’d been watching him, Cyrene began to laugh. “It’s not that cold.”

He’d like to see her try to adjust to being frozen after millenia of burning herself on a pyre. Maybe then she’d understand how utterly jarring it was.

“You’re biased,” Phainon shot back.

Still, he didn’t have any choice but to dip his foot back into the icy bath. It was just as cold as before - perhaps even colder. If he didn’t get in now, Cyrene would probably make it even colder until the bath became a pure block of ice.

…Was he really going to let the cold defeat him? Of all things? Absolutely not.

He took another step into the water and resisted the shudder that ran down his spine. Another step and it became physically difficult to keep himself from glaring at Cyrene and that little smirk on her face. To avoid it, he submerged himself into the water completely, hoping the plunge would help him acclimatise more quickly.

It didn’t. It was still really fucking cold.

Water and ice crystals dripped from his hair. His body trembled from the glacial sting. Unpleasant, yes, but also a somewhat welcomed change to the ever present burn of his body. The shock of it was enough to keep his eyes open as he sunk into the water. If the water had been any warmer, he’d have heard the siren call of sleep.

He settled opposite Cyrene on a bench carved into the bath, running his hand across the grooves in the tile. His back was like a rod, unwilling to slouch against the curve of the wall.

“Any better yet?” She asked.

He shook his head. Then, he asked, “Why exactly is Remembrance linked to ice so much?”

“Why is Destruction linked to fire—” Cyrene wrinkled her nose. “Wait, no that’s a stupid question. Fire’s pretty obvious. I’m not sure why it’s icy. Maybe it helps preserve memories better - meat keeps better in ice, why wouldn’t memory be the same?”

Yeah, alright.

“Literally freezing the memories in time, huh?” Phainon said.

“Exactly.”

“Doesn’t exactly sound inviting though, does it?” He continued. “Whether the memory fades or not, surely it’s better to feel its warmth than to look at it so… clinically.”

Cyrene let out a small laugh. She said, “Guess that’s the difference between the Paths, huh?”

Phainon hummed. They’d not really had much time to ask the express crew about the various Paths - there hadn’t really been time for history lessons on the universe outside of Amphoreus that awaited them over the past few days. He’d had a small introductory explanation on the Aeons from Dan Heng during the final cycle but after everything that came next, the knowledge was difficult to remember with any clarity.

All he could remember about the Paths was that of three Aeons who had overlooked Amphoreus.

Fuli, the Remembrance, who had dragged a world into existence from simulation using the many memories that had been collected and thus was regarded with positivity. Nous, the Erudition, to whom Phainon tried to remain indifferent.

And then there was Nanook.

Something snarled deep in his chest at the name. Phainon had proven that an Aeon could bleed. And if They could bleed, then They could be killed too. And he’d find a way. Once Okhema was pieced back together, when he’d paid the price of all his crimes, he’d figure a way to kill a god. He’d take Dawnbreaker and—

Cyrene let out a yelp.

Phainon jerked out of his thoughts and had to look through thick steam to find her.

“H—hot,” she stuttered.

Eyes wide, he couldn’t help but curse. “Sorry. I didn’t mean to—I just—”

“It’s okay,” she said, though her smile was a little more concerned than before. Lacking self-preservation, she waded through the water until she was by his side, laying a hand on his arm. Her fingers, ice and bone, looked like they were melting. “Just breathe. And try to cool down.”

“Cyrene—” The panic from days before was rearing its head again. It caught in his throat, dry as charcoal. “Your hand.”

She shushed him. “Remembrance can reform anything good as new, right? It’s fine. We’re fine.”

Ha, were they?

“I’m sorry,” he murmured and tried his best to contain the heat inside of him.

“These things happen,” Cyrene said. “Before they left, I accidentally froze Stelle in ice when we were bathing together. You’re not the only one.”

Freezing people was one thing. Melting them was another. He knew that his was the worst of the two crimes.

Still, Cyrene was doing her best to give him a distraction. Phainon grasped it like a drowned man to land.

“How did she take to being an ice cube?” He croaked.

“Unsurprisingly well,” Cyrene hummed. “Apparently it wasn’t her first time. I hadn’t even thawed her out when she told me that I should open a dessert store selling exclusively shaved ice.”

Yeah, that sounded like something Stelle would suggest.

He wondered where the Express was now. How long would they be in open space for before they reached the site of their delivery. They hadn’t specified a time frame for which they’d arrive at their destination, or a date of return. Could’ve been days. Could’ve been weeks.

Hopefully, they’d find no trouble on their journey. Even if they did, they’d probably be able to fight their way out of it. They’d probably find most foes easy to fight. So long as they didn’t come face to face with—

“Hey. Don’t start hiding in your head again,” Cyrene said. “We’re here to relax, right? So… Hm. Tell me about this. There must be a story behind it, right?”

She pressed her finger—reformed and no longer melted—to the top of his arm, where a ring of scar tissue stitched the flesh to his shoulder. They ran around the entirety of his arm, a deep canyon of golden scarring. Though it no longer leaked the way it had days ago when he’d first noticed the amputated limb was no longer unattached, it was still far from being fully healed.

Looking at it, the wound didn’t look all that bad. There were no accompanied bruises or scabs. His arm looked more like a porcelain doll’s arm that needed its cracks filled.

How he’d reached this point following amputation was difficult to say, but the arm had been rethreading itself ever since he’d been shoved inside of Irontomb. Objectively, regrowing an arm was better than not having one at all, so Phainon hadn’t questioned it too much. Sometimes, bodies were weird.

“I got it while fighting the black tide,” he said.

“After passing things on to Stelle and I?” Cyrene asked. When he nodded, she let out a long hum, contemplating. “Wow, it must’ve been a tough fight even with all those coreflames. You’re lucky you didn’t lose an arm.”

An ironic humour caught in his chest. His smile was a small, wry thing. “I did.”

The admission came with a still silence that froze him at the core. Cyrene’s eyes widened, mouth dropping open in surprise. When she spoke, her voice was a squeak. “You did?!”

Phainon shrugged. It was hardly worth being surprised about - it wasn’t even the first time he’d found himself down an arm. Dismemberment got kind of old after a while. The most surprising thing about all of this, really, was that he’d not had to die to get it back. In the absence of another cycle’s Phainon, he’d simply… reattached it himself.

“You’re kidding me,” Cyrene breathed. She poked at the scar, alarmed. “You really lost your arm? It actually came off. Like… properly dismembered?”

“Why would I lie about that?”

Cyrene stared at him. Then, she punched his arm - the one that had not been dismembered previously - and let out an incredulous laugh. She said, “Phai, why didn’t you tell me? This is the kind of thing you tell people!”

Phainon really didn’t know what the issue was. He blinked at her, confused and too tired to begin unpacking what the true problem was. She hadn’t asked before now and Phainon’s arm was reattached - did it really matter all that much?

Clearly the answer was yes.

And yet even seeing her worry, he couldn’t bring himself to care that he’d lost it.

“Am I supposed to tell you about every limb I’ve ever lost?” Phainon asked.

The fact that Cyrene had to take the time to think about this showed just how absurd their lives had become.

Eventually, she said, “Only the ones that have stuck. Or, er—only from your final cycle onwards.”

Better that he only need to tell her about three than an entire slew of them, he supposed.

“Okay,” Phainon said. And when she opened her mouth to continue, he cut her off and said, “So I should probably mention that my wings were cut off too?”

Cyrene opened her mouth, said nothing, and then closed her mouth again. The look she sent him was purely bewildered. “You had wings?”

He nodded. “Still do, I think.”

If he really focused on the sensation of wings, he could feel a burning itch, thousands of pinpricks against bone. It was possible they were growing back. Wouldn’t surprise him, really. There were too many coreflames to be fully contained in his body, so he’d needed the extra space. His wings were as much an extension of himself as they were the coreflames.

Maybe that was why he was so tired. Regrowing two limbs seemed like the kind of thing that could explain away the exhaustion plaguing him.

“Okay.” Cyrene said, slowly. “Um. What does Hyacine think about all of this?”

He stared at her blankly. Tilted his head as if to ask ‘why would Hyacine have an opinion on this?’

“You didn’t tell her about any of this during your check-up?”

“...What check-up?”

From the glower sent his way, this was clearly the wrong thing to ask. Cyrene looked appalled at his question.

“After the fight with Irontomb, Aglaea sent us all to have check-ups,” she explained. “You didn’t go?”

It was probably for the best that he just shook his head instead of coming up with any kind of excuse. Admitting that he’d hardly been listening seemed like something that’d only get him told off more. She might not be openly angry at him yet, but Phainon really didn’t want to push his luck.

“You really are a disaster, aren’t you?” Cyrene sighed. “You’re the one who needed that check-up the most! Don’t you realise that?”

“I feel fine,” he said, because objectively, compared to the agony from the cycles, he was. Tired, sure, but his pain was hardly there anymore. Even the echo of pain had long since passed. The absence of it was actually kind of overwhelming. “Truly.”

“Yeah, well, I know not to believe you on things like this without proof,” she said. “After this bath, we’re going straight to the Twilight Courtyard.”

Luckily for them, when Cyrene said they were going to the Twilight Courtyard, she was not talking of the one that was situated in the Grove of Epiphany. She was speaking of the Okheman branch that was typically founded near the end of most cycles.

As the true clinic was in a state of disrepair, Hyacinthia and the many other healers of Okhema had converted a school on the outskirts of the city into a makeshift hospital. Classrooms had been converted into bays for long-term patients. The gymnasium turned into a rotating clinic seeing not only those injured during Okhema’s destruction but those with unrelated sicknesses as well.

Cyrene led him through the gymnasium doors and towards a receptionist sat behind a small desk. From the moment they’d left the bath and headed out into the street, she had not let go of his hand. Even when he’d told her he wouldn’t try to run.

“Aitee, wasn’t it?” Cyrene asked, with a soft smile.

“Ah,” the receptionist said. “Lady Cyrene, yes, you remembered!”

“We’re after Hyacine,” Cyrene continued. “Is she around?”

Apparently she was. They’d received a delivery of bandages salvaged from the ruins of another infirmary and the healer had taken it upon herself to check that they were all in good condition. They were given brief directions to the storeroom and before Phainon knew it, they were in motion once more, weaving around healers and patients alike.

They knew they were heading in the right direction when the gentle whinny of little Ica reached their ears. Small and relaxed ‘doots’ echoed down the hall, accompanied by the steady flap of miniscule wings.

(Even after 33 million cycles Phainon still didn’t know how the pegasus managed to keep itself afloat with such tiny wings. He supposed some things were just supposed to remain a mystery.)

They saw the pegasus first. A few steps afterwards, there was Hyacine.

Phainon… hadn’t actually seen her since the ill-timed debrief post-Irontomb. She’d gotten just as wrapped up in work as he had - with all the injured, he doubted she’d done much outside of seeing to the wounded and resting when her shift ended. She looked well. In her element.

When— responding to Ica’s trill— she turned to face them, her lips spread into a warm smile.

“Hyacine!” Cyrene called, dragging them forward at speed.

The healer had arms filled with bandages but that did nothing to dissuade Cyrene from enveloping her in a hug.

“Cyrie!” Hyacine responded. “And Phai, too! Hi, how are you?”

Her warmth and kindness were infectious.

“Oh, I’m fine,” Cyrene said. "We're here for this fool," —at this she gestured towards Phainon,— "he’s been a little silly. We were hoping you’d be able to give him a check-up and make sure he’s alright.”

Hyacine’s gaze immediately narrowed on him. Phainon couldn’t help but squirm beneath her gaze. She said, “Is something wrong? No one passed along your notes so I’d assumed everything was fine but has something changed?”

Phainon glanced from Cyrene, to Hyacine and then towards an open window a few metres past both women. He was probably agile enough to get out before either of them could react—

Cyrene’s hand closed over his wrist once more. Clearly, she was a mindreader.

“Well,” Cyrene said, with a smile that was certainly not as pleased as it could have been. “Like I said— it’s all a little bit silly. Phainon never had a check-up. I thought it was better late than never, right?”

Hyacine’s eyes narrowed. If her arms were not filled with bandages, it was likely that she would have planted both hands on her hips. Instead, in a voice teetering on calm, she said, “Phai didn’t come to have a check-up at all?”

Phainon’s smile was small and apologetic. She was definitely going to lecture him, wasn’t she?

“He hasn’t, no!” Cyrene said, because clearly she was angry about this as well.

“You’re right, Cyrie, that was pretty silly of him.” Hyacine pressed her lips together. “Come on, Phainon. We’ll do it now.”

…Yeah. Hyacine was definitely pissed.

Chapter End Notes

next time: hyacine is not pleased. a check-up is had.

chapters.html:
Chapter Notes

i need you all to know that this chapter was written purely as procrastination from doing laundry. now that i've finished i actually have to do it. rough times. sad times.

ANYWAY, i had fun with this one. thanks for all the comments and support - i'm glad you're all enjoying the au as much as i am.

Phainon was marched into the clinic as if he were on death row.

Between Hyacine, Ica and Cyrene, they’d come up with the perfect formation to keep him from fleeing. Hyacine, in the front, led the way, concern and exasperation rolling off her in such strong waves that people turned to see the cause of such a drastic mood change. Little Ica floated to Phainon’s left letting out warning whickers every time Phainon’s gaze so much as lingered on a window. Cyrene, in the rear, simply smiled every time he looked back as if daring him to try and bolt.

“Some things really never change do they?” Hyacine asked, once they had passed through the crowd and reached a free bay. She waved him towards one of the chairs and closed the curtain behind him.

The seat was, unfortunately, a little too small for his frame. His legs folded up in a small v-shape, leaving him a gangly mess of limb. This is what he got for being over six feet tall in a clinic repurposed from a school. He felt ridiculous.

“This time,” he said, still smiling apologetically, “it really was unintentional.”

He really had to fight to keep the smile on his face. If he didn’t, it was just going to go either blank or wholly nervous and neither would be received well. It’d either make everyone angrier at him or it’d make them worry. Neither were viable options.

“Unintentional?” Hyacine echoed, disbelieving.

“Yes,” Phainon said. “I didn’t realise the checkup was mandatory. And either way, I feel fine. I’d have come if I thought I needed to—”

Cyrene, who had perched on the bed by the far wall, said, “Apparently, re-attached dismembered limbs don’t count as ‘needing to see a healer’ these days. Who would’ve known?”

Phainon’s eye twitched. Irritation throbbed at his temples like a migraine. “Cyrene.”

“Oh, oops,” she said, blinking innocently at him. Her voice was too chipper, as if she knew how ‘helpful’ she was being. “My bad. But that is why we’re here. You know that. You can’t go around hiding actual dismemberments.”

Phainon hated her so, so much.

“I’m sorry,” Hyacine said, cutting in before their bickering truly began. “Dismemberment?”

He winced at how shrill her voice sounded.

Cyrene nodded. “Plural.”

“You’re making it out to be worse than it is,” Phainon said. “My arm is working fine now. It’s like I never lost it.”

Hyacine’s expression was pure, wide-eyed horror.

“You lost an arm.” She said, slowly. “And didn’t come to see me? ”

“He lost a pair of wings too,” Cyrene added, helpfully.

She was lucky that she was outside of his reach because Phainon was about two seconds away from kicking her. The distance was too far for petty violence so he settled on glowering instead.

Cyrene stuck her tongue out at him. Phainon bit the inside of his cheek, shoved his agitation down into the depths of his stomach, and fixed an extremely strained, yet doubly apologetic, smile on his face.

See, totally fine!

“Cyrene’s making it sound worse than it is,” he repeated. “Look at me. I’m still in one piece aren’t I?”

It was for the best that he didn’t add ‘do I look like I need a healer?’ because if he had, it would no doubt push Hyacine further onto Cyrene’s side. Words like that weren’t reassurance, they were a challenge.

“I’ll determine how bad it is,” Hyacine said, finally, massaging her temples. “Alright. For now, I’m going to ignore talk of dismembered limbs and just conduct a general check-up. After that… We will be coming back to this.”

She began with the typical tests one would expect. The standard checks were taken: temperature (too hot), blood pressure (too low) and pulse rate (regular for a civilian but, sadly, too fast for a Chrysos Heir in his prime).

Hyacine took his weight and frowned. She pressed a stethoscope to his chest and made him inhale in long, deep breaths. Once she’d finished listening to his lungs, she moved on to his heart.

It was as if she was analysing every part of him.

She shone light into his eyes to see how they dilated, depressed his tongue with a long metal strip to see into the back of his throat and even pressed some sort of —of thing (he didn’t know what it was called)— into his ears to check that they were healthy too.

Definitely excessive for a typical check-up. At least a quint had passed and she hadn’t even seen his re-attached arm yet.

“Isn’t—” Phainon had to resist the urge to bat her little reflex hammer away when she began knocking it into his knee in an attempt to test his reflexes and spinal health. “Isn’t this more than you’d expect for a usual check-up?”

“This isn’t a usual check-up Phai,” Hyacine answered and knocked the hammer against his knee. Phainon’s knee spasmed. That probably meant his spine was fine, right?

“...Why…not…?”

Hyacine looked up at him with raised brows, as if she’d expected him to figure it out himself.

“You’ve been carrying coreflames into each new cycle, right? I’m checking to make sure that holding them isn’t causing any long-term damage.”

…She was a little too late on that one, unfortunately. A couple million years too late. Or well—actually, he supposed not. Only the thousand years or so that he’d been trapped inside of Irontomb.

Had it been that long? Or had the time dilation been different? Difficult to know for sure. He hadn’t exactly had any way of tracking time while he was in there.

“And even if you do turn out to be fine— which you’re not— this is the best time to gather a baseline of your health in case you become sick in the future.”

Damn her. She’d found the perfect argument that meant Phainon couldn’t even argue against the continued tests.

“Alright,” He sighed. “How many more of these are there?”

Hyacine’s half-smile was a small thing. Apparently, that meant there were a lot. All Phainon could do was go along with her and wait for it to be over.

By the time she finally got to his dismembered arm, his shoulders were sagged and he was half-melted against his chair. Hyacine took to the healing wound with a mixture of medical intrigue and personal dismay.

“Does it feel stiff?” She asked, prodding at where scar tissue melded into muscle. “The scarring might not give you full motion of your shoulder if it pulls on the muscle too much.”

Phainon shrugged. The crevice of scarring bulged slightly at the movement but wasn’t accompanied with discomfort. He said, “Feels like it did before.”

Hyacine’s fingers twitched.

“Actually,” he said, contemplative. “It feels better than it did previously.”

Instead of the burning skin and boiling blood in his veins from before, his arm actually felt like an arm again.

“…Right,” Hyacine said.

She glanced towards Cyrene and the pair shared a look that was entirely too weighted. Something flashed across their faces, small signals embedded into the twitching of lips and wriggling of their noses. Cyrene pressed her lips together. Hyacine sighed. It was a language he did not speak and yet Phainon knew they were somehow talking about him.

“Let’s keep going,” Hyacine said and turned back to him.

When she finally exhausted the list of possible examinations, Hyacine dropped onto a chair opposite Phainon, and let out what was probably the deepest sigh he’d heard from her in billions of years.

Cyrene, who had been her scribe this entire time jotting patient notes down on a scroll titled with his name, lowered her quill and said, “We’re finally done?”

“We’re done,” Hyacine confirmed.

It was probably stupid to ask, but Phainon did. “So… What’s the verdict?”

Hyacine simply sat in silence and watched him. Then, she lifted a hand and pinched the bridge of her nose.

…Well, that wasn’t very reassuring.

“I don’t even know where to start,” Hyacine began. “Only you would call this ‘fine’.”

Despite being at a loss for where to begin, she did a pretty good job at pointing out all of the irregularities in his tests. Phainon was granted a crash course in all the ways his body was acting out - though the medical talk went over his head, he got the main point pretty well: It was a testament to his own stubbornness that he’d been able to go about his day without collapsing.

Seemed a bit dramatic to blame it all on his stubbornness but Hyacine looked somewhat incensed so he wasn’t willing to point that out.

“I don’t understand how no one noticed before now,” she muttered. “You don’t even fit into your clothes properly. They’re so baggy and you’re way too pale. Someone should’ve sent you to me days ago.”

Phainon opened his mouth, remembered how often people had been asking him how he was feeling during his rounds of the city and then promptly closed his mouth. He’d thought that people were just being polite.

“Wait,” he said. “My clothes aren’t baggy. They’re just spacious.”

Hyacine crossed her arms. “They’re practically hanging off of you! I’m surprised Aglaea hasn’t made you new ones already, you’re drowning in fabric.”

That was probably because he was avoiding Aglaea as much as he was avoiding the rest of them. Being able to see where her threads were really helped to avoid them. The anonymity that came with staying outside of her sight was kind of nice.

“They are not at all,” Phainon muttered.

“You’re way too skinny,” Cyrene said. “I can’t even imagine how much energy you waste holding onto all those coreflames. Aren’t you tired?”

Phainon grimaced. That was neither here nor there.

He said, “Not really. Only a little. Because of the wings.”

As soon as he said it, he knew he’d added another nail into the coffin.

Hyacine’s voice was very low when she said, “Oh yes. I forgot about the wings.”

Phainon closed his eyes in surrender. No matter how many of Orynyx’s coreflames he’d gathered, he was sadly unable to reverse time and memory. He didn’t have any of Cyrene’s finesse with time. The only way to go was forward.

“Why would they make you tired, Phai?”

“They’re maybe, possibly, growing back in?” He murmured.

From the curve of Hyacine’s brows, she was probably wondering how exactly she could’ve gone on to miss any changes to the bone structure of his back and shoulders. There had clearly been no wings.

“I put them away,” Phainon said. When the two women continued to look at him, waiting for some explanation on what, exactly, that meant, the words were snatched from his throat. “They’re kind of… folded away inside of a synthetic black hole so I don’t always have to walk around with them out?”

Stunned, Hyacine said, “You store your wings inside of a collapsed star?”

He stored a lot of things within a collapsed star. Mostly the black tide monsters and titankin that had gotten in the way during his many cycles. They were all space dust now.

Phainon said, “Where else am I supposed to store them?”

Their disbelief was palpable. That was fair; It was a pretty odd use for a black hole. Most of the universe tended to avoid them - they didn’t tend to harness them as their own personal storage for unwanted limbs.

“...I… Alright.” Hyacine pinched the bridge of her nose again. This time, the pinch left little indents in her skin. “Sure.” A minor pause. “Show me.”

“The black hole…?”

“No, Phainon,” she said, exasperated, “show me what’s left of your wings.”

“I can’t really…” He paused, grimaced and just as quickly gave up. “Well, here’s not really the best place for them. They’re a little… warm.”

“A little warm,” Hyacine repeated, unimpressed.

“They might set the building on fire,” Phainon clarified.

Another long stare. Cyrene buried her face in her hands as if his words were causing her physical pain.

“Alright,” Hyacine said. “Outside, then.”

They went outside.

Hyacine led them down a path to what had once been the school’s sports field. It’d been ravaged by falling stone during the disaster and now the ground was lumpy and uneven.

“Does this work?” Hyacine asked.

Phainon shrugged. Depending on how far his wings had regrown, there was a possibility that the grass might get a little singed. Looking at the state of the field, it really didn’t seem like the risk of burnt grass was going to be high on the list of prioritised fixes.

“It should be,” he said, and removed his coat and shirt.

Shooing them both away, he waited until they were halfway across the field before focusing on his wings once more. It wasn’t difficult - the itch was easy enough to focus on. Flame rippled against the inside of his shoulder blades. The sensation was strong enough that Phainon was certain he’d be able to unfold them with little difficulty. It’d be an easy thing - tear open a hole in reality, retrieve his wings, stitch said hole shut again.

The threads of space and reality weren’t difficult to find when you had thirty-three million of Mnestia’s coreflames. Phainon didn’t even need to close his eyes to control his focus anymore. He just considered where he wanted the tear to stem from, grabbed hold of the seams and ripped.

Sound scraped and distorted. The world went from stable to overtly dense. Loose dirt and pebbles were drawn into the gaping maw of a hungry, deceased star, the space crumbling under the weight of its gravity.

Phainon glanced at the nothingness as if it were, well, nothing. He reclaimed the space where his wings would have been. And then, as easily as he’d torn through reality, he stitched the void away for later use.

Once it was fully closed, Phainon lifted an arm and waved to the pair standing at the edge of the field. He called, “All done!”

They returned to his side, gaping. Even Cyrene, who had some understanding of what he could do and as such shouldn’t have been so surprised, stared as if she’d seen something that shouldn’t have been possible.

Phainon rubbed the back of his neck, cheeks flushing gold as they continued to stare at him. He said, “Do you think Aglaea will be mad about the field?”

Cyrene’s lip twitched in a small smile. “We won’t tell, if you don’t. Right, Hyacine?”

They received a hum. Hyacine was more focused on the wings that were now sprouting from Phainon’s back. While she didn’t dare reach for them - the heat radiated from his back to such a degree that the air around them grew hazy - she was clearly getting as close as she could without being burned.

“They really are growing back,” she said, a mixture of awe and confusement in her tone.

“Again,” Phainon muttered, for the second time that day. “Why would I lie about that?”

His wings had grown far more than he’d thought they would have. Phainon had been expecting smaller nubs against his back, the beginning of bone and at most, a few feathers of blood and flame. Nothing bigger than his hand, at a push.

Before, the limbs had been almost double his arm length. Currently, if stretched out, they reached the curve of his elbow. The feathers, moulded from liquid flame, were covered in so much stardust and debris that he had to resist the physical urge to bathe them in an even more intense flame.

“I can’t get close enough to properly examine them,” Hyacine sighed. “Phai, is there any way you could make them cool enough for me to touch?”

He grimaced. “I’m not sure…?”

A sigh. “Right. Well. If you don’t know and I certainly don’t know, then there’s only one person who could possibly figure it out. I’m going to message the Professor.”

This day was already long enough trying to act normal among these two heirs. Now he had to contend with Professor Anaxa as well?

“Is that really necessary?” Phainon asked.

Hyacine did not answer. Instead, she took out her teleslate and began to type.

Chapter End Notes

next time: a scholar makes his entrance. maybe. phainon's already long week of avoidance becomes even longer.

chapters.html:
Chapter Notes

i'm running late to head to a family dinner to upload this, so apologies if i've missed an immediate typos. i didn't manage to write as much in this one as i'd planned, but that's bc this scene ended up a lot bigger than expected.

To Phainon’s immense relief, Hyacine’s message to Professor Anaxa was not an immediate summons but a query.

“I’m just asking him if he has any recommendations,” Hyacine said, upon looking up. Maybe she’d seen how his exhaustion had ballooned at the idea of interacting with three of them in one sitting or maybe he just looked confused. “It’s a little late for him to visit now.”

Phainon wasn’t sure. He wouldn’t put it past Anaxa. If the man deemed the concept interesting enough then time would cease to exist. It all relied on whether the concept of Phainon growing wings caught his interest or not.

He’d say the odds were an even 50:50. It depended, really, on whether Anaxa would link the wings back to his study of Nousporism.

…What was he thinking? 50:50? It definitely fell within the confines of Nousporism. The transformation of coreflames into biological matter, using divine fuel to create equally divine wings? The Nousporists were going to have a field day with this. It was an application of transmogrification that hadn’t been seen before in Amphoreus.

Something acidic and unpleasant curled under his ribs and squeezed at his stomach. His insides churned. Bile rose in his throat.

…That was probably a sign to stop thinking about the possibility of becoming the Nousporist’s latest case study.

Which was fine by him! He was a pro at burying things away and forcing himself not to think about them.

All Phainon needed to do was remind himself that it was only Anaxa looking at his wings, not the entire grove. He wasn’t going to be paraded around as their latest research subject.

“Phainon?” Cyrene asked, her voice cutting through the static of his totally fine thoughts. “Is everything okay?”

“Never better,” he said.

“…Are you sure? You’ve gone even paler than you already were.”

Phainon smiled and waved the comment away with a well timed shrug. His wings dragged up with the rise of his shoulders, burning with the pull of aching muscle and flame. He said, “Just a trick of the light. Has Anaxa responded yet?”

Typically, when messaging the professor, Anaxa either responded within 5 minutes or after three days. There tended not to be an inbetween.

“Not ye—Oh, wait, now he has, yes.” Hyacine’s gaze flicked back down to her teleslate as the buzz caught her attention. “Apparently the method of cooling differs depending on how high the temperature of your wings is. Do you have any idea of how hot they get exactly?”

Phainon was pretty sure that Amphoreus did not make thermometers that could withstand the force of his flames at their highest temperature. Most tended to melt. They’d probably melt at the lowest burn too, but hopefully not before offering some kind of number.

“Pretty hot,” Phainon said. “I’ve never really tested it before.”

“Hm,” Hyacine nodded and continued to type. Clearly, Anaxa’s attention wasn’t elsewhere because the responding message came almost instantly. “Anaxa would like to know if you’d mind showing him your wings tomorrow morning.”

Phainon blinked. “Tomorrow morning?”

“At the second quint of the Lucid hour.”

“Uh.” He’d kind of expected Anaxa to send a time and location without any care for whether it actually suited him, so having a choice was somewhat disorientating. He said, “I… That sounds fine?”

Hyacine’s lips pulled into a gentle smile. She said, “Great. I’ll let him know.”

…If Anaxa wasn’t going to be seeing them until the following day, then that probably meant he was fine to put away his wings, right?

Phainon folded his wings back into unreality, pulled on his shirt and coat and fixed his gaze onto the two women before him.

“Is this check-up all finished for now, then?” He asked.

Hyacine’s lips pressed together into a thin line as if remembering his seemingly poor results. “We’ve gone over some of your results already but I think it’s probably for the best to go over a more thorough treatment plan when we get back to the clinic.”

Ah. Hm.

What if they didn’t do that, though?

“...Can I have a brief overview instead?” Phainon asked.

He wanted to be a good friend but the idea of coming up with a plan for his continued good health drained what little energy remained in his bones. As much as he wanted to indulge her worries, it all seemed like a waste of time.

Hyacine said, “I think it’s probably for the best to admit you into the clinic so we can keep you under observation.” (No.) “Put you on bedrest for the time being until your symptoms ease.” (Double no.) “And then slowly work into easing you into light, non-strenuous tasks.” (Also no.)

“That seems like a lot,” Phainon said. “It seems like too much, actually.”

Crossing her arms, Hyacine’s brows threaded into a frown. She said, “I’m sorry, which one of us is the doctor here?”

“I could be a doctor,” Phainon said, before his brain caught up with his mouth. “There could’ve been a cycle where I became one. You don’t know.”

Hyacine stared at him.

Beside her, Cyrene asked, “Did you ever become one?”

…33,550,336 cycles and not once did he ever entertain the notion of becoming a healer. By Kephale, that was actually kind of sad. Then again… Deliverance didn’t really go hand in hand with a stethoscope now, did it? Typically required a lot more stabbing. Doctors tended to look down on that kind of thing.

“...I did not,” Phainon said.

“Then,” Hyacine said, heaving out a long sigh, “considering how I am the only doctor here, you’ll just have to believe me when I tell you that this isn’t too much at all. It’s quite proportionate to your current needs.”

Phainon grimaced.

“How about,” he tried, “I go home now and get an early night’s rest?”

“This—” Hyacine’s cheeks went gold with the force of a frustrated flush. “Your health is important, Phainon. You can’t talk down the treatment and expect your wellbeing to do anything but plummet.”

He could definitely see her point. Which meant he’d have to give at least a little bit. He could do that.

“Alright,” Phainon nodded. “A very early night’s rest then. ”

It was probably a testament to Hyacine’s patience that she didn’t immediately try to strangle him. Her mouth opened and closed multiple times, reminiscent of a goldfish, before she finally settled on breathing out a long-suffering sigh that made her sound more tired than he felt.

“You aren't going to stay no matter what I say, are you?”

Phainon’s lips pulled into another apologetic smile as he shook his head. It was really nice of her to offer to treat him as if he were just another one of her patients but her efforts weren’t necessary. There was no reason to stay - he neither needed the bed, nor would he have deserved it if he did.

“I appreciate the sentiment,” he said, because he did. Truly. It was sweet of her, actually, if you ignored the fact that the sentiment was also a little silly when aimed at him, a man who was objectively in much better condition now than he had been in the millions of years prior to this moment. “But there are people who need to be here more than I do. I wouldn’t want to take a bed someone else might need.”

…That was clearly the wrong thing to say. Hyacine’s eyes were beginning to glisten with frustrated tears. From the way her bottom lip was trembling, her frustration was clearly a few minutes away from spilling over into a lecture on self care. Though she bit her tongue, it was clear she wanted to argue with him.

Honestly, Phainon hadn’t seen her this angry at him since… huh, he wasn’t sure he could remember a time when Hyacine had actually been frustrated at him. Back in the cycles, whenever she was faced with his then failing health, she’d only ever been sad. Devastated, even.

He preferred her frustration over her grief. Though he felt guilty to be the cause of both, anger sat better in his stomach. He could understand her frustration better than he could understand her worry and concern. Phainon wasn’t willing to play along? Yeah, of course it made sense that she’d be irritated by that. That, out of everything, made sense.

Cyrene placed a hand on Hyacine’s shoulder, leaning in to whisper something in her ear. It was quiet enough that he couldn’t hear the words.

Hyacine looked to her and Cyrene offered a small smile.

“...Alright, fine,” Hyacine relented, heaving out a sigh. The words were unwilling but she managed to drag them from her throat regardless. “You’ll go straight home and rest?”

That was definitely a thing he’d said he would do but probably wouldn’t. He nodded.

“And you’ll come back for another check-up tomorrow? After you’ve visited the Professor?” She added.

Phainon was pretty sure that if he didn’t come back tomorrow, she’d track him down and forcefully drag him back to the clinic so it was probably for the best that he agreed. He said, “I can come back tomorrow.”

Hyacine stared at him, quietly, for what must’ve been at least a full two minutes. Then, finally, she jerked her head in an unwilling nod, “Fine. I guess that works too. As long as you go straight to bed.”

“I will, I will,” he lied.

Squinting at him as if to see how genuine he was being, it was clear that Hyacine was not fully convinced. Her skepticism would’ve been hurtful, had he actually been telling the truth. Since he wasn’t, it felt more than a little warranted. Phainon raised his hands in surrender as if the motion would do anything to placate her. It didn't, but Hyacine didn't outright call him a liar either so it hadn't not worked.

He would try to go to sleep early - he could probably ensure that didn’t end up being a lie. He just had some things he wanted to get finished first before he did.

For one, he still had a patrol to finish. And Phainon had promised to return to Kephale Plaza and remove any debris that had been too large to be removed by Okheman hands alone. After that he would gladly return home, change into his night clothes and rest.

Probably.

If nothing else requiring his immediate attention turned up then definitely.

“Okay,” Hyacine said. “I’ll see you tomorrow, Phai.”

Phainon shot her his best attempt at a wide grin. It came out plastic and quite forced, but hopefully the sentiment was still there.

“See you tomorrow, Hyacine.” Phainon said. And then, before Cyrene could open her mouth to even contemplate joining him as he made his escape, he added, “You too, Cyrene. See you later.”

Was it a blatant dismissal of her company? Maybe.

Did he particularly care at this point? It was debatable.

A little bit of guilt festered in his chest like an ache, but compared to the ever present guilt he harboured for having killed his friend over and over, it was like a drop in the ocean. Hardly noticeable - he was going to feel bad anyway, so why not feel a little more comfortable while he did?

That sounded antithetical in theory but theorists had clearly never felt this drained of their social battery.

“Sure,” Cyrene said, and lifted her hand up in an almost hesitant wave. Her smile seemed the same though so maybe he was just overthinking it and he wasn’t outright dismissing her at all. “I’ll see you later, Phai.”

He fled. His steps may have been slow, slightly stumbled movements but there was no doubt in his mind that he was fleeing.

Titans, he was tired. When did talking to his friends become so exhausting?

(Probably around the time his mind had stopped hesitating each time he killed them, but hey, who was to say for certain?)

The sun was setting by the time he stopped in a small alleyway, all threads in the city accounted for. He’d fixed any fraying threads he’d found - rebinding them with stronger knots and lattice-like webbing.

That was one task completed. One more to go.

He checked the time on his teleslate - they still had half of the Parting hour to go and, as such, it was still possible that he could get the ‘early’ rest he’d promised Hyacine - and spotted a new message on his teleslate.

Ah. The express must’ve reached a pocket of the galaxy that was connected to the intergalactic web. The trailblazer had messaged him a single emoji: a chimera with its head tilted, a question mark rising from its head. Phainon returned Stelle's emoji with one of his own. Also a chimera, though his was half melted into the ground, its soul trying to escape its body.

His teleslate buzzed with a single sentence: 'Disappointed, but not surprised.'

…Rude, but not terribly unwarranted.

He sent a quick report of how he’d been forced to go to the clinic, received zero sympathy (he didn’t know what he was expecting, honestly), and several confusing memes. Then, as quickly as he’d found the trailblazer online and able to respond, Stelle was out of service and his messages could no longer reach her.

“I guess that’s as much a sign as anything else to get back to it,” Phainon murmured, and began the long trek back towards Kephale plaza.

Chapter End Notes

next time: kephale plaza. and then anaxa. (for real this time).
