angst and humor.

definitely rears its head in the first half of this one. so, uh, yeah. please be careful if you're not in the headspace for angst.

Okhema’s ruins were bearable during the day, but when night struck they quickly became haunting.

Daylight was linked with safety. Evernight with danger. To walk through a ravaged Okhema during the day meant to walk through a city that was preparing to rebuild, a city that held hope that it would one day fix itself. To walk through the same ruins at night was to succumb to the danger of entropy and the Black Tide.

Adjusting to a new rhythm of day and night would take time. Hopefully, the people of Okhema would one day begin to associate the dark with restfulness and not the harrowing need to grab the nearest available weapon to protect oneself. The change would come, but it would take longer than the four days they’d lived within the Era Nova.

Until then, the citizens would settle into their new routine - lighting as many candles and torches as possible, locking themselves and their flames inside their living quarters and hiding from a sky dotted with stars.

Phainon couldn’t blame them for it. An Okhema enshrouded in shadows was a harrowing place - shadows slunk just outside of one's peripheral vision, sounds amplified until even the slightest crunching footstep sounded like the prelude to battle, and meagre moonlight illuminated the worst of the damage in such a way that it seemed as if the world was still actively ending.

…This was the Okhema that lingered in his mind each time he thought of deliverance. It was a tide-torn emptiness that he alone had walked for millenia.

Though wild flames were not actively dancing between the buildings, the glow of candles was enough to spark the memory. It swallowed him whole and Phainon could do nothing but fall into it.

Heat licked across his cheeks as he made his way to Kephale plaza and he knew it was imagined but that did not ease the memory of the burn.

It did not help that speckled rays of light from the moon and stars created ghosts. Refracted light off of closed window panes created corpses in the streets - most of them faces he’d forced himself not to remember, some of them too memorable to forget.

He turned a corner and instead of seeing rubble pushed into piles in front of abandoned infrastructure, Cyrene’s broken bodies lined the street. He climbed down stairs and a cluster of three broken pillars removed from the path were the corpses of the three remaining Tribios priestesses, doll-like strings frayed, fabric peeling. His foot caught on a loose rock and when he looked down it was not rock but the bloodied hand of Hyacine, wanting - even in death - to reach out to him.

He grit his teeth, ground his jaw until it ached and kept walking through Okhema’s warped streets. The city was disfigured, trying desperately to embellish itself in fanciful decoration - unfortunately, it was trying to use his memories to do it. That meant he was faced with a merciless mural of murdered companions and fragmented cycles.

None of this was real.

Phainon knew it wasn’t. It was not the first time that the world had glitched around him and it would not be the last.

And yet his chest ached at the sight, regardless of the knowledge that what he saw was false. His eyes burned and his blood boiled. He leaned into the flicker of anger - it was better than grieving - and lifted his head high.

He’d fought against a crazed intellitron, a Lord Ravager and even an Aeon. He had not bowed his head to any of them - not once. Phainon was not about to bow his head to false ghosts and aching memories.

The false images followed him all the way to the gate of Kephale plaza. Then, they lingered, unwilling to follow.

Phainon did not look back. He never did. He simply stepped over the threshold into the ruined square and made his way towards whatever piles of debris had been left for him to remove.

There wasn’t much.

In his absence, the construction workers had done a commendable job of clearing things.

Where there had been many fallen stones and pillars, now there were only a few left behind. Phainon did a quick count - four. Whether they’d been left for him to remove or left for the following day’s work was difficult to say. He removed them regardless.

It would be an understatement to call them heavy. Even a Chrysos Heir would have struggled to pull them along. That was fine - reinforcing muscles with thread would keep them from tearing under the strain, and hardening bones with Georios’ coreflames would leave them unbreakable.

The weight didn’t feel lighter but moving things became easier.

In no time at all, the rubble was gone and Phainon found himself in empty silence with nothing to do.

Probably for the best to head home then, like he’d promised.

He cast his gaze around the plaza one final time to ensure he hadn’t missed anything major. It fell on another pile of debris that seemed more organised than one would have expected. A small thing, light caught on flecks of gold.

Ah.

That.

Phainon was moving before he could properly think about what he was doing. The shimmer of gold etched into stone left his blood sizzling against blood vessels.

They’d collected whatever remains of Kephale they could find. Not for his sake, he knew that, but it felt almost like some sort of gift regardless. Now he wouldn’t need to go looking.

Squatting on the ground, Phainon reached for the first fragment of mural. Nothing but stone painted gold. Without any detailing, it had probably been part of the depicted dawn device.

‘Do you not see the truth behind this place, Lord Khaslana?’

The words were so clear in his mind that Phainon stiffened and searched for their owner. The plaza remained empty - no life, artificial or otherwise, existed except for him.

He grit his teeth and snarled, “Even destroyed, you won’t shut up.”

Curling his fingers around the stone in his hand, Phainon heaved out a staggered breath. Unlike before, where it had disintegrated into a fine dust, the rock melted. Molten, liquid rock dripped from his fingers, sizzling against the stone courtyard.

The ground beneath him was becoming pockmarked with gold and Phainon couldn’t bring himself to care. All he could bring himself to do was reach for another piece of mural and continue to burn.

‘Kephale is to Amphoreus what the Destruction will be to the galaxy. The peace that the people thank the Skyfather for is nothing but a… fickle falsification. It is nothing but a prelude to—”

“Enough.” Phainon snapped.

Before he could think, he was moving. A piece of half melted rock left his hand with the force of a million coreflames, aimed in the direction of a nonexistent voice. It smashed into a wall at the edge of the plaza and then kept going.

Phainon scrambled to his feet, eyes wide, his pulse thudding rapidly against his ribs.

The wall crumpled on itself. Brick collapsed to the floor and shattered as if it were glass.

Behind it, Phainon watched a building stagger, groaning under its own weight. There was no time to support it with Mnestia’s threads. Within seconds, it had succumbed. A plume of dust ballooned in the air like smoke.

…He really hadn’t meant to do that.

His hands were trembling. Strange - all of his body was. It was difficult to know if it was caused by shock, rage or regret. Could’ve been a combination of all three.

“...Oh…” Phainon murmured, the words deafening in the aftermath of his destruction. “...Oh that is… not good.”

At least a second building hadn’t collapsed. Or any more walls. Was that a silver lining? Probably not.

This was all probably just a sign that he needed to get the fuck out of here before anyone came looking.

Bolting wasn’t necessarily the best idea but it was the only option that Phainon could think of. His muscles tensed, his head swam and there was nothing else he could do.

He darted past the exit with such speed he hardly clocked the curl of a tail hidden behind the edge of the gate. Cipher? …No, it was probably just another hallucination.

Phainon kept moving. His steps were rushed, frantic things. His chest was heaving not just from exertion but his rage. It was difficult to put out the flames and let them die - it was difficult to want to. Still, he had to do something about the thrum of destruction currently sitting in his veins.

When he eventually stopped, it was in a small dilapidated courtyard just off of an abandoned alley. Alone, he pressed his palms against closed eyes and tried to drink in air with long, deep breaths. It didn’t really help, but he hadn’t expected it to do much.

He sighed, dropped his hands and opened his eyes.

“Sleep now,” he murmured. “Figure this out tomorrow.”

The world warped around him, blurred and twisted.

Oh. Okay, no, it wasn’t the world, he was just lightheaded. That was fine - he just needed to wade through it. A few seconds and his body would sort itself out. Then he’d head back to his room.

Phainon waited and it did not sort itself out.

Instead, his body wobbled. Spots of black entered his vision and there was little time to catch himself before his legs gave way beneath him.

“Wait—no, no—” He stuttered, realisation spreading through now numb limbs.

His body had already waited long enough; It would not wait any longer. Instead, it dragged him to the ground and, as his chin bounced off of stone, it dragged him into sleep.

Consciousness returned with warmth caressing his cheek and daylight prickling at closed eyelids.

Phainon would’ve been lying if he said he felt particularly rested or that his exhaustion had settled purely because he’d been unconscious long enough for the sun to have risen. He’d clearly rested enough that his body was satisfied enough to return control of its functioning back to him though, which was always nice.

The warmth of the sun had not woken him, though. Nor had his body’s relent of control.

He had been woken by the gentle drift of conversation. The voices were those he knew well - though the combination of them was a puzzling thing.

“—breathing appears steady, and past the bruising there’s no external signs of injury. Like I said, there’s little risk in moving him.”

“You can’t check for internal signs?”

“Observation shows he’ll be fine until he wakes. That will suffice. Any other tests have already likely been undertaken by Hyacine already - I see little point in redoing them. Now, are you going to move him or do I need to send for someone else?”

“You don’t need to call for anyone else.”

There was a shuffle from nearby.

The idea of being carried elsewhere was so mortifying that Phainon forced his eyes open before he was truly ready to be awake. He flinched back - not from the pair nearby him, but because his head was angled in such a way that the first thing he saw was the literal sun.

“Ugh,” he moaned, lifting an arm that felt like cement and throwing it over his eyes. “Sun’s bright.”

“Ah,” Professor Anaxa said. “So you’re finally awake.”

Finally? That implied he’d slept for a long time. The ache in his bones made it evident that he had not.

Phainon turned his head and opened his eyes a second time. This time, no longer staring straight into the sun, he was able to see outlines. Though his eyes stung from staring into a blaze, he could still clearly make out a pair of bodies. Professor Anaxa was staring down at him with crossed arms.

Beside him stood Mydei, who looked a mixture between exasperated and concerned. He was a step closer to Phainon than the professor was - though that wasn’t too surprising. From the little he’d heard, Mydei had clearly been brought along as a means of transport. It made sense, Mydei had the most experience in lugging his unconscious body around.

“Mostly awake,” Phainon murmured, and lifted a hand to rub the sleep from his eyes. He paused halfway when he caught sight of just how messy his hands were. A layer of dust and rock had dried against the skin. Flecks of gold had mixed with burnt, speckled grey.

He dropped his hand - his eyes had gone through enough when staring at the sun, he wasn’t going to make them withstand a dried dusting of granite. Instead, he sat up. Swallowed down the groan that came with the first aching movement of the day.

Mydei opened his mouth to say something and Phainon, knowing he wouldn’t necessarily like whatever he said, cut him off before the words could begin.

He said, “Funny coincidence that I’d see you here. What brings you both to this neck of the woods?”

Mydei closed his mouth. The suddenness of his frown left Phainon wishing he hadn’t woken up.

“You were late to our meeting,” Anaxa said. His gaze was an unmoving thing, a relentless force designed to keep Phainon fixed in place. The design worked - Phainon did not move an inch. “Naturally, I thought it best to come find you myself.”

Their… meeting. Hadn’t that been during the Lucid hour? Surely he hadn’t slept for longer than the ten quints it would’ve taken to see them into the Lucid hour.

No, that was absurd.

Yet, with the sun as high in the sky as it was, doubt began to trickle in.

“Imagine my surprise,” Anaxa continued, when it became clear that Phainon had no response ready for him, “when I found you unconscious in this courtyard. It is not the place one would assume Okhema’s deliverer would take a nap.”

He said it in a tone that seemed to imply he had not been surprised in the slightest. As if he’d been expecting something like this to happen.

Napping… yeah, that was definitely what he was doing.

“I was branching out on location,” Phainon said.

Mydei’s frown deepened. He said, “You passed out.”

“Nope,” Phainon said, because denial was his best friend and it would always be there for him. “You can’t prove that.”

“You’ve got bruises that prove that.”

Hm. That wasn’t proof enough. It was intangible at best; The prince was clearly reaching.

“Could’ve gotten these bruises anywhere,” Phainon said. Again, before Mydei could respond, he glanced back to Anaxa and said, “I didn’t realise I was late. That explains why you came,” —hardly, when did Anaxa come looking for those who stood him up? It was utterly absurd— “but it doesn’t really explain why Mydei is here…?”

For a moment, the pair simply stared at him.

Then Anaxa said, “Well, I’m hardly capable of carrying you home. I brought Mydeimos here so he could.”

Oh yeah. Scholar.

Anaxa wasn’t exactly well known for his physical strength. Phainon had watched the man struggle to carry a particularly large pile of books - he wasn’t exactly someone capable of carrying the dead weight of an unconscious warrior over his shoulder.

“I don’t need to be carried anywhere,” Phainon said.

“Not now that you’re awake, no.” Anaxa agreed.

“Debatable,” Mydei said, gruffly. “Can you stand without collapsing?”

That sounded almost like a challenge. It probably wasn’t one, but Phainon was going to take it as if it were.

“Of course I can stand,” he said.

He went to push up, felt his legs tremble and steeled himself.

Mydei, who had been watching him closely, sighed and held out his hand. Phainon stared, not quite registering the meaning. He only took it when Mydei let out an exasperated huff.

Once he was on his feet, his trembling ceased. The change in position had shocked his system enough to allow his body the space to remember how to support itself.

“It’s later than I’d have liked,” Anaxa said, “and I have some errands I require completing, but we can still continue with our meeting. Are you still available?”

Phainon had just woken in the remains of a ruined courtyard. It was pretty clear that he had no other plans for the day.

He brushed dust from his clothes and sighed. “Yeah, I’m still available.”

“Perfect,” Anaxa said. “Mydeimos, you may join us as well.”

The look in Mydei’s eye seemed to suggest he would have joined them whether Anaxa had given his permission or not.

“Come along, then,” Anaxa said, and led the pair out of the courtyard and back into the streets of Okhema.

Chapter End Notes

chapters.title: Chapter 7
chapters.html:
Chapter Notes

it's been a while, huh? as apology, have a longer chapter! (it was going to be shorter but the scene started to get away from me and I really wanted to stop where I did.)

hope you all enjoy!!

Okhema’s weather seemed uncertain whether it wanted to entertain sunshine or rain, and thus, had settled for a humidity that clung to the skin like a film.

It was a horrid thing. Though Phainon hadn't noticed it upon waking in the courtyard - his mind hadn’t been able to focus on anything other than the fact that Mydei and Anaxa had found his sleeping body among rubble - he was certainly feeling it now.

For the rest of Okhema, they must’ve been hating how warm it left them. For Phainon, the wet vapours tickled his skin and offered him chills. The water helped cool his boiling body, yes, but the more his temperature dropped, the more he wanted to burn.

Also, his clothes were growing more and more damp. Which was an inconvenience. The fabric was beginning to stick to the skin like glue, bunching up uncomfortably. Tugging at the hem of his shirt did little to help; Cyrene had been right when she'd claimed that there was too much loose fabric. Every time he unbunched the front of his shirt, the back half would bunch in a way that left his skin crawling and vice versa.

If he really wanted to, he could've used his coreflames to dry his slowly saturating clothes. But that ran the risk of singing the fabric. Or, if his control wavered too much, outright setting them on fire and burning them so thoroughly that the ashes would be too fine for the human eye to pick out. Walking through Okhema without clothes was already a horrendous idea - walking through Okhema without clothes because he’d set himself on fire was even worse.

Yeah, that wasn’t going to happen.

Instead he tugged on his shirt one final time and decided that he’d just have to grin and bear it. Mydei’s stare had been prickling at his back each time he moved - no doubt watching as he tried to smooth out all of the unflattering folds and bunching of fabric - and he didn’t want to give him any further signs that this walk was uncomfortable.

Luckily, Mydei hadn’t commented yet. He hadn’t said anything since they’d begun walking, but that didn’t mean that he wasn’t going to speak eventually.

Maybe he was waiting for Phainon to fill their empty silence. During the cycles that had been their dynamic. Well, not the dynamic of Khaslana and Mydei - that had mostly included fighting until his sword pierced Mydei’s tenth thoracic vertebrae, at which point he’d leave Mydei’s body in a puddle of his own blood and walk away with the stolen coreflame of Strife—

Something caught in his throat. Bile probably. Phainon closed his eyes, tripped over his own feet and managed to catch himself before either Mydei or Anaxa had a chance to right him.

— but, yeah. Phainon and Mydei’s dynamic had always included Phainon filling the silence. He should’ve been doing that. Right now would’ve been nice. And was probably expected. But he couldn’t think of what he could say. All he could think of was that with the current humidity, the water trickling down his neck was beginning to remind him of blood.

“You okay?” Mydei murmured, moving quicker to reach Phainon's side.

Phainon flashed him a porcelain smile - it was easily breakable yet beautifully artificial. “Just peachy. Loose tile, that’s all.”

It hadn’t been and they both knew it.

But Phainon really wasn’t about to start talking about how the weather was reminding him of the times he’d murdered his best friend and left his body behind without looking back. At least he’d buried Cyrene each time he killed her. He’d only ever buried Mydei’s body once.

Their walk quickly descended into an awkward game of ‘who will break the silence next?’

Anaxa and Mydei might have been seasoned pros at keeping to their silence, but they did not have Phainon’s current dedication to the cause.

Eventually, it was Anaxa who spoke next. They’d just turned onto one of the larger roads that had been built as a private walkway for droma deliveries, heading towards the outskirts of town in the direction of the Path of Parting. The professor said, “So, tell me about your wings. What were the circumstances that led to their development?”

Before Phainon had the opportunity to respond, Mydei’s voice cut through the silence. Confusion filtered into his words. “Wait. What wings?”

“My wings,” Phainon said. Which was probably just stating the obvious and didn’t actually offer any clarification at all. Or any answer to Anaxa’s question.

Was Mydei frowning again? Ah - yep. That was definitely a frown. Still mostly a confused one - Phainon was pretty sure the Kremnoan had a frown that displayed every one of his emotions. Well, except for happiness, of course. That was the rare emotion that allowed the softening of his eyes and the slight tug upward of his lips.

That was a nice thing to imagine - Mydei’s smile. It’d been a thousand years since he’d seen it but the memory sat warm behind his ribs.

“You have wings now?” Mydei asked.

Phainon hummed, affirming.

“Yes, Mydeimos,” Anaxa said, waving the question aside as if he’d expected more from the prince than confusion. “He does. Do keep up.”

Despite himself, the faintest smile tugged at Phainon’s lips. It was a rare thing - this duo interacting with one another often enough within a cycle to develop enough familiarity for Anaxa to speak to Mydei in such a way that could be viewed as minorly teasing - but whenever he got to see it, he was always reminded of how dear his friends were to him.

He knew, of course, that he loved all of the Chrysos Heirs to - literal - death, but there were some combinations that always reminded him of it more than others.

“Since when?” Mydei asked.

From the way he was eyeing his coat, it was clear he was looking for any sign of the additional limbs. Phainon rolled his eyes. Anaxa had also cast his gaze over his shoulder, steps slowing as he fixed a questioning gaze onto Phainon.

…What was a good amount of years to have had wings for, again? It wasn’t like he could just outright say that he’d had his wings for the past 315 million years. That would leave his lies redundant and sure, Phainon wasn’t the best liar in Amphoreus - that was definitely Cipher - but he should’ve been able to keep things together for at least a week, surely.

“I couldn’t tell you exactly how many,” he said, rushing the math in his head to figure out what would be the best number to give. How many cycles ago made the most sense? How many coreflames was, in his lie of 33 cycles, too many coreflames for a body to hold? “Maybe… some time between the twentieth or twenty-first cycle?”

Yeah, those numbers worked. He’d have had at least ten thousand years for the wings to have grown in and 240 coreflames were probably enough flames, in this retelling, to need extra space in his body to store them.

“If you have wings,” Mydei said, “where are they?”

Currently, the old pair had been abandoned in the depths of the Archforge, buried beneath the many piles of abandoned bodies that would go on to be repurposed into anti-matter legion puppets. But Phainon knew they weren’t asking about the previous pair.

“Stored away,” he said. “Staring at my coat isn’t going to make them magically appear.”

The prince scowled.

“Yes,” Anaxa said, oblivious to the weight of Mydei’s scowl. Or, perhaps, fully aware of it and simply unwilling to highlight its existence. “Hyacinthia did inform me of your storage methods. Inside of a black hole, was it?”

“Inside of a what.”

“Yes,” Phainon said.

“How fascinating,” Anaxa hummed. “To use gravitational collapse and spatial distortion in such a manner. And to manage to do so in such a way that avoids degradation of what is stored inside. Surely this requires a subsectory layer of reality within the sphere of unreality of the black hole.” He nodded his head. “It’s truly remarkable.”

If the professor thought it was remarkable, then it probably was.

Phainon didn’t necessarily agree, but then, he was hardly a scientist. There wasn’t much he knew about gravity or black holes or reality in the first place. He knew how to alter it in the same way that he knew how to breathe - instinctually. It didn’t feel special anymore. It just felt like another tool utilised to reach the Era Nova.

“Though,” Anaxa said, finally, “from what I have been told, the action of opening and closing the space hasn’t been fine tuned and so the accompanying destruction might not be cost–effective.”

“Yes, well,” Phainon said, absently, “If you ever need help with landscaping, then it definitely becomes cost-effective.”

Or if ever Amphoreus needed to fight more monsters. A little bit of ruined land was always favourable to letting it become overcome with the Black Tide.

Anaxa set unimpressed eyes onto him and shook his head. “As lucrative as demolition companies might find your skills, it is still necessary to figure out a way to keep the damages minimal.”

“Figure it out?”

“I would hope you are not intending on destroying Amphoreus’ landscape every time I request to see your wings. Are you?” Anaxa said.

Well… no. But Phainon hadn’t exactly planned on bringing them out all that often, either. There wasn’t any point to it. Why bother flying when most places in Amphoreus were easily navigated by foot? Even if he needed to go anywhere further than walking distance, he could travel via the space anchors that the trailblazer had left behind. Surely they weren’t that hard to use?

“How often are you going to request to see my wings?”

Anaxa turned his gaze back to the road. It had opened up even more - they weren’t quite at the path of parting yet, but they could see the bridge at the edge of their vision. Beneath it, the river that bisected the city shimmered - people had clearly been doing well in removing debris from it; the water was much clearer than it had been at the beginning of the Era Nova.

“Arguably,” Anaxa said, “any number higher than zero should be enough to want to minimise gravitational damage.”

Alright. Well, yeah. He can't really deny that one, can he?

“...Right,” Phainon said. “Well, if you don’t mind offering your help on that, Professor.”

He wouldn’t typically ask for the help but - this wasn’t for his sake. It was for the sake of Amphoreus. And… even if it wasn’t… the idea of figuring out how to minimise destruction left him wanting to curl up under a blanket for… at least a decade. As much as he hated being so destructive, it felt impossible to figure out how to counteract it whenever he was.

Just like Lygus had said: For him, it was an inevitability.

He was always destined to be better at destroying things than he was at keeping them in one piece. Amphoreus. The Chrysos Heirs. Himself.

Knowing how to mitigate damage didn’t come naturally to him. If he needed to swallow his pride and have Professor Anaxa tell him how to do it so that he wouldn’t ruin the Era Nova and watch it crumble in his hands, then he’d do it. He would add it to his penance - another goal, another wish, another—

Titans, he was tired thinking about everything that still waited for him.

“It will act as an interesting thought exercise,” Anaxa said.

Well, at least one of them would find it interesting.

What were the chances that Anaxa would find the destruction in his chest as interesting? That he’d take it upon himself to try to deconstruct it, to remake him the way Nanook’s gaze had atomised him, had left his body trembling as he’d fought, knowing that he was simultaneously being unwound and reshaped at the same time.

Would he be enthralled by the concept? Or would he be horrified?

…Ha. As if he’d ever share that.

“Thanks,” he murmured, and tried to put all thoughts of the Aeon from his head before he destroyed something else. Before the rage returned with such a vengeance that they were able to see past the cracks of his porcelain smile to the flames within and see that the Phainon they knew wasn’t ever coming back, he was just a monster now, only fuelled by hatred and bloodshed and—

“We’re here,” Anaxa said, and his whirring thoughts settled.

They had reached a large building that had been used for hosting smaller community events. Phainon had been to a few over the many cycles. A couple of weddings. Once or twice, literature conventions filled with handwritten scrolls, visited with Castorice after pulling some strings to let the pair explore after the hall had closed to the general public.

Currently, the main hall was being used as a makeshift mess hall.

Tables lined the hall. Most were filled - it must’ve been some sort of dinner rush, as the hall seemed almost packed full with Okheman and Kremnoan alike. A roar of chatter that seemed cacophonous. It was the sort of noise that was currently missing from the inner sections of Okhema. Lively and welcoming, if not a little too loud.

Why had they come here of all places? If he was going to bring out his wings, surely they wanted somewhere far emptier.

Oh, of course - Anaxa had mentioned chores that he needed to get done, hadn’t he? Phainon wasn’t sure why he’d assumed the man would be completing those after they’d seen to his wings.

Why had they come to a mess hall, though? It was hardly the sort of place he could see Anaxa coming to willingly. Usually, the professor was far more antisocial - he’d always been one to keep himself isolated.

…Surely that hadn’t changed during the single cycle he hadn’t been present for. Stelle hadn’t caused that big of a deviation as the Deliverer, right? He knew his fellow Chrysos Heirs. Nothing could change them that much.

“Why…?” He murmured, before remembering that it wasn’t actually any of his business and that questioning their location wasn’t the politest thing he could do.

If Anaxa thought his question rude, he wasn’t bringing attention to it. He simply spared Phainon a momentary glance and said, “They’ve delivered some reagents here from the grove. The two of you can entertain yourselves while I receive them. This might take some time.”

He had led them into the hall but now deviated down one of the corridors, disappearing into its depths. Phainon watched as he walked away until the tasseled edges of Anaxa’s billowing coat followed him around a corner.

Then, he was left alone with Mydei.

Mydei, who was waiting for him to finish staring after Anaxa as if he’d lost a lifeline - which he had because now he had to interact with Mydei, alone.

He wasn't ever going to be ready for this.

“They’re delivering things here?” Phainon asked, when it seemed that Mydei wanted him to say something. Anything.

Mydei dipped his head in a nod and led them into the hall. They weaved through city guards, kremnoan soldiers and civilians alike as they ventured towards one of the empty tables at the far end of the hall. Phainon’s lips pulled into a half-smile each time he made eye contact with anyone, trying to ignore how his name rippled through the room as if he were respectable, one of their saviours and not a murderer trying desperately to atone.

“It’s difficult for couriers to run packages through the city,” Mydei said. He was paying the crowd less mind - most of his focus remained on Phainon. “They don’t know what’s structurally stable and what isn’t. So they’re sticking to deliveries on the outskirts of Okhema, for now.”

That made sense. Most couriers weren’t capable of walking away from a collapsed building with only a few injuries. If they entered the wrong part of the city, they’d be risking their lives. It just wasn’t worth it.

…Phainon could offer to run deliveries through the city too. It was something to think about - with Zagreus’ coreflames, it wouldn’t take too long to get from A to B.

Though, really, the need would be made redundant if he put more effort into rebuilding Okhema and keeping it structurally stable.

“No one’s been injured since the evacuation, have they?” Phainon asked.

“Not grievously," Mydei said. “Most people aren’t stupid enough to go outside of the reported ‘safe zones’.”

He sighed, and added, “Though, Aglaea’s going to have to update those reports. Apparently, some areas aren’t as safe as we thought they were.”

A shiver ran down Phainon’s spine. Had he… missed something with his threads?

“What do you mean?” He asked.

“A building collapsed last night by Kephale Plaza,” Mydei said. He wasn’t looking at Phainon pointedly or anything, and yet, as they settled into their seats, Phainon found him unable to sit still. Squirming beneath a gaze that didn't know it should be judging him.

Ah. That had been him. He hadn’t missed anything with his threads; He’d just lost his mind during the night and subsequently lost his temper. Ha.

Yeah, no, he wasn’t going to own up to it. He’d rather—

Well it was probably best not to consider all the things that he’d do to keep this a secret. Probably wasn’t the healthiest thing to entertain such thoughts.

“No one was hurt?”

Mydei shook his head.

That, at least, was a relief. He swallowed the sigh of relief before it could give him away and tapped his fingers on the table instead.

“Aglaea’s looking into it,” Mydei said, which sent a wave of dread crashing against Phainon’s spine. Something caught in his chest. He was going to have to keep avoiding her, then. Lest she realise he was the culprit.

“I see,” Phainon said, and stared at the cracks in the wooden table.

They fell back into silence.

It unspooled like thread, extending further and further, until it became unbearable and Phainon—

“Ah, Lord Phainon, Lord Mydeimos,” came a voice from behind them.

—was fine, actually. He looked up and smiled because he was fine. And he wasn’t losing his mind. And Aglaea wasn’t looking into the destruction that he had caused.

The man wasn’t one that Phainon remembered the name of. He recognised him though - a chef from Janusopolis who he succeeded to save from the black tide and bring to Okhema more often than he’d failed. He had a teenage daughter who had wanted to be a poet. Millions of cycles and she’d only ever made it to Okhema alongside him three times.

She was standing beside him now, delivering food to the various patrons. Currently, she held a tray that held two bowls.

Stelle had managed to save her this time.

(Or maybe… he could congratulate himself for the fact she was here. He’d kept the black tide away from their last cycle, right? So maybe he could pretend he’d managed to save the both of them in a fourth cycle?

..

…No, he shouldn’t take that accomplishment from Stelle. She’d kept them all alive. He’d gotten himself trapped inside of Irontomb.)

“We just wanted to thank you both for saving Amphoreus,” the man continued. Phainon really should've known his name. Why couldn't he remember it? “I know it’s not much but we hoped a meal would show our thanks. Please, enjoy.”

His daughter set down the tray between them, offered a smile and quiet thanks of her own, and before Phainon could think to refuse said offering, they were gone. He stared into the space they had once occupied, eyes wide.

Mydei took one of the bowls and placed it in front of him.

Staring down at it, Phainon froze.

They’d brought out stew - something filling that was easy to make large amounts of for all those utilising the mess hall. It smelled… inviting. Nice. They were wasting it on him. He didn’t need to eat. Hadn’t in… millions of cycles. Hadn’t been a point in doing so.

“What is it?” Mydei asked, as he took the other bowl for himself.

“Ah,” Phainon said, guiltily. “I don’t—”

He couldn’t really bring himself to look up from the stew. Carrots and potatoes floated in the broth. They’d used Droma meat in it too - either that, or there was some other meat with a purple hue to it that he’d never heard of across millions of his lives.

Mydei was waiting for him to continue, so he forced out the words. “I don’t need to eat anymore. You know... because of all of the coreflames. I don’t even get hungry anymore.”

The exhaustion hadn’t just brought him weariness - currently, it had brought him uncertainty too. He didn’t know why he hadn’t refused the offering while they were still there. Politeness, probably.

“They didn’t need to— I don’t need—” Finally he dragged his gaze up. Mydei was watching him as if he’d determined that Phainon was not a person but simply a bunch of puzzle pieces that he needed to clip together. “They should’ve given this to someone who needs it. That’s all.”

Mydei continued to stare at him. It was as if Phainon could see the cogs moving behind his eyes. Churning away, around and around, as if trying to figure out the best thing to say. Mydei had always been serious about nutrition and eating well; He was probably going to turn this into an argument, wasn’t he?

Apparently not.

Because eventually, Mydei just shrugged and said, “Okay.”

That was it…?

“...Okay?”

He wasn’t going to make any comment? He wasn’t going to push, or tell him that he needed to?

Mydei was just going to… accept it?

“Yeah.” Mydei said. “You don’t have to eat it. We’ll just send it back.”

Phainon couldn’t do anything but stare as Mydei began to eat.

No arguments raised. They would simply… send it back?

…Well. No, they couldn’t. That would be rude. And past being rude, it would be a waste.

33 million lifetimes of growing up in Aedes Elysiae had all included his mother teaching his child self never to waste food - especially in the winter months when their harvest had been sold and fresh produce became more scarce. While those memories didn’t always feel real anymore after all of the truths he had learned about Amphoreus, the lessons they instilled stuck with him.

Waste not. Want not. And all of that.

So no - he couldn’t just let them throw it out. Phainon couldn’t do that. Disregarding the kindness of the people whose dreams he’d decided to carry for eons, wasting things that he shouldn’t have received in the first place—

Phainon’s breaths caught in his chest as he reached for the spoon.

(“When,” a part of his brain hissed, rattled and raging, “did the idea of food become so stressful?”

“Probably,” the part of himself that was stuck in eternal grief replied, “around the time we realised that we’d killed everyone we could ever share it with.”)

The first bite was the worst. He’d forgotten that his body was inhospitable to anything that couldn’t withstand intense heat, and a bite of potato was quickly rendered ash against his tongue. He choked, coughing flakes into his hand.

Mydei’s stare was a weighted thing but he did not say anything.

Phainon had to figure something out so that the other man wouldn’t worry. Before Mydei could ask, he shoved another spoonful into his mouth. This time, he let instinct take over - a thin layer of water courtesy of Phagousa’s coreflames, to keep the intense heat from burning the food so quickly. He managed to swallow it down before the food started to burn. There was only an aftertaste of burning.

On the third bite, he adjusted his coreflame usage enough that he could begin to taste the stew. There was a hint of spice to it, possibly paprika. And herbs, too, though they’d been mixed into the broth well enough that they didn’t feel gritty against his tongue.

The flavours were explosive. He wasn't entirely sure if it was in a good way or not. It tasted good, yes, but it was all accompanied by something he couldn't name.

How long had it been since he’d let himself indulge in tiny kindnesses like this? Even if it was only to ensure things were not wasted? Even if it left panic rising in his chest?

…His stomach lurched. Not with nausea, but as if, after lifetimes of being ignored, it was glad to have finally found itself of use once more.

When he’d finished - stew filling consumed and broth drained - Phainon placed his spoon down on the table beside his bowl and stared into the now empty crockery.

He felt… strange.

Like he didn’t understand himself as well as he thought he did.

“I guess you were hungry after all,” Mydei said, as he continued to stare into the empty bowl. As if this hadn’t just opened a bag of worms and he wasn’t currently questioning when, exactly, he’d reached a point of not understanding his own mind anymore, or his body, or—

—Phainon really couldn’t think about it. If he did, he was going to cry and if he did that then what happened if he couldn’t stop?

Remember, he reminded himself, trying to add some cheer into the thought and falling flat. I’m fine. This is fine.

“Maybe,” Phainon murmured. “Mostly I didn’t want to waste it.”

Over his head, he did not see the way that Mydei lifted his gaze up. He did not see the way he made eye contact with Anaxa from across the room. He did not see the small exchange of nods. Nor did he see their rising concern.

All he saw were the cracks at the bottom of his empty bowl.

Was it strange, if it reminded him of himself?

Chapter End Notes

next time: anaxa finally, actually gets to look at phai's wings. phainon thinks that he's maybe probably having a minor breakdown.

chapters.html:
Chapter Summary

in which phainon's having a bit of a meltdown and today becomes even worse than yesterday.

Chapter Notes

you ever look at your characters and wonder why they're refusing to go along with your original plot ideas? yeah well, that's me currently. i had set ideas and then this chapter was written and now we're going elsewhere with it. whelp. it be like that sometimes.

also, just a reminder - i don't have a beta so I typically look for typos and the likes on my own. if you ever spot any that i've missed, pls feel free to point them out!! thanks~

oh, also, if y'all want to speak with me or get lil updates on my writing in general. find me on twitter under @MintCLeaves

He couldn’t stop staring at the bowl.

Phainon’s attention was laser focused on it. Each ceramic crack burned itself into his retinas. He ran his fingers absently across a chip on the rim - it was the faintest thing, only visible if one truly looked for it, not even enough to prick skin if he applied pressure.

“Phai—n.” Mydei must’ve been saying his name but the words felt like they were coming from somewhere far more distant. As if he’d plunged his head into water and was struggling to hear through all the pressure and the chill. “—n’n.”

It was difficult to snap out of it. To look away. Phainon could only stare as his thoughts started to stick like syrup - difficult to traverse, trapping him like a fly that couldn’t break free. Maybe passing out had knocked things out of place in his head. His thoughts were rattling against his skull. His senses rippled and he was certain that the world around him was glitching more than ever. Everything was tinged red. Errors in the code. The only way to stop it was to start over—

“Phainon.”

He jolted as a hand blanketed his own. A mixture of warmth and cold. Colder than the fever that was his permanent temperature. Warmer than hands wrapped in gauntlets should have been.

Phainon’s gaze jolted from bowl to flesh and something caught in his chest as he saw the bare skin of Mydei’s hands. One moment, they were clean, a grounding touch that had brought him back to the present. Next, they were sticky and stained with gold. Mydei wasn’t wearing his gauntlets. Had Phainon not noticed this whole time? What if something happened?

(If Phainon tried to kill him now, Mydei wouldn’t even last a second).

“...Yes?” He murmured, and tried to blink the glitching hallucinations away. It was only half successful. They disappeared but never for long.

“Are you alright?”

…He was beginning to think that maybe he’d gotten a concussion when his body had decided it was time for a quints long siesta without consulting him prior to the event. A concussion would explain why his thoughts were moving strangely and his senses running haywire.

“I’m fine,” he said and, looking up, smiled at Mydei in an attempt to dislodge any remaining embers of concern that the prince was holding on to.

Mydei did not look like he believed him.

—The world glitched, his sight blurred and for a moment the Kremnoan didn’t even look alive. Just glassy-eyed, just choking on the remaining embers of life left inside of him—

“...Right,” Mydei said. “Are you… sure? You seem…” He paused, as if trying to find the right word. “...Dazed.”

“Never better.” Phainon said. His voice sounded far away; As if it wasn’t his own. A dead, dying thing that held no warmth. And yet, his body felt warm. Too hot. Something inside of him was burning. “...Where are your gauntlets?”

“My… what?”

Phainon lifted Mydei’s bloodied-clean-bloody-clean-bloody hand and held it up between them as if it explained everything. “Your gauntlets. You’re not wearing them. Where are they?”

Mydei’s brows furrowed. He said, “I put them away. I don’t need them while rebuilding Okhema.”

Ha. Something bitter and ironic rose in Phainon’s throat and it took all his effort to stop it from emerging. Mydei didn’t realise that he was sitting opposite his murderer because Phainon refused to tell him. Didn’t realise that all it would take to kill him at this point was a single slash of his sword. Didn’t realise that he wasn’t safe enough to set his weapons down.

“You should wear them,” Phainon murmured, releasing Mydei’s hand.

Brows furrowing even deeper, Mydei stare was unending. “Why?”

…Why was Phainon’s mind currently snagging over Mydei's lack of weaponry? Probably the concussion. Or maybe the panic from eating had opened the floodwalls to all the rest of the worries lurking at the edge of his consciousness. The numbness he’d gained after millions of cycles, courtesy of the coreflames, had left him. Now something had to fill its place.

Was his mind cracking at the edges? He didn’t know. All Phainon really knew was that something wasn’t right. Something was wrong. With him.

“You might need them,” Phainon said.

“Why don’t you have Dawnbreaker with you, then?” Mydei asked.

Phainon flinched. He couldn’t stop it. It was a full body thing. His muscles seized and his eyes widened and he could not stop the dread that filtered into his blood like a curse.

Dawnbreaker was currently held prisoner in the same place he trapped his wings. After breaking free from Irontomb, he’d barely been able to look at it - let alone touch it. So he’d let his powers swallow the sword up, out of sight. There wasn’t a soul in the world capable of being harmed by it now. Not even by accident.

Because he was never going to bring Dawnbreaker out. Not in Amphoreus. Not until he left the planet behind to end the Destruction once and for all.

“Phain—”

“Anaxa’s been gone for a while,” Phainon said, hands slamming onto the table with enough strength that the wood split with spiderweb cracks. Luckily, he still had enough hold on himself that it didn’t begin to burn. He pushed up to his feet. “We should go look for him.”

“He said he’d find us,” Mydei said. “Just sit back down.”

Yeah. Phainon couldn’t do that. Ash was beginning to catch in his throat and he was all too aware of the fact that his temperature was rising in response to his agitated state. He needed to get out. If he didn’t, he was pretty sure he’d end up setting something on fire.

“He’s got to be here somewhere,” he said and looked over his shoulder, scouring the room for any signs of the professor.

Too many people. Yet not many with Anaxa’s green hair. Most people had more neutral hair colours - there were few people in Okhema that Phainon had met with mint shading. He squinted, trying to disregard Mydei’s voice behind him and made his way through the crowd.

There, near the exit, the man was leaning over a box and inspecting whatever was inside. Components. Ingredients for whatever soul study he’d decided to investigate next.

Phainon kept moving until he was beside Anaxa. His smile was only slightly unstable when the professor looked up.

“There you are, Professor,” he said.

“Phainon,” Anaxa said, brow raised, his working eye widening. “You’re creating steam.”

“Am I?” He asked. Sure enough, a quick glance at his shoulder showed that faint ripples of steam were rising from his body. The edge of his collar was singed. “Oh. Well. Sometimes that happens. It’s fine.”

“...I see.” Anaxa’s gaze flicked past him, to Mydei who had followed close behind, and then settled back onto Phainon. “I’ll survey the rest of these later. Let us depart.”

The sigh of relief that Phainon exhaled was so deep that it felt cavernous. He ignored Anaxa’s stare, pointed towards his box of components and asked, “They look heavy. Would you like me to carry them?”

The professor’s widened eyes had settled. He'd returned to his usual assessing glances. He said, “Best not to. They’re sensitive to heat. Mydeimos will carry them.”

Phainon was about to open his mouth to argue that he was more than capable of lowering his body temperature when the edge of a flame caught on his sleeve. He felt the burn as if it were an extension of himself. Slapped a hand over it in an attempt to snuff it from existence.

“Sure,” he said and Phainon’s wide smile wobbled but refused to fall.

Their next walk was even more awkward than the first.

Luckily, there was a lot less conversation this time. Phainon was left to focus on settling the flames before they could take root and burn him completely. Anaxa and Mydei were content to leave him to cool off, to settle his body that currently steamed in response to raised stress levels.

They talked, but mostly between themselves. Quiet murmurings that Phainon wanted to believe weren’t about him and, as such, was willing to believe related to the professor’s experiments. Probably wasn’t true. But Phainon didn’t care.

He just wanted this day to be over. Even more so than he’d wanted yesterday to be over.

Reality was still a half-moulded thing around him. Last night, at least he’d been able to blame his dead friends in the streets on the strange lighting of the Evernight and the flickering of candles. Now, he couldn’t blame it on anything but himself.

Phainon kept his gaze on the backs of his living friends and did his best to ignore all the dead ones. Reminded himself that the dead ones weren't real. He was just a little stressed. And concussed. Probably. Those two things were making the usual hallucinations worse. If he pretended they weren’t there then maybe they’d go away.

A dry chuckle caught in his throat. Yeah, right. Like it would be that easy.

They left the outskirts of Okhema behind, headed across the Path of Parting and made their way outside of the city. Sunlight continued to bathe them as they walked - it was foreign, to be able to walk away from Okhema and not feel like its light was abandoning them.

Veering off of the path, Anaxa led them towards an abandoned expanse of grass by the riverside. Luckily it was not too overgrown, though some patches were much taller than others.

“Try to minimise the destruction and bring them out quickly,” the professor said, as he waved Phainon forwards. “We’ll stay here until you’re finished.”

Phainon nodded, and removed his coat. Once he'd removed his shirt, he folded the clothes and held them out to Mydei, who took them with a quirked brow.

“I don’t want to set them on fire,” he explained.

“Of course,” Mydei replied, slowly. Then, “That’s a risk?”

“Coreflame wings,” Phainon shrugged.

Mydei opened his mouth, considered, sighed and then closed his mouth. He said, “Sure. Makes sense. Why not?”

“Go on then,” Anaxa said, waving him towards the open expanse of field. “We don’t have all day.”

There wasn’t any reason to delay so Phainon headed further into the grass and began focusing on the feel of his wings. Like usual, they were not hard to locate. The feel of them never really disappeared, it just got a little harder to track. Not quite a numbness, more like he’d pushed the sensation of them to the furthest recess of his mind.

Then, it was just a matter of reworking space.

Easy work. Just like the day previous. A rogue clump of wet grass smacked into his shoulder as the gravity of his black hole settled into Amphoreus. Phainon let out a faint hiss of annoyance, but past that, it was routine as usual.

Open the black hole. Take out wings. Close the black hole.

(He was half tempted to kick at loose dirt out of sheer pettiness, but Phainon knew that he was being watched. He shoved the irritation down and told himself that he was above being angry at grass.)

The flames engulfing his wings were burning hotter than they usually did. Each feather - usually golden, dappled with white at the edges - shone a dazzling white. Blue flame tinged at the edges. Any dusting from the black hole was washed away in the blaze.

Before bringing his wings out, he'd reinforced himself with coreflames to keep himself from burning. His body - capable of withstanding the heat - held up fine with the faintest reinforcement of water, but the buckle of his choker began to melt and he was forced to remove it before it melted into skin.

His clothes too, struggled against the heat. Luckily, Phagousa’s coreflames kept them from the worst parts of incineration. The grass around them was not as lucky. Grass boiled from green to yellow before his eyes. Then, the longer stalks began to crumble into ash.

Phainon sighed.

“Hm,” Anaxa called, from a distance, making his way over. He lifted a hand to his chin, contemplative. “From what Hyacine informed me, I had thought the temperature was lower than this.”

“The temperature fluctuates,” Phainon said, tiredly, once both the professor and Mydei came to a stop a few feet away.

“Do you have control over it?”

“To a degree.”

Anaxa nodded, considering. “Does utilising coreflames make the burn worse or better?”

Well, he was currently using them to stop from burning everything and it hadn’t exactly made the heat any worse. No, it seemed that the burn was purely controlled by his emotions. Whenever exhaustion slunk in, the flames were lazier. When his rage burned at its highest, the coreflames resonated with it and scalded everything in his immediate vicinity.

Currently, Phainon was learning that panic and guilt manifested heat in a similar way. Though, luckily not quite as molten as his rage. The coreflames weren’t combusting in the same way as when he was enraged. The heat wasn't as volatile, or explosive. It was just there.

“Neither,” he said. Anaxa didn’t need to know that the heat was determined by his emotions. If he did, then he’d realise how wild said emotions had become. “The coreflames just burn. Using them doesn’t change how hot they are.”

Again, Anaxa hummed.

Beside him, Mydei crossed his arms and narrowed his eyes in thought.

“Very well.” The professor nodded. “I assume you’re capable of using more than one titan’s power at a time?”

Phainon nodded.

“First, I’d like you to try dousing these flames. Phagousa's coreflames should work effectively in doing so.” Anaxa said.

That was… well. Phainon glanced towards the nearby river and pressed his lips together.

“That’ll only put them out for a few seconds,” Phainon said, after a moment. “I don’t think I'll be able to control enough water to permanently put out—”

“Yes, yes, I know that. As soon as the flames are doused, you’ll use Orynyx’s coreflame to halt the time around your wings. You'll only need to put the flame out for a matter of seconds.”

Alright. Well that was a little bit more plausible. Hopefully. While he wasn’t able to reverse time or mould it in the ways he wanted, it wasn’t an altogether impossible task to halt it in its tracks, though the longer he wanted to pause things, the harder it would become. He'd done it a few times. Only for a few seconds at a time and only ever in his divine form, but he had proven that it was possible.

Holding it in place for longer than a few seconds though… Maybe if he utilised Mnestia’s threads, he could keep the clock firmly in place and that could help keep the time attached to his wings from moving forwards?

“Will I need to do anything else?” Phainon asked.

“Not yet,” Anaxa said. “Try that first.”

Nodding, Phainon made his way to the river. Phagousa’s coreflames thrummed in his blood, bringing with it the scent of sea salt on the breeze. River water rippled in recognition of the power in his veins. Small bubbles of water rose like teardrops falling in reverse. Then, larger spheres.

Phainon raised a hand and the water followed suit. His brows twitched as he focused. Fire was so much easier to control - he wasn’t nearly as practiced with liquids.

He brought the water spheres together, - winced as they rippled between transluscent, red and gold, - merging them into a single ball, heavy and distorted under the swell of it's own weight. Then, he tilted his head, considering how best to drench his wings.

“...No point in overthinking it,” Phainon murmured, and - considering it was the easiest and only option he could think of - proceeded to loosen his hold on the water and drop it over himself like a balloon. He staggered under the sudden weight that crashed over his shoulders and rooted himself in place with the help of Georios’ coreflames to keep from toppling over.

Hm. Okay, so he could’ve thought a little bit more about that plan. A quick glance over his shoulder showed that the water had snuffed the flame somewhat, though not entirely.

Already they were beginning to burn again.

Hair clung to his forehead. Phainon scraped it from his face with his fingernails and let out a long sigh. Every part of his body was dripping and soaked.

…Titans, he was an idiot.

Phainon turned back to Anaxa and Mydei, somewhat helplessly, and said, “I don’t know what I’m doing.”

“We can see that,” Anaxa said. He was absolutely judging him. “You’ll need running water to keep the flames doused. Create a moving stream between yourself and the river.”

Oh right. Yeah, that made more sense. Phainon could do that.

Why couldn’t Anaxa have offered that before he’d dropped several tonnes of river onto himself?

Creating a moving current of water was more difficult than simply altering the gravity of a set amount. He had to weave a route for this new river to follow and then alter the directional flow into something that was mostly contained. Then, let it crash across his back and wings - he shuddered at the sustained cold it brought - and move it along before his own body temperature boiled it.

By the time he was finished, Phainon’s chest was heaving from the exertion.

…Orynyx’s coreflame wouldn’t be any easier to use. Still, at least he knew how to pause time. Now it was just a matter of focus.

Visualise a box around the space he wanted to freeze in time. Each atom inside the box would need to be slowed - Mnestia’s coreflames could help with that. Thread space into a fixed state and reinforce it with the force of hundreds of Orynyx’s coreflames. Time cracked at his mental fortitudes. Phainon added a few thousand more coreflames into the mix.

It took seconds at most but it felt longer. Using Orynyx’s coreflame always felt like that. Time sat weird in the mind whenever the titan’s power was utilised.

It was altogether exhausting. The exertion left him feeling like he’d run a marathon. Phainon leaned forward, hands on his knees and inhaled deep pockets of air. Keeping the altered time in place around his wings wasn’t quite as hard as pausing time in the first place, but it was still difficult. His heart raced in his chest.

“Fascinating,” Anaxa said, as both he and Mydei moved closer. “I hadn’t thought that you’d be able to do it immediately. With the amount of coreflames you have, it should’ve taken a lot more practice to reach this point.”

Phainon control over the river cracked. Like a waterfall, the floating stream of water crashed into soil, soaking the three men.

“What?” He gasped, his chest heaving.

“Time rarely wants to hold still. It’s in a constant state of movement,” Anaxa said, wiping the water from his face as if it were little more than a minor inconvenience. “Whether moving backward or forwards, it’s always moving. To halt it in place… I’d have expected it to take more than thirty-three coreflames.”

“I—” Phainon stared, wide-eyed. “—What?”

“Perhaps the power of other coreflames strengthens them? I’ll have to rework my equations - I hadn’t accounted for this.” Anaxa said.

His gaze narrowed in on Phainon’s wings. Doused as they were, it was now possible to see each individual feather, and the slow growth of bone beneath them. They were back to their gold colouring, glowing softly like embers in a fire. “How large were they before they were cut off?”

Mydei muttered, “Cut off?”

Phainon ignored him and said, “Approximately… double the length of my arms?”

For a moment, Anaxa simply stared at his now much smaller wings.

Then, his eyes narrowed. “I see.”

He said it in the tone of someone whose mind was beginning to spark with multiple realisations. A shudder rippled down Phainon’s spine.

“...Three hundred and ninety six coreflames, was it?” Anaxa asked.

Mydei’s gaze flicked to Anaxa, questioning.

Phainon swallowed down dread. Then, because it had caught in his throat on the way down, he cleared his throat. Sweat caught on the back of his neck. He said, “Yeah.”

Anaxa continued to stare. His gaze had caught Phainon in a vice - There was nothing he could do but stay rooted in place, let out a small, shaking breath and attempt to keep his expression as neutral as possible.

“...Is that so?” the professor said, dryly.

Chapter End Notes
