chapters.title: Chapter 9
chapters.html:
Chapter Summary

in which, phainon crashes tf out.

Chapter Notes

oh boi. oh, oh, OH BOI.

Phainon’s wings were twitching with the instinct to hunch his shoulders.

If he did anything at all in response to Anaxa’s questions it could not be that. To hunch his shoulders would imply that he was guilty of something. If he showed any weakness, then Anaxa was going to read him like a poorly constructed pamphlet that was beginning to curl at the edges.

So, he tried to ignore the twitching that rippled across every feather. Straightened his shoulders and pushed any guilt down into the pits of his stomach alongside every other emotion he’d deigned unnecessary for the current moment.

Then his wings twitched again, accompanied by a full body shudder that racked down his spine with enough force that Phainon’s body trembled in the aftermath.

Ah.

That wasn’t guilt but something more physical. The trembling of his body wasn’t caused by repressed emotion - he was shivering. He’d quenched his flaming wings, drenched himself in water and now the gentle breeze felt like a winter gale. Bumps rose on the flesh of his arms, hair standing on its ends.

“Cold,” he murmured. He reached out to Mydei, footsteps slippery in the now-muddy field and said, “It’s freezing. Pass me my shirt?”

Mydei passed him the shirt. It only had a little bit of blood on the fabric from his bloodied-clean-bloodied hands. He said, “Cold? It’s the middle of summer.”

“I run a little warmer these days,” Phainon said.

There was no way he was getting this shirt over his wings without struggle. He squinted at the fabric, considering how best to move forward and eventually settled on ripping an extra hole into the fabric. His finger fumbled at a first attempt, but luckily, he managed to tear through the fabric much easier on his second. Pulled the new shirt over his head and wiggled his wings until they were freed from a prison of shirt. “Coat?”

The coat was more gold than white. Glitch-stained in blood. Phainon did his best to ignore the stickiness of it as he wrapped it around his shoulders. Probably best not to rip this - Aglaea wouldn’t be too pleased if he did. He could replace the shirt easily enough with just about anything but this coat was irreplaceable. Aglaea had made it for him herself.

He pulled the fabric around his arms in an attempt to soothe his shivering. It didn’t make him feel warmer - it felt about as useful as wrapping oneself in a loose paper towel - but at least the breeze no longer caressed bare skin.

“The coreflames have severely increased your temperature,” Anaxa noted. Since he’d asked about the coreflames, his eye had been narrowed, flicking between Phainon’s wings and face. As if observing every single secret that was hidden behind both. “It seems you regulate your body temperature through your wings. With the flames put out - the cold sets in.”

Phainon grimaced.

“Though, to think that your body is already showing signs of hypothermia…” Anaxa trailed off. Frowned. “Three-hundred ninety six coreflames. From thirty-three cycles?”

Dread coiled in his stomach. Phainon pulled his coat closer around him and said, “yes.”

“That can’t be right,” Anaxa said. “The temperature difference wouldn’t be this extreme with that many coreflames. The body wouldn't react as severely. There must’ve been more coreflames.”

Mydei’s gaze flicked between Phainon and Anaxa, lips pressing in a thin line.

“Phainon wouldn’t have…” The Kremnoan muttered. His focus settled solely onto Phainon, the press of his lips twisting with grim understanding as if realising that yes, actually, he absolutely would have done whatever Mydei was currently thinking.

“How many other cycles were there?” Anaxa asked.

Beside his dread, something hotter was beginning to curdle in his chest. It didn’t help with the shivering, or his base temperature; This, he knew immediately, wasn’t physical. It was something that needed to be pushed away. Something that was better ignored; Better not to think about it lest it settle in his blood like a disease.

“How many other cycles were there…?” Phainon repeated, the words catching against his tongue as if glued there. His eyes widened. What… the hell? How did someone figure out the truth from casual observation? It didn’t make sense. “Professor. What are you talking about? There were only thirty-three.”

The only way out of this was through it. He was going to have to play the clueless baby chicken that Stelle had once said he was.

Phainon tried to meet their eyes - found that the flicker between lifeless glass and wakeful suspicion was too much, even for him - and cast his gaze to the ground by their feet. It was littered with their corpses. How… wonderful.

Phainon’s lips twisted in distaste.

“Like I said,” Anaxa said, “the temperature difference with four hundred coreflames wouldn’t be enough to cause hypothermia in their absence. Chills, perhaps, but the body would adjust quickly. So how many—”

“Thirty-three cycles.” Phainon repeated, more forcefully. One of the dead, not-really-there, Anaxa corpses twitched its fingers, as if trying to tear himself back into life and join the argument. Sunken eyes stared at him, demanding the truth. Despite himself, Phainon leaned back, away from the corpse.

“Disregard the temperature fluctuations then,” Anaxa - the real one, the one that he hadn’t killed yet - said, forcefully. “There are other indications. With your coreflame usage and what I’ve observed of your wings, it’s not feasible for it to have been that small a number. It doesn’t fit with the math —”

“Have you considered,” Phainon said, thickly, “that maybe your math is just wrong?”

The words were torn from his throat before Phainon could really think them over. Thick. Warm. Tingling against his tongue alongside the beginning of blossoming irritation. When he tried to push it down alongside all the rest, it sprung back - indignant - even more inflated than before. It was like someone was shovelling coal into his chest, throwing dying embers and lit matches alongside it, encouraging the burn.

It didn’t make sense. The suddenness of it all was enough to stagger him. Wasn’t anger supposed to build more slowly? Curated over a long time, the fire tended to over eons, flame stoked bit by bit?

This was more like a flash flood. It seemed as if it had come out of nowhere.

“If it had only been one equation faltering I would consider it.” Anaxa said. Which was even more infuriating because what kind of person assumed they were only capable of being wrong once? “But there are multiple factors pointing to this theory being the truth. We already determined that one would expect more than thirty-three of Orynyx’s coreflames to be able to—”

“—And now you’re an expert on Orynyx’s coreflame too? How do you even have a frame of reference for what each coreflame should be capable of? That’s— That’s ridiculous—”

“Would you quit interrupting me?” Anaxa snapped. “Getting defensive only proves my point further, Phainon. I have a frame of reference from when the Trailblazer inherited the coreflame in the previous cycle. Now. If you’d simply listen, I’d explain that it’s not just these two things that act as indicators.”

Phainon’s breathing was a fast thing. His eyes narrowed on one of the not-there corpses. They— it— was smirking at him. As if to say ‘you’ve lost this debate, Khaslana. What, you thought you could win?’

“Unless you are lying about the previous size of your wings - which I presume you were not, for there is little reason to lie when time will have them regrow back to a similar length - then they would be too large a container for a mere ‘four hundred coreflames’. You would need to hold more.”

The anger in his chest was beginning to boil. It was as if, in pausing the burn of his wings, he’d set the rest of himself alight. His chest ached. Familiar rage trickling in, making itself at home as if it’d never truly left. Just momentarily disguised itself as something weak and less predatory.

Why was he feeling so strongly about this?

This was Anaxa - of all people, he was the one most likely to approach the truth. He was the smartest person that Phainon had ever met. He always figured out the truth, eventually. The truth of the world. The truth of the Flame Reaver. The truth of… of everything.

And it wasn’t even as if he was all that attached to this particular lie, anyway. It’d been an accidental thing. Stelle wasn’t going to let him keep it forever.

…Maybe it was because it’d been billions of years and Anaxa had never once let things go. Couldn’t he have just dropped it, this time? Let Phainon rest and tell them the truth on his own?

Couldn’t he just let Phainon keep this lie of his for a little while longer? He hadn’t even had it for a week.

“And how would you determine how much space a coreflame takes up?” He challenged, because… well, in this regard, he and the professor were quite alike. Phainon wasn’t very good at letting things go either. “These wings are the perfect container, no matter the number. Flame spreads, professor. It fills whatever container you put it in.”

Anaxa crossed his arms. “I’ve possessed coreflames of my own, Phainon. I know their dimensions. Four hundred flames in that large of a wingspan? They wouldn’t burn with nearly as bright a flame as what we witnessed earlier.”

Something cold was collecting in Phainon’s eyes.

His gaze flicked up to the professor - ha, he was flaking away like he always did upon ripping the coreflame from his chest and disintegrating upon the wind - and ground his teeth together. Gnashing things, something wild was prowling inside of his veins, begging for release. He wanted to blame it on the Destruction’s influence but this, he knew, was all him.

(Beside him, Mydei’s golden gaze had shuttered. Realisation had caught him in its tight grip. From his heavy stare, it was clear that— if asked— he would take the professor’s side in a heartbeat. Something in the back of his head snarled at the betrayal he felt over the idea of the prince taking anyone else’s side but his.)

Phainon’s fingers twitched as if reaching for his sword. Muscle memory preparing to solve the problem in the only way he knew how.

Maybe it should’ve been sickening, the realisation that - after billions of years - his first instinct was murder. Maybe it should’ve rattled him.

It didn’t.

It just made the rage filling his chest burn even brighter - a supernova that was cracking at the edges of his skin, of his consciousness, of his very being.

Phainon was so sick of his own mind. Of the anger and exhaustion. Of all of the hate.

“Fine,” he said, finally. “How many coreflames would I need to have?”

His voice was dull. Though the bite had not faded, though his words were saturated, it was less explosive. Colder now - in the way that fire confused the senses when its heat had reached a level that nerves could no longer process.

“...Excuse me?”

“How many of Orynyx’s coreflames would I need,” Phainon said, frost catching on each syllable like sharp fragments of glass. It sliced sharp as a needle. “In order to pause time on my wings. How many?”

Both Chrysos Heirs were staring at him.

Of course they were. Phainon had all but confessed to them. This was the closest one got without actually saying that he’d lied, wasn’t it? Why they seemed surprised was beyond him - this was what Anaxa had pushed for. Phainon had been trying to protect them, to spare them the pain of the truth, but what did he care?

He’d been willing to tell them the number of cycles in the beginning until they’d gotten upset over such a miniscule number. If they wanted to force him to increase that number, then fine. That was on them. They could impale themselves on the truth of something larger if they really wanted to. Who was he to stop them?

“Well?” He pressed.

Professor Anaxa looked less resolute now. Less determined. Having the truth confirmed had allowed for something wary to catch in his eye.

Apparently that weariness didn’t breed hesitation, though. He said, “Hundreds for the initial pause. To keep time paused for as long as you currently have though, without any visible struggle, it would take thousands.”

Fine.

Fucking. Fine.

Phainon threw his hands into the air and said, “Thousands! Alright. Thirty-three hundred cycles then. That’s how many cycles it’s been. Does that fit with your math?”

Mydei, wide-eyed, lifted a hand and pushed the Professor back. He said, “Deliverer—”

Something ugly and violent caught in the back of Phainon’s throat. It tasted of blood and ash and millions of shattered dreams.

“Don’t,” he spat. “Don’t call me that.”

“I—” Mydei’s brows raised. Almost infuriatingly, he lifted his arms, almost as if placating some wild beast. Phainon would show him wild. His teeth ground together with enough force that he wouldn’t have been surprised if his jaw cracked from the aftershock. “Sorry. Phainon.”

Oh. This was Mydei trying to calm him down, wasn’t it? Well, tough shit. He didn’t want to be calm. He wanted to burn like he always had, to fall into the sweet release of his anger and let it carry him through into tomorrow. Every other part of himself was something that he was carrying for others - this anger was the only thing that was his.

“No,” Phainon snapped. “I’m not done. He hasn’t answered if it’s enough yet. Right?”

His gaze fell back onto Anaxa. His body was glitching so much between real-unreal, dead-alive, smirking and afraid, that it was difficult to tell what the true Anaxa currently looked like.

“Tell me,” he continued, “is three thousand cycles worth of coreflames enough to fill these wings of mine? Or is that number too small? You tell me, Professor. You’re the expert here.”

Around him, Phainon could feel something cracking. Probably time. Maybe his own mind. He didn’t care. Let it do so. What did it matter?

Anaxa said, “...I would expect the number to be even higher. Tens of thousands.”

Bitterness caught in Phainon’s chest. Swollen, like a festering wound that had been infected by years and years worth of self-flagellation.

He laughed. Sharp. Harsh. The edges of it distorted. His mind was melting. “Fine. Thirty thousand then. Does that work for you? Does that fit the narrative of your equations?”

Anaxa opened his mouth but no words came out.

Ha. Haha. So even the great Professor Anaxagoras could be stunned into silence, huh? He’d been through millions of cycles but this? This was new. Anaxa always had something to say.

Did that mean that it was finally Phainon’s turn? To say something and not have to be so fucking polite about it all the time?

Maybe it was.

The words bubbled from his throat against his will. A fresh, burning sludge formed from years of silence and trauma, from buried rage and having reached the edge of sanity time and time again.

“You know Professor,” he snapped, “you’re not nearly as smart as you think you are. Maybe if you were, you’d have actually survived at least one time.

You would think that at least once in all of these cycles a certified genius such as yourself would have managed to keep himself alive?”

Breathless, he tried to catch his breath but it was impossible - the words continued. Phainon couldn’t bring himself to stop even to breathe.

“But no. All of your math and equations and theories, it never factored in survival, did it? I mean, why would they? Your theories only ever focus on subjects that are utterly inconsequential. Titans? The Era Nova? Who even cares about any of that? You’re seriously—”

“Phainon,” Mydei said, cutting through the words with a chill so deep that it caught hold of his words and froze them in place.

Phainon cast his gaze from the heavily glitching Anaxa and let it settle on Mydei. He was still pushing Anaxa back, step by step, widening the gap between them and him.

A corroded, glitching version of Dawnbreaker burst free from his ribcage.

He couldn’t stop the laugh that caught in his throat. Nor the rage that now found itself focused on the Kremnoan.

“And you,” he snapped, because now he really couldn’t stop. If he didn’t keep speaking, he was going to tear Dawnbreak free from unreality and do something that couldn’t be reversed. “Mydei. Don’t get me started on you. Ha. Mydeimos the Undying. What a false title that is. If you were truly immortal, you’d have come back. You’d have made it to the end too. It’s pathetic. You’re path—”

Time cracked in full.

One moment, he was trembling with rage and shivering from the cold of suppressed flames.

The next, his wings reared with a blazing inferno. Flame licked at his skin, at the grass around him, at his clothes. It burned everything. His clothes, the grass, his own hallucinations - even clumps of dirt were sizzling away into cinders. Behind him the river erupted with steam, like a volcano ready to erupt.

Mydei yanked Anaxa into his arms and threw the pair of them back. Away. Flame caught the edges of their clothes, their hair, but past being slightly singed they were relatively untouched.

Phainon heaved in a long breath. It rattled against his lungs. This fury that had raised its head and now ran rampant in his blood was an ancient thing. Transformed from grief, he’d been holding it longer than the universe had drawn breath. It was eternal. The deadliest thing that lived between the curl of his ribs.

…Ha.

Haha.

He hated them. Mydei. Anaxa. His fellow heirs. Okhema. Amphoreus. All of the people that lived within the planet's atmosphere. He loathed them. For all the dreams they’d placed on his shoulders. For the title they’d forced him to bear, over and over and over, without any promise of release.

Hated how easily they died.

Despised them for the fact that his mind could replay the stuttering melody of every final breath, every failing heartbeat.

Loathed them for every set of final words they’d ever given him.

Detested the fact that even now, in what was meant to be an era of peace, he still couldn’t protect them from anything. From the truth. From himself.

…Hated how after everything, after 33 million cycles of suffering, they were still the most precious of people. That he still wanted to carry everything so that they’d never have to. That even while he burned, he wanted to plunge himself into ice so that when he held them in his arms, they would not burn with him.

He hated Amphoreus and cherished it. He loved his friends and, simultaneously, wanted them dead.

Grief caught in Phainon’s throat. Tears evaporated before he could summon the strength to cry. In the absence of a sob, he laughed, because it wasn’t fair. It was meant to be over and it wasn’t. He was meant to be fine but how could he ever be, after everything?

It took Mydei pulling himself and Anaxa to their feet for the haze of flame and rage to settle enough for him to think.

“I—” His breaths shook with the weight of momentary restraint. “I—I’m sorry. I shouldn’t have—”

Nope. Even trying to talk was fraying the edges of his mind.

He met Mydei’s gaze. He was watching Phainon as if he were going to shatter. Ha. That was laughable. Out of all of them, he was the least breakable. The Kremnoan let out a shaky breath and opened his mouth—

—And Phainon lifted a hand, pulled on every single one of Orynyx’s coreflames at his disposal and trapped his fellow Chrysos Heirs in time before any words could break the silence.

Staying here wasn’t an option. He couldn’t be here. If he stayed…

No. He couldn’t think of what he’d do if he stayed.

So instead of thinking about it, he moved. He curled Janus’ coreflames around his fingertips, summoned an infinity gate and fled from his friends.

Chapter End Notes

Chapter Notes

Iny drew an amazing comic of Phainon's crash-out last chapter. Like. My god, my guy. I am still in awe. I keep going back and looking at it because I'm in love with the way Phainon is illustrated??

Now that we're on chapter 10 - I want to say thanks to everyone for all the comments and kudos. I typically try to respond to all comments but y'all are treating me so much and I'm struggling to keep up ahaha. If I miss your comment in my replies, then I'm sorry, but I definitely appreciate each and everyone. Thank you all for enjoying my little au!!

(Oh, also, I've updated the tags a little. Not much, but you know. Ye.)

The infinity gate spat him out into the decaying remains of the village that had birthed him.

For a moment, Phainon simply hovered above what remained of Aedes Elysiae. Suspended in space, his gaze snagged on crumbling buildings and half-collapsed barns. Thick vines of ivy had attempted to reclaim the buildings to no avail - they’d long since withered alongside the village that had always been destined to die. Then quivering wings drooped, unable to keep him held above the destruction, and Phainon was dropped down onto scorched earth.

It was dry and coarse against his toes - sizzling beneath his feet as lifeless soil ruptured into ash.

There had been a time when the thought of Aedes Elysiae would have halted his anger; When it had offered a sense of peace, past an initial wave of grief and loneliness. But that had been whenever he thought of before. Of back when it had stood, when it had lived and breathed.

Seeing this version of home, knowing that both his own and Cyrene’s foggy recollection of the life that had come before was not enough to reform it into something alive, that there were simply too many memories of a destroyed Aedes Elysiae to ever bring it back to what it had once been, only managed to stoked the rage in his chest.

His flames reached a temperature so high that his skin was beginning to sit wrong around his bones. Tight. Malleable. His flesh was incandescent with molted gold - less like he was a person and more like a half-forged weapon awaiting the strike of a hammer.

Trembling, Phainon managed two steps closer to what remained of the village. It was as close as he could allow himself before he was forced to admit that, currently, the task of entering was impossible. Physically, his body resisted each step, working against him and the rage that this place wrought within him. Mentally, he just couldn’t. He could see people burning at the edge of his vision, could hear their screams, but he couldn’t get closer because they weren’t his to save.

Exhaustion caught in his chest, cracking it open. His mind swam through a tide of light-headedness and glitching memories.

A snarl caught in his throat; Even his body was trying to temper him. Clearly it had not received the memo that Phainon wasn’t willing to douse this flame just yet. If this current form of his was unwilling to let him burn and burn then he’d force himself into another that would.

Lifting a hand to his chest, he dug nails into flesh and tore. Flame poured free from the tear, speckled with sizzling drops of ichor. The surrounding skin charred, blackening like hardened ash, forming a chrysalis for his transformation into a divine form.

Coreflame crystallised, wrapping him in a sphere of gold as his transformation progressed. They burned against his hands, blistering the skin in black and gold. Coreflame tore through the stitches of muscle, jagged deposits bursting from his shoulders with such violence that it hitched his breath.

Divinity leaked out of the cracks in his chest. Burning. Soaring. The temperature of it crackled the air, condensing it like a half-drawn breath held over eternity. It washed over him, staining him with the poison of destruction, seeping into every part of his being. Into the sun tattoo that now burned like a brand. Into his eyes, unseeing but for the glint of promised - revenge - salvation on the horizon.

It even filtered into his blood, singing its shrill song, harmonising with all of his hatred and his rage.

Sound burst free from a burning throat. Guttural and filled with wrath. Not a yell, or a shout, but something that could not truly be described. A sound unlike any other, it wasn’t something that should have been formed by human vocal chords. It had reached abyssal depths of despair, broken and distorted.

Phainon’s legs buckled beneath him and his knees crashed into ash.

The earth trembled beneath the weight of his anger. When curled fingers dug into ashen soil, it quaked alongside his trembling hands. When he screamed, unable to keep the broil of his hostility inside of his chest, the ground split, cavernous, reaching deep into Amphoreus’ core.

It wasn’t fair.

Above him, the sky responded to his own volatility as if his rage was its own. The atmosphere splintered under the weight of its oncoming storm. Thunder resonated with the heavy pound of his pulse, lightning striking out at everything in the vicinity that the blazing inferno of his divinity had left untouched.

It had never been fair.

At the further edges of the village, gentle waters grew tumultuous. Waves crashed against the edges of a rotten pier, consuming decayed slabs of wood, swallowing half-standing structures and dragging them into the depths of sea.

He’d just wanted to help. To protect everything he held dear. To keep everything from falling apart for just a little bit longer. Why weren’t they letting him? Why did they always—

Space rippled around him. Distorted. It did not quite sit the way that space should. Heavy, the sky pulled down, squishing the atmosphere as if pressing on a sponge. Infinity gates opened, and closed, opened, closed. Fragmented passages leading to nowhere and everywhere. Into endless blazes and hungry stars. Into spaces encased with death, with trickery, with strife. Fractals of impossible dimensions, ripped open with golden thread and sewn back together just as quickly, only with uneven stitches that left reality an uncanny appropriation of what it should have been.

Phainon heaved in gasping breaths. With each one, the space filled around him.

His friends had come for him.

Bleeding, decaying things but they had come. Aglaea, stitched with gold, lifeless but for the strings that walked her closer like the puppet she was. Tribbie, fracturing over and over, like she always did, reaching out with a smile and the promise of tomorrow.

Anaxa, trying to step closer but disintegrating further with every breath of storm around them. Castorice, skeletal and never quite there - just smiling as time ground bone to dust. Cipher, always just outside of view, only visible in his peripherals, constantly moving even despite all of the holes stamped into her body. Hyacine, reaching out, always reaching out, even as her body burned.

All of them with thousands and thousands of duplicates. Thousands piling up around him, weighing down on his shoulders, adding to the weight of deliverance. Various deaths, all of them the result of his action. Of his hatred.

Phainon felt something bump against his skin, and there he was. Just the one copy, considering the fact that he always died in the same way.

Mydeimos the undying, glassy-eyed, lying face down in the ash. Dawnbreaker sticking out of his back as if a natural fixture to his body. Blood pooling around his torso. Staining his hair, his face, his hands, his—

Phainon’s lips trembled. Something caught in his throat and he wasn’t sure what it was. He reached for the false Mydei’s hand, lying limp at his side, and pulled on it so that the corpse was half in his lap, half collapsed on the earth before him.

“Tell me, Mydei,” he murmured, rage giving way - momentarily - to pain that wracked his very core. He pressed Mydei’s hand against his cheek and let his eyelids shutter. “Is there still any tenderness left in my eyes?”

No response.

Of course there wasn’t.

The only answer that Phainon received was the way Mydei’s glitching body began to crumble into ones and zeroes. It would’ve been kinder if he’d been reduced to ash - at least, then, Phainon could’ve convinced himself that Mydei had once been real. Instead—

Instead, Phainon curled now-empty hands around clumps of hair and screamed.

And around him, whatever remained of Aedes Elysiae ceased to exist.

—

Eventually, the rage plateaued.

Not for lack of a spark, but because even this divine vessel was unable to sustain itself against the heavy weight of exhaustion weighing down on him. His anger remained, though now it was an unconscious thing. The coreflames took hold of it and acted in his stead. A flicker of flame wrapped around his shoulders like a blanket. It pressed against drooping eyelids and promised to continue burning in his stead while he rested.

Emotionally drained, but for the rage that would never cease, Phainon closed his eyes.

He slept.

At the edge of his consciousness, he could feel the extended burn of his divinity reacting to his emotional state since his mind was not present to guide it. The sky wept tears of rage and continued with its tempest. The earth shook, manic laughter as it split itself, as it remoulded the landscape and began tearing itself apart once more. Even space continued to contort. Misshapen, it wrestled with itself, trying to make sense of its new reality.

Each time he opened his eyes, fatigue reared its head and stared at him.

Phainon could not see the point in refusing it any longer. Suspended in what looked like the end of the world, he simply closed his eyes and leaned into the collapse.

It was difficult to know how long it took for the exhaustion to claim the coreflames as well. But eventually, even they too began to tire.

First, space began to unfurl. Gates closed. What was compressed began to ease, the pressure lifting slowly. The quaking earth’s trembling became soft shakes. And then, they ceased all together. The unruly waters of Aedes Elysiae returned to the same peaceful ebb and flow that remained in half-faded memories.

The rain lightened. The storm settled.

And with a gentle caress of wind, the remaining traces of grey were nudged from sight and the skies of Aedes Elysiae cleared.

Phainon woke to the warmth of sunlight against his cheek and the scratch of fabric across his back.

…Fabric?

Even after this extended period of rest, Phainon’s body still felt heavy. It resisted movement. Even lifting his arm to tug on the fabric felt like a large undertaking.

Pulling it from his body, he was surprised to find that it was a blanket. It felt like wool, but as tired eyes tried to comprehend its sudden existence, he could see that it was more than that. The memory of wool. A blanket stitched from memoria. It was slightly singed but clearly capable of withstanding the heat of Phainon’s wings.

For a moment, all he could do was stare at it.

Then, Phainon wrapped it around his shoulders and burrowed into its warmth. He closed his eyes, not for the sake of rest, but for the sake of bathing in the quiet comfort of something soft and gentle.

When he convinced himself that he should open them again and take in his new surroundings, Phainon was met with a desolate wasteland. Everything was ash. Though the earth had reshaped into something jagged and violent, there was little around but rock and cinders.

Mostly.

Because several feet away, there was a bag. It was an old, fraying thing. Well-loved. Most likely waiting for him.

Wariness caught in his chest.

And curiosity.

His legs shook with each step. By the time he dropped to his knees before the bag, the entirety of his body was trembling. He pulled the blanket closer around his body and just… looked at it. It wasn’t anything special - simple fabric, neutral colouring. The handle was torn at the edges and the threadwork had clearly been loosened under a lifetime of strain.

Someone had loved this to its end. And now it was… here. Waiting for him to find it. To open it.

So he did.

It was not filled with much. A bottle of water. Two rolls of bread, wrapped in brown paper to keep them from growing stale. A yellow chiton, its bright colouring vaguely familiar. A recognisable pair of purple trousers. A teleslate. And lastly, a folded piece of scrap parchment.

Hesitant, he unfolded it.

The writing was both familiar and unfamiliar. Something he had once known as well as his own, and yet, over time, had began to forget.

Phai,

A care package for you. I hope you slept without nightmares. If you need anything - you always know where, in this place, I’ll be. Take your time, my dearest friend, and rest well.

He stared at the words for a long time. Reminded himself to breathe. Closed his eyes and held the note as closely to his chest as he held the blanket.

And when his breathing began to even out, Phainon stood.

Because the note was right - he knew where she would be, and he was not so cruel as to force Cyrene to wait for him any longer than she already had.

Chapter End Notes

Chapter Summary

a meeting in what was once Aedes Elysiae

Chapter Notes

look, phainon and cyrene - to me - are so sibling coded. they love each other so much. i adore them. i want to hug them both and squeeze them and never let go.

Back before they had been forced to watch Aedes Elysiae die, there had only ever been one place that Phainon had needed to search if he’d wanted to find Cyrene: The pond west of the Sacrament Courtyard.

She - and subsequently Phainon himself - had spent so many hours playing in the water and climbing the nearby trees that their parents had decided to spruce the place up for them both. Cyrene’s father had fixed up some old chairs and a table so that they could always draw and write stories within the shade cast by their favourite tree. Phainon’s father, Hieronymus, had climbed up onto the thickest branch, armed with several pieces of rope and tied thick knots around it, using the branch to hold the large swing that he’d carved from leftover wood that had been lying around ever since he'd fixed the hole in their leaking roof.

They had spent their early childhood swinging on it. When they’d been little, it had been big enough for the both of them to sit on, shoulder to shoulder, with plenty of leftover space. As they’d grown, however, it had become Cyrene’s swing. She spent more time patiently swinging, while Phainon - filled with energy and the endless need to tire himself out - had raced through the village and trained his swordsmanship skills.

Whenever she was not busy, she was always there. Swinging. Or writing in her book and designing more oracle cards for her divinations. Or sitting at

the edge of the water, feet submerged, simply enjoying the sunlight that slowly baked them in the oven of summer.

The tree supporting her swing had long since burned down. The table and chairs had decayed - though whether by his hand in this era or the last, he wasn’t sure. Nothing remained but murky water and large deposits of grey ash.

And, of course, Cyrene herself.

She was knelt at the edge of the water, one hand pressed against the earth to keep her balance, the other reaching out into the pond. At first, it was difficult to see what she was doing. It wasn’t until Phainon shuffled closer that he could make out the fact that she’d fashioned a net out of ice and was now scooping debris from the water’s surface.

For a moment, it was too much to simply look at her.

Phainon closed his eyes and pulled the blanket tighter around his shoulders. The earth trembled gently beneath his feet - a minor quake rippling in response to his discomfort.

Cyrene paused.

Then, she turned to face him.

There was no freeze in her expression. No uncertainty. From the second she spotted him, her gaze softened and a warm smile spread across her lips. There was ash in her hair and she looked exhausted, but upon seeing him, there was nothing but clear relief and affection.

“Hey Phai,” she said, without even an inkling of hesitation. “Did you sleep well?”

He stepped closer. Not because he particularly wanted to but because he wasn’t sure whether he’d be able to speak loudly without the words scraping against his throat. A fist clenched the handles of the bag Cyrene

had left with such force that Phainon was surprised it wasn’t merging with his skin.

Had he slept well? Doubtful. All he could really say was that he had slept. There wasn’t much more to it than that. Well? Poorly? Who cared?

“What are you doing?” He asked.

Cyrene shifted as he made his way closer - not in an attempt to get away, or closer, but simply to allow him the space to settle near this pond without being forced to climb over the many  sharp deposits of razored stone that now encased the water. She said, “Filtering the pond.”

Ah.

His fault.

She was stuck trying to undo the mess that he had caused. Phainon had only caused trouble for her in the aftermath of what could only be labelled a tantrum. His foot paused, midair, freezing as if he were the one with an affinity for ice.

This time, the tremble of earth beneath them was enough to stagger him. He tripped, displacing a pile of dust that caught in his chest and left him wheezing around heavy coughs.

Cyrene’s hand pressed into the ground. Half-lifting to her feet, she began to stand—

“Don’t.” He gasped, frantic.

She halted. “Phainon—”

Despite himself, he raised a hand and shooed her away. “Just… Just stay there. I don’t…” He shook his head, trying to speak around his coughs. “Just stay there. Please.”

Cyrene’s smile had dropped. Concern had trickled into the gaps of her furrowed brows and though he could see that she wanted to argue with him,

she slowly lowered back onto her knees. Soft, her voice only a whisper on the wind, she murmured, “Alright. I’ll stay here.”

He didn’t thank her. Just tried to dislodge ash from his chest and settle his rapidly beating heart.

“There’s water in the bag,” Cyrene said, as his hacking continued. “It’ll help.”

He tore into the bag and grabbed the bottle, uncapping the lid and drinking in long gulps. She was right. It helped. Though his throat remained raw, the splash of water helped soothe the ache like a balm.

They fell into silence.

Tucking his knees close to his chest, Phainon pulled the blanket around his body even tighter. It would be impossible, he knew, to hide behind it entirely but the idea of being able to hide even a little helped to settle some of his… rising panic? He wasn’t sure what this tightness in his chest was.

Cyrene’s gaze flicked between him and the blanket. Then, watchful eyes flicked away completely. Gaze averted. A quiet kindness that she had not spoken of, and yet Phainon had identified almost immediately. She’d realised he couldn’t handle her attention, and thus, had removed it.

His shoulders loosened. Strange… he hadn’t realised that they had ever tensed. When had they done that? Maybe when he’d woken… Or when he had opened the bag and found Cyrene’s note hidden inside?

Or had it maybe been when he’d seen her outline and realised that he’d ruined yet another thing for a person he loved— and despised— so deeply?

“Are the clothes I left you alright?” She asked. Perhaps, even without looking at him, she’d identified that his thoughts were beginning to rise like a tidal wave, prepared to pull him under and deemed him in urgent need of distraction. “I thought you might be warmer with them too. Mixed with the blanket, you’ll be nice and toasty.”

The clothes? …What clothes?

Oh. Right. The clothes that had been included in her care package. Bright yellow and deep purple. An outfit that Aglaea would’ve hated. Had hated. Cycle after cycle. Whenever she had seen him show up in such clothing the seamstress had declared him an affront to fashion and decided there and then to sew him a whole new wardrobe.

In this, the goldweaver had seen fit to declare war against his poor fashion choices.

“I thought…” He frowned. “...Aglaea threw them out. Didn’t she?”

“Well, not these ones, no.” Cyrene said, moving her hands so that they rested in her lap. “They’re not the same clothes you wore in the past. But.. they’re pretty close to it, I think? I’m pretty sure they should be your size. They might be a little big, if anything.”

Absently, he pulled out the purple-stained trousers. The fabric was not quite as soft as the blanket around him, but they weren’t coarse either. A little worn. Not brand new. A thumb-sized tear in the leg had been messily stitched back together.

That they weren’t brand new was a relief. And yet, he couldn’t help but feel guilty to receive them regardless. This… wasn’t something he could accept. It didn’t fit the image that he’d been forced to uphold for millenia.

“I can’t wear this,” he said, bitterly. Behind him, his wings flared at the realisation that this was a kindness that he was not supposed to accept. For Okhema’s sake. “They’re not the kind of thing you’d expect an upstanding Chrysos Heir to wear.”

Objectively, he knew why Aglaea had always taken these clothes away from him. There was an image he’d had to uphold and haphazard, second-hand clothing wasn’t a part of that. Pristine white was better for the cause - unmarred by the black tide, untouchable and clean. Gold because it symbolised both the flame chase and his allegiance to the goldweaver. Blue because… well, because it looked good.

Even knowing all this, it was hard not to be angry that he’d not even been allowed to keep this part of his identity. No room for individuality of this kind in any of the flame chase journeys. No joy to be allowed in bright, contrasting colour schemes.

Not that is mattered, anymore. It was difficult to be anything but that perfectly curated role. A fake deliverer not only by prophecy but in costume and personality as well.

Cyrene let out a loud, somewhat overtly dramatic hum. More like she was trying to capture his attention than because she’d seen any actual point in humming.

Phainon glanced up from the trousers and waited.

“Phai,” she said, once she was certain she held his focus. “Do you still like brightly coloured things?”

…Did he?

Phainon wasn’t sure. He hadn’t thought about it in… a truly long time. He’d always been stoking his rage and that had meant bathing in hate and reminding himself of everything he loathed. Focusing on things that he liked would’ve been counterproductive. Somewhere within the cycles he’d started to forget any of the details that humanised himself.

Did he like bright colours? Well, he didn’t hate them. Was that the same thing? He didn’t know.

“I don’t…” His brows dipped, the beginning of stress curling his shoulders. “...really remember.”

Cyrene lifted a hand to her cheek. As she always did when thinking deeply over something she thought was of great importance, she tapped the pads of her fingers against her cheek. As a child, she’d said it was to stimulate her thoughts. As an adult, she stuck by the same words, though they both knew it was just a habit with no further meaning.

“Alright,” she said. “Let’s start a little smaller, then. Do you want to wear these? Or would you prefer it if I collected something from your current wardrobe?”

“Aglaea—”

“—Isn’t here,” Cyrene said, both firm and gentle. “It’s just us. What do you want to do?”

Phainon reached into the bag and pulled out the chiton. He stared at fabric that looked like it’d bathed in sunlight until it’d absorbed the colour into each thread. It was old, and yet, it looked like the colour had never once dared to fade.

From yellow chiton, to purple pants. He looked between each as if Cyrene had asked the world of him. Had asked him to solve some intangible problem that was incomprehensible, impossible to even begin solving.

He closed his eyes. Breathed in deeply and held the air in his lungs. Which option would he hate less? The options left him feeling both exhausted and... and strange, so it was just a matter of choosing the least uncomfortable option.

He breathed out a sigh. Ran his fingers across old seams and steeled himself.

Then, he made a decision.

One that did not regard deliverance, or the fate of Amphoreus, but rather something that solely regarded himself. Who he was.

“...I still like bright colours,” he decided. Hesitant, yet also tinged with the finality of someone who had just stumbled upon one of the truths of their own being.

When he opened his eyes again, Cyrene was grinning. Unabashed, her expression was as warm as moonlight. Gentle in much the same way as the blanket around him felt.

“Then,” she said, “I’ll close my eyes and you can go put those on, alright?”

“I—”

“Unless,” Cyrene continued, grin widening, “we want to go find something even brighter.”

His lips quirked for half of a moment, before falling flat. He shook his head. No. These would be fine.

“Or,” Cyrene continued, “you can just stay wrapped up in the blanket. That’s an option as well. It’s up to you.”

Phainon let out a half-sigh.

It shouldn’t have been this hard to salvage parts of himself, his own wants, but here he was, clearly struggling. It was exhausting. He’d just slept for… however long he’d slept, and he’d only managed to wake more tired than when he’d fallen asleep.

Another sigh. It was a full thing, now.

“I’ll wear them," he said. "Close your eyes.”

He reverted back into a more human form and got changed.

If he tried to don them while still wearing this divine form, the clothes would simply melt from his skin like butter against flame. After all, unlike the blanket, this new outfit wasn’t reinforced with memoria.

Once dressed - his wings tucked away for another day, the coreflames stored away and now much less reactive to his emotions - he padded back towards Cyrene, wearing the blanket around him like a shield.

The trousers were too short on his legs. The fabric of the chiton was loose around the biceps. Phainon probably looked ridiculous.

Yet, this outfit felt a million times more comfortable than the clinical clothing of Amphoreus’ ‘Deliverer’.

“So,” Phainon said, quietly, as he returned to her side. He hesitated several steps away, unsure whether he could force himself closer. “What now?”

“Hm?” Cyrene tilted her head towards him, half opening her eyes.

“You didn’t come all this way to bring me clothes and ask what colours I like,” Phainon said. “So… what next?”

She didn’t say anything, not at first. Instead, Cyrene patted the earth beside her, a mushroom cloud of dust and ash whooshing into the air at the movement.

Phainon squinted at the ground as if it was going to morph into a horrifying beast. .

Then, reluctance showing in the heavy dragging of his feet, he sat beside her. His knees were pulled close to his chest, arms wrapped around them protectively. Resting his chin on his knees, he stared out at stagnant water. He could see physical clumps of ash floating atop it like a film. Either the clumps hadn’t been in the water long enough to settle, or the pond was simply that full of waste that it could not be poisoned any further.

“That depends on you, really,” Cyrene said. “I’m not going to ask if you don’t want me to.”

He didn’t.

Since he’d been awake, his mind - while scraped raw from the weight of his own rage and grief - had been wrapped inside of what he could only describe as a bubble. Trapped inside, everything felt… distant. Far away.

He could feel the heat of his own rage, but there was a disconnect. Though he knew it was there, it was as if his connection to it had been halted, momentarily. All he felt now, was tired. Worn.

If he talked about it, then he’d burst the bubble and everything would come crashing back. Later he would ask. Later he would learn everything he could about what had happened while he’d slept and explain what had happened on his side, but right now…

“Don’t ask me about it,” Phainon mumbled.

“Alright,” Cyrene said, “I won’t.”

Hesitant, she lowered her head onto his shoulder. Together, they stared at what remained of their home, a landscape that was as unwelcoming as every one of their previous experiences. They lapsed into a silence that was only interrupted by a docile breeze.

An age later, Phainon tilted his head and let it rest against Cyrene’s. He closed his eyes.

“What are you thinking about?” Cyrene asked him.

Honestly… not much. His thoughts remained as thick as syrup. They all existed outside of this bubble of dissociation. Currently, the only thing he could think of was how thoroughly drained he felt.

Not just physically, but mentally.

“...I’m so tired,” he murmured.

Cyrene reached for his hand. Clasped their fingers together and admitted, in a voice far more serious than he’d have expected from her, “Me too.”

“It was too much to bear,” Phainon continued.

“It was,” she agreed.

When he sighed, it was just as light as the breeze around them. A whisper against the wind. She squeezed his hand, and he— after some hesitation— squeezed back.

More silence.

“I just want to rest,” Phainon admitted.

Another hand squeeze. “Then let's go back. You can climb into bed, and I’ll keep guard over your room to make sure no one disturbs you.”

He wasn’t sure whether he was ready to leave this place yet. To return to Okhema and face his fellow Heirs. To face his friends and the questions they no doubt held for him.

“Cyrene?” He murmured.

“Yes?”

“...You don’t need to guard my room.” Her hold on his hand loosened, as if to pull away. He tightened his own hold so that she couldn’t let go. “But… Can you stay for a while? I don’t…”

He couldn’t get the words out. That she’d offered him the first semblance of choice, of comfort, that he’d felt he was able to take in millenia. That he wasn’t willing to let that disappear just yet.

“I’ll stay,” Cyrene promised.

Breath rushed from his lungs with heavy relief.

“Well then,” she continued, voice no louder than a whisper. “Should we go home?”

chapters.title: Chapter 12
chapters.html:
Chapter Summary

phainon and cyrene return to okhema. they rest. they talk. there are glitches.

Chapter Notes

maaan, i wanted to get this out sooner but i was struck with a bunch of fatigue this week. work really has a way of draining you out, huh? or well, it does to me. anyway, i hope you all enjoy!! i like this chapter a lot, actually.

In the end, their return to Okhema was quite underwhelming.

After a final, solemn farewell to the empty space of Aedes Elysiae, Phainon rid space of any remaining crinkles and proceeded to open an infinity gate that led to his Okheman quarters.

Through the gate, his room was exactly as he’d left it: Closed curtains. The space dimly lit and leaving the room dull and lifeless. Dust had yet to settle but even still the room looked stifling and aged - the only sign of life being that of his unmade duvet, thrown over his mattress with little care of whether the bed was properly made or not.

Phainon tightened his hold on Cyrene’s hand and stepped through the gate.

When the gate closed behind them both, Phainon’s room became much darker. Little light settled around them and the only thing that Phainon could see clearly was the mattress. It beckoned him closer like an old friend.

Phainon shuffled forwards. Didn’t even lift his feet properly as he moved, weighed down by exhaustion as they were.

When he reached the mattress, he collapsed onto it, surrendering himself to gravity.

Cyrene, still holding his hand, was pulled along with him. She yelped, weight falling entirely onto Phainon, who let out a loud grunt as his breath caught in his throat. He face planted his pillow at force. Cyrene’s elbow split his side with such force that he gasped.

For a moment, they both existed in silence. Cyrene, blinking at the wall as if trying to process what had just happened. Phainon, trying to catch his breath.

Then, Cyrene broke into a breathless set of giggles.

Phainon didn’t laugh but his lips twitched with the beginning of something that could one day evolve into a smile.

“Some warning next time, please?”

Yeah, maybe. He was definitely going to have an elbow-shaped bruise across his ribs. And a Cyrene-shaped bruise on his back.

“Mmph,” he breathed into his pillow, closing his eyes.

“Are you alright?”

Another ‘mmph’ into his pillow.

“No clue what that means,” Cyrene continued, lying beside him. Then, she began wriggling, trying to settle comfortably. A task made more difficult by the fact that her hand was currently being held prisoner by Phainon’s own. The position she settled on was an awkward thing - jutting his elbow out at an acute angle that reminded him of a chicken’s wing. “But I’m going to assume that you’re not dying and that you’re fine.”

Phainon nodded into his pillow, and then, considering how uncomfortable their current positioning on the bed was, proceeded to drag Cyrene closer. Once she was close enough, he freed her hand and threw an arm over her shoulder.

A breath caught in her throat. Torn from Cyrene in a way that was purely accidental - instinctual and without any forethought. Her body tensed, momentarily, as if even she’d been caught off guard by her reaction.

Phainon froze. Then, he began to lift his arm.

A hand whipped out and grabbed hold of his wrist before he could pull away entirely. Then, whispering, Cyrene said, “Phai?”

“Yeah?” He murmured, half into his pillow, half towards her. Guilt tried to swim in his voice but he forced it away before it could settle. Some things were only meant to be felt internally - his guilt wasn’t something to plague others with.

“Can I hug you?”

It was phrased as if it were just like any other question. As if it were not important. And yet, there was a quake to Cyrene’s voice, a thick loneliness to it that she’d been unable to hide entirely. And in that way it ceased to be a question, instead shifting into a quiet plea. He had little doubt that this was a question she’d been wanting to ask for a very long time. Perhaps millions of years.

Phainon couldn’t quite bring himself to answer her with words. The idea of answering without the sincerity that Cyrene deserved in this moment was so overwhelming that nausea settled in his stomach. She deserved kindness, and understanding - not the ruin and bitterness that festered in his soul.

Even after seeing what he had done to Aedes Elysiae, she was still requesting comfort from him? That was foolish of her. Stupid. It warmed him and he wasn’t sure whether it was in a good way or a way that filled him with dread.

Instead of speaking, he raised his arm and held it in place, leaving Cyrene enough space to shuffle up to his side.

It took her a few moments to move. When she did, it was first with the slowness of someone waiting to see if the gesture would be rescinded.

Then, upon realising that he would not drop his arm before she could cross said barrier, she moved with a speed that sang of the end of an eternal wait.

Cyrene’s arms wrapped around Phainon’s waist, her forehead pressed against his collarbone, holding him as tightly as she possibly could. It was as if she were worried that, at any moment, he might disappear like a memory on the wind.

Phainon lowered his arm around her and, though he had noted it, did not mention how her shoulders had begun to shake. Instead, he murmured, “Get some rest.”

“You too,” Cyrene said, in a voice both thick with unshed tears and bursting with inconceivable joy. “Sweet dreams, Phainon.”

Between periods of sleep, whenever wakefulness caught hold of him, Cyrene informed Phainon of what he had missed.

Squinting at rays of sun that had broken through the gaps of his curtains, he forced glassy, sleep-filled eyes onto a tangle of pink hair and tried his best to ignore how the sun bathed the room in fire and burning fields of wheat.

“You were gone for six days,” Cyrene told him, when finally he asked. It was between his second and third attempt at sleep. His stomach squirmed, sharp nails digging into his intestines.

Almost a week of… of what? A tantrum?

It was a week that he could have spent rebuilding Okhema.

“Six?” He murmured, dull and dispassionate.

“Yes.” Cyrene, bless her, was doing her best to filter the worry from her voice. It manifested instead in the way she rubbed circles into the back of his hand with her thumb.

What a waste of time.

And yet, even knowing he’d wasted so much time, there was little want to get out of bed and make up for it. He should’ve been pulling his weight, taking the time to fulfill the duties that had been passed onto him as a Chrysos Heir. Instead, Phainon could not bring himself to do anything but close his eyes.

He simply held his best friend closely in his arms and let out a long sigh.

“Did you spend all that time sleeping?” Cyrene asked. Her voice was gentle. She continued to work circles into his hand. Phainon’s thumb twitched as if to copy the task, before falling still. Best not to try. He didn’t want to hurt her.

He hummed, managing a half nod. Sleep’s outstretched hand was similar to Cyrene’s and he fell back into another doze with the sensation of her hand in his.

Between naps, he learned more.

Cyrene had been with Castorice when it had all happened. The pair had been taking a break, talking over poorly brewed tea - Cyrene had tried her best but she was shockingly out of practice - and rating their favourite romance novel tropes. Then the sky outside of Okhema had lit with a streak of fire so bright that it could have been confused for starlight.

Of course, Chrysos Heirs that they were, the pair had done what no sane person would: They had run towards the perceived danger. Through crumbling streets, along the path of parting and towards an expanse of field that now had gouges of earth ripped free from its core.

The field was also burning.

Not good. Especially since, in the middle of the flames, protected by a ring of water, were the frozen bodies of Mydeimos and Anaxagoras.

Not frozen in ice but in time.

While Castorice had not known what she was looking at, Cyrene had known from a single glance. There weren’t many people who could alter time like this within Amphoreus. The answer of ‘this must’ve been Phainon’s doing’ wasn’t hard to settle on. Knowing Mydei and Anaxa, they had likely pushed too far and this was the result.

The why hadn’t been important to Cyrene at the time. What mattered more to her, then, had been the where.

Where, exactly, had Phainon gone in the aftermath?

“Of course that wasn’t hard to figure out either,” Cyrene murmured. At this point in her story telling, they’d shifted on the bed. Cyrene sat against the wall and Phainon lay with his head in her lap. Her fingers carded through his hair, gentle, detangling any knots and kinks. “Ever since we were little, you’d always go to this same wheatfield on the southernmost edge of the village whenever you were overwhelmed. Since you can open gates, why wouldn’t you have gone there?”

Subsequently, she’d asked Trianne to transport her to Aedes Elysiae as well.

It was at this point that the others realised - in part - what must have happened. Things had gotten loud. Concerned. Without Mydei and Anaxa around to explain, they had little explanation available.

Yet, the explanation didn’t matter.

All that mattered was finding him. A gate was opened and…

And that was when Cyrene had realised that things hadn’t just gone a little wrong, a momentary dispute or argument bubbling over, but that something very bad had happened. More extreme. Less overfilling a cup with water and spilling the remains, and more… shattering said glass under the weight of a waterfall.

Because… Trianne’s open infinity gate did not open the way that it should have.

The gate had rippled. Liquid silver showing an image of an Aedes Elysiae that was actively tearing itself apart. The sky snarled. The ground buckled. Past the opening in space, they could see other gaps leading to places that the brain couldn’t fully comprehend. Space was contorting on the other side of the gate.

One moment, they were just observers. Then, the destruction caught hold of Trianne’s infinity gate too and its shadow began to creep through the opening. It dug claws into the ground around them and seeped through with a roar. The edges of space sharpened and curled. It moved in ways that were not tangible.

Their gate, infested as it had become, glistened with unshed tears as instability bled into Okhema and began to shake the earth. Heat leaked through the open expanse between city and village and began to burn. The air was static with electricity so intense that it sparked thunderclouds into being, a storm biting at the skies of Okhema and settling there as if it belonged.

“Trianne had to close the gate so that nothing else could break through,” Cyrene said, with a sigh. “And we had to wait.”

“I didn’t mean for it to reach Okhema,” Phainon murmured.

“I know.” Her fingers paused in his hair but she didn’t pull away. Less like she was rescinding her kindness and more like she’d stopped in an attempt to think more on her words. “Past what broke through we only felt small quakes and rain. And what did break through didn’t stay for too long. Just a day or two. Everything else was contained to Aedes Elysiae.”

Phainon breathed out a sigh.

More mess. All his fault.

And yet, still, he couldn’t bring himself to care.

He would start caring again later. It was a promise. When the tiredness left him, when he didn’t feel so far removed from his body that emotion began to feel like it could sit right in his body, he’d try. For now, he closed his eyes and bathed in the comfort of Cyrene’s presence.

She returned to running her fingers through his hair, and Phainon slept.

Sometimes, Cyrene was not there when he woke and Phainon would find himself alone, wrapped in a bundle of memoria and blanket.

She always made sure to tell him in advance, of course. A note left on the bedside table, written in bright pink ink that seemed to shine like ice in the dark of the room. There was always a half-remembered memory of the warning being uttered after a gentle shake to his shoulder had roused him enough to receive a hum of acknowledgement, half-awake. Always a warning to explain that she’d left to get food, or because her duties had called and she couldn’t step out on all of them.

He never thought twice about where she was going because that wasn’t important. He didn’t care why she was leaving. All that mattered was the promise that she was coming back.

Still… It was difficult to exist in this space without Cyrene there to ground him.

The first few times, he managed to slip back into unconsciousness before it became too difficult. He woke, and Cyrene was not there so he slept.

Except, this time, after the second nap, she was not there either.

This time, when Phainon woke to an empty room, his perfect bubble of disassociation thinned to such a degree that it felt like it had popped. Heat spread through him, hatred catching hold of his soul like a flare, filling both his room and lungs with smoke.

He burned through several layers of mattress. His pillow incinerated to ash. Phainon choked on a laugh, or a cry, and stared silently at his wall with wide-eyes until, in her absence, the world once again began to glitch.

It was as if his mind, seeing how desperately he wanted the comfort Cyrene brought him, had decided that it would be better to fill the room with countless copies of her. The room dripped with her blood. The burnt mattress glitched until, horrified, Phainon crawled out from a pile of her burning bodies.

A shattered version of Cyrene stared from behind the mirror.

And then, after he’d launched a shoe towards the wall, his chest heaving, dead eyes stared at him from the hundreds of shards he’d created.

Cyrene - the real one, probably - had returned to smoke. To shattered vases that had once mattered so much but no longer held any worth. To Phainon in the middle of the room, covered in soot and unable to breathe properly as he pulled and pulled on the loose threads of the Deliverer’s clothing, tearing them to pieces.

He did not hear her return.

He did not realise she was there until a balm of ice had settled over his burning skin, holding his shoulders firmly. Then, her frantic voice reached his ears. His name, repeated. Over and over. And he’d realised she wasn’t a memory but something real. All the other Cyrene’s burned. The real one was accompanied with frostbite.

“Cyrene,” he gasped, and threw himself into her arms.

She wasn’t ready to take the brunt of his weight. Together they toppled onto the ground. Phainon’s hand cupped her head to keep her skull from cracking open on the harsh floor. The glitch of gold blood on his hands disappeared in a string of dispersed code.

Now that she was back, the dead Cyrene’s in his vision were clearly dolls. They hardly looked like her at all. He choked on a bitter laugh and closed his eyes so that he couldn’t see them anymore.

“Phainon.” Cyrene said, voice shrill and panicked. “What happened? Are you—” A pause. Then, as she pulled him close into her arms, “I’m back. I’m here. You’re alright now.”

She repeated the words and he held her with a tightness that must’ve been painful but she didn’t comment on it.

When they settled, Phainon half-slumped against her shoulder, he murmured, “Cyrene?”

“Yes?” The worry was still there. And fear. She was scared but he couldn’t think of why she would be. He hadn’t done anything to make her feel unsafe, had he? If not, then why would she be scared?

“Is any of this…” He crinkled his nose. Disassociation was beginning to catch in his eyes again like mist. “Is any of this even… real?”

“Any of this…?”

“The Era Nova,” he elaborated, staring at the shards of glass past her shoulder and all of Cyrene’s additional eyes trapped within them. “It’s not just in my head, is it?”

When he managed to tear his focus from the glass back onto Cyrene, she looked seconds away from tears. Her pupils wobbled with flickers of light caught in the ocean of her stare.

“Yes,” she said, voice cracking under the weight of her own sorrow. “It’s real. It’s not just in your head. I promise.”

He couldn’t think of any reason why she would lie. Not when looking as distraught as she was. And either way…

Either way, he knew what Cyrene looked like when she lied. Her nose twitched. Her right brow would dip, minutely. She wasn’t doing any of these things - therefore, she must’ve been telling the truth.

(Or, at least, she thought that this was all real.)

“Alright,” he said, numbly.

“Does it not feel real?” Cyrene asked.

He wasn’t sure. Maybe in the beginning, when Stelle had been present it had felt real - because it was impossible to make someone like Stelle up. She wasn’t fiction in the way the people of Amphoreus were. Her and Dan Heng and the other outsiders from the Astral Express. They felt real because they were unfamiliar.

They were unknown variables. With them gone…

“I don’t know,” he said. It was better than saying ‘no’. “Sometimes it’s…”

He paused.

Shook his head.

He couldn’t immediately find the words and he was too tired to try, so why bother?

“I don’t know.” He said. And then, “You promise that this is real?”

“Yes,” Cyrene said. Tears spilled from her eyes, finally, no longer able to contain them. “It’s real.”

Phainon’s fingers twitched by his sides. He reached a hand up and wiped them away with his thumb. He murmured, “Why are you crying?”

“Because you aren’t,” she said. “Because you won’t.” She paused, her lips wobbling. “It’s real. I promise this is real. We made it. Our plan worked.”

He wiped away more tears. Then, he pulled Cyrene back into his arms and held her while she cried all of the tears that he could not.

“I believe you,” he murmured.

He didn’t know whether he was telling the truth or not.
