chapters.html:
Chapter Notes

should be resting, probably, but hey guess what. i wanted to upload this chapter regardless. i like writing. it's like a secret medicine for the soul. anyway, i hope y'all enjoy this update. i enjoyed writing it.

cutiepie on twt has created some wonderful art for moments from ch11 and ch12. and also for a moment from this chapter too, but i'll put THAT link in the end notes!!

anyway. yeah. look at how long this one is in comparison to the other chapters. are y'all proud of me? i'm proud of myself. haha.

Once her tears had dried and the burn of rosy cheeks had settled, Cyrene pulled Phainon to his feet and fashioned his blanket around his shoulders like a protective shield.

“I know you’d rather go back to sleep,” she murmured, when he let out a sigh in protest, wavering on uneasy legs, “but we really can’t stay here. There’s too much smoke and soot. It’s not safe.”

Phainon blinked at her, blankly. Then with a sigh, he said, “Where are we going?”

“Silly question,” Cyrene said. “If not your room, then obviously we’ll go to mine.”

He pulled on his coreflames until space felt malleable enough to open a gate between the two rooms. Then, Phainon paused, his brows furrowing into a deep v-shape. It was all fine preparing to warp space, but he didn’t know where to place the receiving gate. He didn’t actually know where Cyrene’s room was.

Had she ever told him? No. Probably not. There hadn’t been a need. Phainon didn’t know where to find any of the Chrysos Heirs. Which was kind of stupid, actually, because avoiding them would’ve been a thousand times easier if he’d had any idea of where they find them at any one time.

He released his hold on his coreflames, letting the power dissipate back into his blood. Then, he dropped his hand back to his side, limp and useless.

“Alright,” Phainon murmured.

He cast a final glance around his room. Cyrene had been right - it really wasn’t inhabitable anymore. His mattress had been reduced to cinders. The ceiling had been coated in black. The room - once a place of life, had been reduced to a burnt home of torn thread, broken ceramic and smashed glass.

Titans, he’d really made a mess of things, hadn’t he?

Why…

Why had he done that? Why had he gotten so angry that he’d torn this place of comfort to pieces?

…It didn’t matter. It would, later, but right now he hardly felt anything at all. Just a nothingness in his chest as he stared at the destruction he’d wrought.

Cyrene smoothed out the edges of Phainon’s blanket one final time. Then, she took his hand and led him from the room, closing the door behind them with a muffled thud. Other than a layer of soot on the door handle there was little indication of the ruin that lay within.

They stepped out into a long corridor of apartments that overlooked the square leading to Dawncloud. Through sunbleached pillars they could see the movement of civilians in the plaza - some wandering to and fro, going about their daily business, and others making themselves comfortable on the patch of grass at its center to bathe in the sun and peace that Okhema had been gifted with.

Phainon, unused to it all, reared back from rays of sun and lifted a hand to cover his eyes. It must’ve been the middle of the day; The temperature was blistering in a way that was only experienced during the Action hour.

“It’s this way,” Cyrene said, once his eyes had stopped watering from the sudden shift in brightness. There was no rush to her steps. It made it easier for his own lead-lined body to stumble beside her without too much protest.

This area wasn’t one that Phainon was too familiar with.

Well - as unfamiliar as anything could be after billions of years worth of memories within Okhema. It wasn’t an area that he’d spent many years living within. There were two main places he had lived within the city: The Okheman barracks, among his peers in the army and, after being scouted by Aglaea, a room in the western corner of Marmoreal Palace.

The residential district nearby the entrance to Dawncloud hadn’t fallen within the purview of ‘home’. He’d frequented the area in the past but only ever with the intent to visit. Even now, with his quarters here, he knew it was only temporary. He’d probably be relocated again once the city was renovated.

“Is it far?”

Cyrene halted mid-step and turned him towards the balcony. Past the plaza’s grassy center, there were multiple apartment buildings similar to the one they stood within - all painted white, with long swooping arches leading into corridors that overlooked the nearby streets. Many of them were lined with different colours of bunting. Orange. Lilac. Blue. Identical buildings told apart by this simple splash of colour.

“Across the grass,” Cyrene said, pointing towards one of the buildings. “The one with the blue bunting. That’s where we’re going.”

It wasn’t anything more than a short walk.

And yet it felt as if she were asking him to walk miles.

“I’ll open a gate—”

Cyrene cut him off with a soft shake of her head, squeezing his hand. “I know you’re tired, but a walk might do us both some good. What do you think?”

He stared at Cyrene’s apartment building with the blue bunting and then let his gaze flick down to the plaza before it. Phainon’s lips twisted into something reminiscent of a grimace. He said, “There are people down there.”

“There are,” Cyrene agreed, with a shrug. “Does that matter?”

Of course it did. Phainon didn’t have the energy to play nice and be the fake Deliverer that they all thought him to be. It took effort that he just… couldn’t bring himself to expend. The people of Okhema expected him to be put together at all times, ready to lead them into a bright future. To be eager to do so.

The only thing that Phainon was eager to do, was curl up in bed with his blanket and sleep even longer than he already had. Social politics and responsibility was just another hindrance waiting to drain him.

If people saw him as he currently was… what would they think? Wrapped in his blanket, wearing horribly mismatched clothing, his body covered in soot. If they looked at him and saw that his eyes were glazed over with a distance that could not hide his detachment from the city he’d sworn to protect then they would only be disappointed.

The whole point of being forced onto the pedestal of Deliverer was that he would give the people of Okhema hope. That he would free them all from any dismay that ailed them.

“When they see me like this, they’ll…”

Cyrene squeezed his hand again as he trailed off. Her smile was minute, her eyes sad. “When they see you, they’ll be glad to see that their saviour is taking the time to recuperate after saving the world.”

Right.

But… he wasn’t their saviour. Stelle was. She was the true Deliverer.

Phainon was just the one who had held onto the role until she arrived and could inherit it. It’d never truly been his. Phainon had always just been a placeholder until the real deal had shown up.

But he couldn’t say that. He knew that the second he tried, Cyrene would chide him for it. Tell him not to underplay his part in everything. She’d keep trying to convince him that after all of this he was a hero and not one of Amphoreus’ villains.

(He’d bought them all time, yes, but he could’ve been kinder while doing so. Even Phainon knew that much.)

Now wasn’t the time to say any of this.

“Cyrene,” he murmured instead, “I’m not even wearing shoes.”

“Oh, well that’s easy to solve.” Cyrene let go of his hand and unclasped her sandals. Slipped out of them without a second thought. Once she’d leaned down to collect them, sandals dangling from her fingers, she reclaimed his hand. “If I’m not wearing shoes either, then people will hardly judge the both of us, right?”

A cold thumb began rubbing circles into his skin once more.

Of course, Phainon was still hesitant. Why wouldn’t he be? The walk felt less like it would take them five minutes and more like Cyrene had asked him to commit to something that would take five cycles.

But… Cyrene was trying.

Even he could see that much.

Since she’d tracked him down to Aedes Elysiae and left a care package beside his sleeping body, she’d been accommodating his needs without a single complaint. It mustn’t have been easy, dealing with him day in and out. Offering him care when he wasn’t able to reciprocate it.

He’d not been able to voice his appreciation to her yet. So… Phainon could at least try his best to meet what requests she did make without being too difficult. Even if he was reluctant, a little walk was hardly going to hurt.

Phainon didn’t exactly care about helping himself, but he could try if that was what Cyrene wanted.

“Alright,” he sighed.

They trudged down the corridor, sedate and unhurried. Climbed down stairs as if descending a mountain. Headed out into the plaza as if exploring a new, hostile land. Phainon’s shoulders were hunched, muscles pulled taut as he fought to avoid eye contact with any passersby.

Cyrene, noticing his apprehension, began to fill the silence. Her voice washing over him like a gentle balm designed to keep him from getting trapped within his own anxieties. “You know, I’ve been messaging March 7th a lot since the express left. She’s got so many recommendations of movies and magazines from all around the cosmos. Did you know that directors hire out whole planets for the duration of filming. The planet becomes one huge set. Isn’t that insane?”

Phainon tried to focus on Cyrene’s voice.

Tried to ignore the way that heads turned towards them.

At one point, he made eye contact with an older man with hair greying at the roots who lifted a hand in a wave, and Phainon flinched back from the attention before he could begin to think. A bunch of children started pointing at them and Phainon found himself infinitely glad he no longer needed to eat, or drink, because nausea flooded his stomach and he wanted nothing more than to hide.

Cyrene must’ve noticed the rising tension in his body, because she picked up her pace without a word.

Objectively, Phainon knew it would be better to pull back his shoulders and stand straight. To force a smile onto his lips and pretend that everything - that he - was fine. But he just… couldn’t. Instead, he curled his shoulders and offered his best attempt at becoming invisible.

“And she’s also been introducing me to new music, too,” Cyrene continued. If her voice was a little louder in an attempt to distract him further, then Phainon wasn’t going to be the one to point it out. “One of the artists, Robin, is apparently super nice and totally talented. The Astral Express helped her planet too. When we get back, I’ll play you some of her songs. The music isn’t like what we’re used to here. It’s more… peppy and upbeat! You’ll love it!”

He leaned into the sound of her voice.

Lost himself in the feel of grass beneath his feet.

Tilted his head to stare at the ground so he could avoid the watchful gazes of the people around him and wished for time to speed up so that they could reach the end of the plaza as soon as possible.

It didn’t.

Unfortunately, it appeared as if toying with time was something that required conscious thought.

And the second he tried using the coreflames consciously, Cyrene would absolutely know it. He wouldn’t even have plausible deniability - she’d see right through him to the rising sparks of gold in his eyes.

“See, I told you it wouldn’t take long at all,” Cyrene said, tearing him from the depths of his own thoughts. He glanced up to blue bunting and a welcoming shade. “Wasn’t even five minutes.”

Phainon swallowed a sigh and instead tried to smile. He said, “It didn’t take long at all.”

It felt as if it’d been an age.

“Come on,” she said. “Let’s head inside.”

Cyrene’s quarters seemed far more lived in than Phainon’s had ever been.

In one corner, scrolls had been piled haphazardly on a desk, kept in perfect rolls by fraying strings that had clearly seen better days. In another, she had pushed a sofa up to the wall nearest the window. It was an inviting thing, plump cushions buried beneath multiple blankets.

Before it, a small table housed a lifetime of memories. Memoria given photographic form - mostly snapshots of moments not from the cycles but from the days following their end. A smiling Cyrene stood with the Astral Express members. Another photo with groups of the heirs.

The only photo that was clearly from within the cycles were the photos of the two of them. Of Cyrene and Khaslana. One when they’d been gap-toothed children sat side by side on their swing. Which could’ve been from any cycle, really. Another from what was clearly the first - the pair of them in Okhema. Brightly smiling - Cyrene in her priestess clothing, Phainon in the uniform of the Okheman army.

A time before the Flamechase had asked their active participation.

Phainon’s gaze flicked between all of the photos, almost unseeing. Of all the things to remember… Well.. he supposed these weren’t the worst photos in the world.

Cyrene led him to the sofa, pushing him gently onto the seat.

As he sunk into the cushions and the comfort they provided, Cyrene moved to closed curtains. The rails rattled as she threw them open, bathing the room in gold highlights. Phainon squinted, lifting his hand and throwing it over his eyes with a groan.

“Oh, come on it’s not that bad,” Cyrene said, with a small laugh. “Light is good for you. Staying in the dark isn’t healthy, you know.”

She pulled on the window frame until it slid free.

“Plus, I need to air this place out,” she continued. “It’s been a while since I’ve been here. The draft is extremely welcome.”

Phainon didn’t say anything. Simply toppled to the side against the many pillows on the sofa with a faint sigh. The light wasn’t particularly unwelcome. After all, he’d never really spent much time resting beneath the sun within the cycles as either Khaslana or as Phainon, so arguably it was a nice change of pace.

“I’ll close them again in a while, if you want me to,” Cyrene said.

“It’s alright,” he said, and wrapped his arms around one of the pillows. The edge dug into his cheek, like a dimple, and when he closed his eyes the emptiness that met him was tinged with orange. Less like the burn of a flame and more like the skies of a falling sunset. “I don’t mind.”

“As long as you’re sure.”

He hummed.

The room fell quiet. A lack of conversation as Cyrene went about her own business, leaving him to rest. Just soft footsteps as she moved back and forth. The sound of running water and then glasses being placed nearby. The scrape of a chair being pulled back. The unfurling of parchment.

Usually, he’d have fallen asleep by now.

Instead, he was wholly motionless. Leaning against pillows, atop blankets. Thinking of nothing at all, just listening to Cyrene’s movements, bathing in the rays of sun that had been welcomed into this room. Simply… existing.

It was…

Arguably, he’d call it nice. Existing here without any expectations. Without being forced into conversation he didn’t want to have. Without being asked about what had happened to make reality feel false, like it was seconds away from fracturing.

She was giving him the space he needed. From herself. From their fellow heirs. From Amphoreus.

…Because he was taking the time to recuperate after helping to save the world, was it?

She’d said it as if it was warranted. He wasn’t sure whether it was or not but if she was buying him the time to do so, then it was only right that he make use of what she had given him. That meant trying. He couldn’t spend all of this time sleeping. Surely he needed to do more?

Though… He wasn’t sure what exactly trying meant anymore. Not in this capacity.

He’d figure it out. Just like he’d figured everything else out. Start with something small and… well. Build on it from there.

“You were going to show me music from another planet?” He murmured into the quiet.

“Oh,” Cyrene said, surprise colouring her voice. She’d probably expected him to have fallen back to sleep by now. Or maybe she simply hadn’t thought he’d ask, that her words had fallen onto deaf ears earlier when he’d stopped responding to her words. “Yeah, of course. Robin, right? You want to listen now?”

Phainon opened a single eye. When it became clear that he held her attention, he nodded.

“Alright.” She was beaming. A bright, wide-eyed smile as she reached for her teleslate. “Oh, let me think which song to show you first. From her latest album, maybe? Or maybe—”

She was rambling, scrolling through tracks as she struggled to decide on which album to show him first. Eyes crinkling, both opened and forgoing sleep for a little longer, he watched his friend mumble about tracks and whether it was best to show her favourite or the fan favourite.

Finally, she managed to choose.

“Ah, here,” she said at last, pressing play.

A bounce of sound washed through the room. Synthetic but not in a way that seemed false. Rather, it seemed energetic. A steady beat of drums that could be mistaken for clapping hands. A warm voice filled with joy. And… something else. Not a lyre. Definitely strings, but deeper than the stringed instruments of Amphoreus. Cyrene sang along and fumbled over lyrics she hadn’t yet memorised, bopping her head to the beat.

Utterly foreign. It was unlike anything he’d heard in his billions of years.

Something wholly new.

“What do you think? Do you like it?” Cyrene asked, as the track flowed into the next.

Phainon let out a small sigh. The tiniest of smiles tugged at his lips. He said, “Yeah, I like it.”

“Then I guess we’re having an impromptu concert?” she asked.

“Seems like it,” he murmured.

The next time he woke, night had set in.

He didn’t remember falling asleep. Just remembered the steady beat of another planet’s melody and a voice that made the world feel a little more real. Music was still playing, although now it had shifted from Robin’s music into someone else’s. Also unfamiliar. This song was even softer, more like a lullaby designed for sweet dreams.

Candles had been placed on the table, flickering inside the room like friendly stars in the sea of night. One larger candle was scented, circumventing the smell of burning that had been brought on by the various tealights. A familiar scent. Fruity. Pomegranates.

Phainon’s eyelids lifted, lazily, as his gaze went in search of Cyrene. She sat at her desk, nursing a cup that had steam rising over the edges, leaning over one of her scrolls. Wholly engrossed, he doubted it could have been anything but a romance novel.

Best not to distract her while she was reading. She’d always hated being interrupted in the past. Whenever he’d dragged her attention away at the best parts of the romance, her cheeks would always go splotchy in her anger and she’d beat her fists against his arm in her indignation until he’d taken Snowy and raced away.

‘Can’t you let the princess receive her confession in peace!’ He could practically hear the words as if they’d been uttered yesterday.

He’d forgotten about that. It was strange that he was only just remembering it now. Weird that he was remembering it at all.

Phainon didn’t exactly want to interrupt so he shut his eyes instead.

He was just beginning to drift off once again when the candle’s scene snagged on a stray thought that had been floating untethered in the back of his mind.

Eyes snapped open. Phainon jumped up with enough speed that his legs, bound in a bundle of blanket, were strung together as if in a net and he toppled over the side of the sofa with a thud. Letting out a small grunt from the floor, he pulled on the blankets in a weak attempt to free himself from their restraint.

One of Amphoreus’ so-called saviours and he’d been bested by a blanket of all things.

“Phai?” Cyrene asked. When he looked up, she was turned in her chair, one of her brows raised in a perfect arch as if silently wondering what was wrong with him. Luckily, she hadn’t started laughing. He’d… have probably preferred if she had, actually. Instead, she looked like she was struggling to tell whether she should be concerned or not.

“Cyrene,” he said, sitting. And then, since he’d already pulled her away from her reading: “I didn’t restart time.”

He was met with a blank look.

Something urgent caught in his chest. He said, “I didn’t restart time. Have Mydei and Anaxa been stuck out in that field this whole time?”

For a moment, Cyrene simply stared at him.

Then, her lips twitched at the ends and she broke into a fit of giggles so intense that tears collected in the corner of her eyes. As if the idea of him having kept their friends frozen in time for the better part of two weeks was comedic and not a tragedy.

“No,” she said, around her laughter. “They’re not in the field anymore. Nor are they trapped in time.”

Phainon’s cheeks reddened.

“I’d have asked you to free them from the time freeze if they weren’t already,” Cyrene said, with another small laugh.

“I can’t believe I forgot to even ask,” he murmured. Had he undone the freeze unconsciously? He didn’t remember smoothing the ripples in time that he’d created, but if they were free…

He blinked. Remembered who he was looking at.

…Cyrene had definitely freed them from time herself, hadn’t she?

“How angry are they?”

“Not particularly,” Cyrene said, joining him in a crouch on the floor. “Mostly they’re just concerned about you.”

Bathed in flickering candlelight, she continued her explanation of what had happened in Okhema during his absence.

Freeing Mydei and Anaxa from time hadn’t been an immediate thing. It had taken days of chipping at the cracks of time. Considering how Aedes Elysiae hadn’t been navigable, Cyrene had been available to work away at it.

At first, progress was slow. But, of course, considering how many coreflames had been used to press pause on the two Chrysos Heirs, that was to be expected. Persistence was key. The longer Phainon had been away, the less power his coreflames held over the pair.

Two days later, they’d been free.

“They were a little disorientated,” Cyrene said. “For them, days had passed within a second. One second they were with you and then, the next they were with me. I don’t think they really believed it’d been days at first.”

…Titans, the professor was definitely going to add this into his stupid equations of… of coreflame science or whatever it was that he’d named it, wasn’t he? He wouldn’t be surprised if the man was already questioning the number of coreflames again after this show of power.

Phainon tipped his head back onto the sofa’s cushions and stared, unseeing, at the ceiling. “I told them that it was thirty three thousand cycles instead of just thirty three.”

“Yeah…” Cyrene agreed. “Professor Anaxa said as much.”

“He asked you how many there were, didn’t he?” Phainon asked.

Cyrene hummed, affirming.

“Did you tell him?”

Cyrene tilted her head, before breathing out a sigh. She said, “I really should’ve. But, well, we made a really stupid pact, right? That I wouldn’t. So… no. I didn’t.”

For a moment, Phainon stared at her. Then, his lips quivered, disbelief catching in his throat like an abandoned laugh. He said, “You didn’t?”

“Nope.”

“You probably should’ve.” He said.

“Oh absolutely,” Cyrene said. “If you won’t, I really think that I should.”

“But…?”

“But,” she continued, “I was kind of a little annoyed that they pushed you for an answer so much. So I didn’t want to tell Anaxa how many cycles it’d been.”

Despite himself, a laugh caught in his throat. “You didn’t tell them because of spite?”

“A little bit,” she agreed. “But I also didn’t want to tell them before talking to you about it first. That wouldn’t be fair.”

Phainon tilted his head towards her. Didn’t say a word.

“But I do think it’s time that I told them,” Cyrene said.

“It’s not even been two weeks,” Phainon sighed.

“This secret is too heavy to keep. It wasn’t meant to be kept.”

He heaved out another sigh. This one was deeper. The kind of sigh that left the lungs struggling from hyperdeflation.

“Let me think about it?” He murmured.

“Of course.”

Later, after he’d abandoned the sofa for a bed, Cyrene having stolen the duvet, half splayed across the mattress and leaving him with very little space at all, Phainon reached for the teleslate that she’d gifted him and turned it on.

The room brightened with blue light.

Squinting at it, Phainon was surprised to see that it had already been set up in much the same fashion as his old teleslate. Same applications, same background…

Oh. Cyrene must’ve recreated his old teleslate using the Remembrance’s power.

He pressed a thumb into his messages, brows instantly furrowing at the sheer mass of them. He’d not really checked his teleslate since they’d entered the Era Nova, so it shouldn’t have been surprising to see how many unopened messages awaited him.

Messages from his fellow heirs. Some from friends outside of the Flamechase. One from Chartonus. A couple from Theodoros. A few from Dan Heng and March 7th.

And then, finally, of course - Stelle.

He would read the other messages later. Right now, he wasn’t ready to read the onslaught of them all. Didn’t have the energy for it.

Instead, he opened Stelle’s messages and - without reading the messages she’d sent him these past few weeks - began to type.

Phainon When are you coming back?

Her response was an instant thing. As if she’d been waiting for it.

Stelle

i’m not too sure. soon hopefully?

herta wants to do some experiments that she needs me here for but those are usually pretty quick.

why? have they confirmed the next date for seal slammers? is it soon? if it’s soon you HAVE to sign me up. i need to reinforce my status as champion.

Phainon

I think I’m having a nervous breakdown.

For a moment, there was nothing.

Then Phainon was met with three bouncing dots. The jump of an ellipsis announced that Stelle was typing.

He waited for a minute. Then for two. Then, he realised it was probably best to stop counting altogether and Phainon simply settled on watching the screen with wide eyes. When the response finally came, his teleslate buzzed with such ferocity that he almost dropped it in his surprise.

Stelle

oh.

phainon. babygirl. yeah.

we been knowing that.

Phainon

What?

Stelle

33 million cycles? if you didn’t have a nervous breakdown after all of that, you’d be a psychopath.

honestly, i’m surprised it took this long.

Phainon

Oh.

Stelle

also…

partner. sunshine child of mine.

you’re literally insane.

so many screws loose in that pretty little head of yours.

what were you expecting?

Phainon

…

Titan’s above. I’m the dog in the room that’s on fire.

Stelle

yup.

Phainon

Fuck.

Stelle

double yup.

Chapter End Notes

Chapter Summary

“Hey babygirl!” Stelle said, loud and merry, “how’re things on your side of the galaxy?”

Chapter Notes

i know i promised hot chocolate in the previous chapter but circumstances changed. hot chocolate will have to be delayed. i know, i know. i have betrayed you all and i offer only my humblest of apologies.

anyway. we broke 3.5k kudos?? uh. wow. guys. i'm glad you all enjoy the fic as much as i do. i hope you have as much fun reading it as i do writing it.

also, i've been enjoying writing this chapter to octopath traveller's 'Frostlands' which. wonderful track. really kinda captures the ending to this chapter.

In the silence of Cyrene’s room - well, mostly silent but for her soft snores echoing from beside him - Phainon stared at his teleslate and considered how, exactly, he was going to source multiple fire extinguishers.

The extinguishers would need to be metaphorical, of course.

(Though metaphorical or not, it appeared that they were very much needed.)

A nervous breakdown?

Him?

Even while he’d been typing the message to Stelle, Phainon had had his doubts. He’d considered the very real possibility that he was simply exaggerating the state of his own mind. Exhausted? No. He was just a little

tired. People grew tired, sometimes. Anyone who’d been stuck within Irontomb for a thousand years, fighting the blacktide and the force of its corruption would be tired. He wasn’t drowning in his own grief, he was just a little upset.

And then Stelle had responded.

Simple messages yet unwavering in the agreement expressed within. Yes, the messages had taken time to reach his teleslate, but it wasn’t due to any hesitation. If anything, the messages had simply reminded him of the first day of the Era Nova when Stelle had looked at him with such appalled horror for being a complete and utter moron.

Huh.

Wasn’t even on the planet and yet he could practically see her judging him in his mind’s eye for taking so long to come to any realisation on the state of his own mental health.

So far trapped in his own mind, he barely registered the buzzing of his teleslate in his hand. The screen had switched off, releasing the room back into darkness. A single buzz wasn’t enough to catch his attention enough to steal him from his now whirring thoughts.

Phainon could agree that his mental health wasn’t exactly in a good place, but the claim that he was literally insane? Surely not. That, at least, must’ve been a joke. Maybe another meme? Stelle often made references to things he didn’t understand. Maybe this was just another reference.

Another buzz. And then a third.

Until the room lit with blue light once more, and the vibration of his teleslate became a more constant thing. Ongoing in an attempt to reclaim his attention. What was she doing, at this rate Stelle was going to blow up his phone with the sheer amount of messages—

He glanced down.

— Incoming Video Call: Stelle —

Out of pure panic and a little bit of surprise, Phainon fumbled his attempt to answer the call and instead declined it.

Another small, feeble buzz.

Stelle

Rude.

She phoned him again. This time the vibrations felt far more indignant, as if the trailblazer was trying to prove a point from the other end of the galaxy. When he tried accepting the call, his thumb was less shaky and he managed to press the awaiting green button.

The screen burst to life with a glow of warm yellow light as the video call connected.

Stelle, centre frame, looked as she always did. Messy grey hair sticking up as if she’d crawled out of bed without a care, curious golden eyes glistening with mirth. The edges of her lips were pulled up into a loose grin, though her entire body seemed tense. Concerned.

The room she was in was a familiar one. She’d shown it to him the day after the Era Nova. Her room on the Astral Express - photos plastered to the walls courtesy of March 7th, a fair number of bird plushies behind her and a toy clock with legs and a face. She must’ve been sitting at the desk because he could see the sofa and all its many cushions over her shoulder.

“Hey babygirl!” She said, loud and merry, “how’re things on your side of the galaxy?”

Phainon glanced towards Cyrene, to how her brows furrowed as the noise threatened to rouse her and proceeded to lift a hand to his lips and shush the trailblazer with a voice bordering on a hiss. He said, “Quiet. Talk quieter. You’ll wake Cyrene.”

Stelle’s eyes widened. Comically so. She said, “Oh, you and Cyrene out here having a sleepover without me? Makes sense why my screen's all dark and I can’t see shit, but hey, where was my invite?”

He had to give credit where credit was due. She was quieter. Not by much, but there was some hush.

“You—” Phainon grabbed hold of his memoria blanket and slid off of the bed. “You’re halfway across the galaxy. Any invite would’ve— Partner, you wouldn’t have been able to attend.”

“Still would’ve been nice to have an invite,” Stelle sniffed. Though from the smile she threw at the screen, it was clear the offense was all faux. “... Ignores my calls and doesn’t invite me to sleepovers. I’m telling on you to Dan Heng.”

Phainon was pretty sure that Dan Heng would simply roll his eyes and do absolutely nothing, so he said, “You do that, partner,” and moved from the bedroom to the living room.

He ambled towards the small coffee table and the candles that had been previously snuffed out. Considering how Phainon was the closest thing to a living flame in all of Amphoreus, there was little need to start searching for wherever Cyrene stored her matches. Instead, he simply snapped his fingers and small bursts of flame caught the edges of candle wicks, bathing the room in a low flicker of candlelight.

An abandoned mug on the table was quickly utilised as a stand for his teleslate. Once it was in place, he dropped onto the sofa, again toppling over onto his side and reaching for now familiar  pillows.

“Also,” Phainon continued, shifting into a position that allowed him to stare at his teleslate without cricking his neck. “Why do you keep calling me that?”

“Calling you what? Babygirl?”

Phainon hummed, affirmative.

“Well, you never call me that,” Stelle said. “And one of us needs to be babygirl so—”

“Do we?”

“Mhm. It’s totally a thing, trust me.” He trusted the trailblazer on many things, but on this, Phainon remained skeptical.

“Right,” he said, slowly. “It sounds… a strange thing to call someone.”

“Nah,” Stelle said. “Not strange at all. Now you have access to the wider universe, you’ll see it’s just affectionate. One day you’ll even start using it yourself. It’s written in the stars.”

“Is it?”

“Sure is,” Stelle said. “I can’t wait to get to be the babygirl in this partnership. March doesn’t think I can make it take off. But I’m faithful to the ways of the babygirl. We can walk this journey together, partner.”

Phainon stared at her grin and found that once again, he had no true understanding of what she was talking about. He simply said. “Sure. I’ll… note it down for the future.”

Stelle’s eyes lit as if taking the words as a promise. As if she had just won something very important.

Then, they began to simmer, showing more of the tension from before. As if even with her wish to keep things light-hearted and upbeat, the concern was bubbling whether she wanted it to or not.

“So,” she said. “Dog in the room on fire, huh?”

Ah. It seemed they were doing this then.

He didn’t say anything. He simply lifted one shoulder in an aborted shrug and sighed. There wasn’t any reason to deny it, was there? If Stelle had brought up the claim of a nervous breakdown then maybe he’d have been able to pretend it wasn’t all that bad, but a room on fire was always a concern - no matter how many flames currently filled it.

“What are you going to do to stop living the life of that particular meme?”

His next sigh was even louder than the previous one. Pulled from the depths of his soul, it was the accumulation of lifetimes of smothered breaths.

Phainon said, “I don’t know.”

“You don’t?”

He shook his head. Just because he’d identified that things were bad didn’t mean that he knew how to magically fix it. Didn’t even mean that he wanted to. Earlier, he’d felt certain that he needed to try, that for Cyrene’s sake he was capable of making even a tiny start.

But that had been earlier in the day, delirious on the sound of her laughter, with new music in his ears and an adrenaline surge of panic misinterpreted as eagerness. Now it was night and he vacillated between wanting to try to leave his metaphorical burning room and wanting to stare into the flames as his mind burned.

So the room was on fire. So what? At least that meant it was warm.

At least that meant he could still feel something.

“I don’t know,” he repeated. He lifted his gaze from his teleslate to shadows of flame dancing across the coffee table. He brought his knees up close to his chest and wrapped an arm around his shins. “Do I have to do anything?”

On the other side of the call there was silence.

Certain that if he glanced back at the screen, he’d be met only with sadness, Phainon kept his gaze raised. He wasn’t sure whether he’d take back the words if he didn’t keep looking away. If he saw sorrow in any of his friend’s eyes then he’d fold and go back to lying to keep them happy.

“No,” Stelle said, eventually. “You don’t.”

She was halfway across the galaxy and yet Phainon could still feel the way that space could tremble under the weight of unspoken words. The trailblazer was trying her best to find the best words that could help. After all, that was the role of the nameless. Wasn’t it? To build connections and use them to help in whatever ways possible?.

“But I—” She trailed off. Paused. Tried again. “I think…” Another pause.

He could hear movement but from where he’d refused to look down, it was difficult to tell what it was she was doing. It could’ve been anything from resettling at her desk, to reaching for some item that sat past the space captured by the lens of her teleslate.

Quietly, Stelle said, “If you don’t want to do anything, then don’t. There isn’t a person in all of Amphoreus - no, in the cosmos - who could reasonably ask that of you.”

Again, she trailed off into silence.

This time, Phainon wasn’t able to stop himself from glancing back at his teleslate. To Stelle, brows dipped in a v-shape, frustration present in the press of her lips and the way her gaze felt heavier than it ever had during the entirety of their friendship.

She met his gaze through the screen and held it.

Steeled herself.

“Phainon,” she said. “I don’t know if you’ve realised it yet but… if you turned around tomorrow and said you were done, like done-done, that you couldn’t keep going and that this was it, that you didn’t want to do anything ever again… I don’t think anyone would be cruel enough to ask you to keep trying. They’d hate the outcome but they’d accept it. Because you’ve suffered enough. And you deserve the right to choose.”

“I—” Phainon shifted, pushed himself up on the sofa and held his pillow close to his chest.

“At this point,” Stelle continued, after a sharp inhale. As if she wasn’t entirely sure whether her words were helping or not, but thought they were important to say regardless. “You’ve earned the right to do absolutely nothing. No one is going to ask you to. And it’s not because they don’t want to but because it’s not up to them. It’s up to you. You’re the only one who can make that decision.”

Phainon’s brows furrowed.

The last time he made a proper decision for himself, it’d been alongside Cyrene and it had led to billions of years worth of literal hell.

“I—” His teeth pierced his lips with the full force of his uncertainty. “Partner, I don’t… I didn’t mean anything by the question, I just— Well, I was simply thinking out loud. I don’t…”

He held the pillow more tightly within his arms.

More silence between them. Though now some of the tension had eased from Stelle’s shoulders. She said, “That’s fine then. I just thought someone should tell you that. So you knew. Because the other Chrysos Heirs probably won’t say it.”

“Alright,” Phainon murmured.

“Now,” Stelle said, clapping her hands together. With it, the seriousness faded back to her usual half-grin, bright eyes promising mischief “Enough of all the heavy stuff. What are we, bodybuilders? I think not. Tell me, partner - What do you do these days to offer yourself even a little bit of comfort?”

The jump in her mood was so sudden it felt like whiplash.

For a moment, all he could do was simply blink and try to make sense of the words. She had one of those beacon things that ensured he heard Okheman when she spoke and yet he still had to take the time to parse the words.

“Uh…?”

“In the cycles. Before them. As Phainon. Or Khaslana. Any of it.” Stelle prompted.

Phainon blinked, almost absently.

As a child, he’d hidden himself away between stalks of wheat and stared out across a sea of gold, but that wasn’t necessarily a viable option these days. Gold reminded him too much of blood and wheat was a sore reminder of the home he’d spent too many years destroying.

As Okhema’s Deliverer, he had found comfort in connections, in other people. Whenever things became too much, he would find his fellow heirs and converse with them. Days spent helping Hyacine move supplies into Twilight Courtyard storage rooms, or helping Castorice study during their time at the grove. Spars with Mydei. Shared tea with Aglaea while they discussed the latest changes in the internal affairs of Okhema and its politics.

Yet this too had become difficult. He wasn’t that same person, anymore. Every conversation with his fellow heirs felt taut. Uncomfortable. Like each interaction took place on a bed of shattered glass, and there was no way of getting through it without tearing oneself apart and leaving the room bloody and in pain.

So all that really left was the little comforts he had allowed himself as Khaslana.

During his time as the Flame Reaver of each cycle he had allowed himself one single comfort.

A single hope.

Standing motionless, he would stand apart from the world and tilt his head up to the sky. There, he would wait. Watch for any signs of change. For any signs of deliverance.

“I used to watch the sky,” he admitted, finally.

“Perfect,” Stelle said. “Love me a little stargazing at late o’clock in the morning. Well, let’s both go outside and have a staring contest across the cosmos. I bet I’ll win. I’m the universal champion when it comes to staring without blinking. March will back me up.”

Phainon did not know Miss March well but he was pretty sure that she would not be backing Stelle up in this particular claim.

Still, the idea of a staring contest that spanned several galaxies was stupid enough to make him unfold his legs and rise to his feet. After a quick glance into the bedroom to ensure Cyrene was still resting peacefully, Phainon blew out the candles and crept out into the night.

“Are you outside yet?” Stelle asked.

“Yeah."

Cyrene lived on the bottom floor so there were no stairs to navigate. Just the one corridor that led out to the plaza around them. It was sparsely lit. Outside, he spotted a few streetlamps with flames that had long since died out and now held only the glow of still warm embers.

“Can’t exactly see the stars yet,” Stelle said. “You gotta keep moving if we want to see anything.”

Phianon kept moving.

Out of the complex that housed Cyrene’s building. Out into the plaza - empty and devoid but for him and the trailblazer.

“It’s quiet,” he murmured.

“Peace typically is,” Stelle noted.

They kept moving. Or rather, Phainon continued walking further into the plaza, towards the patch of grass that sat at its centre. A little trampled on from all the footfall, but even beneath the glow of stars he spotted a few wildflowers peeking through.

“Get comfortable,” the trailblazer said, as his toes curled around grass, cuffs of his trousers soaking through with morning dew. “You’re about to lose this staring contest in real time, babygirl.”

Though she wasn’t capable of fully seeing it through the darkness, Phainon shook his head. He lowered to the ground, resting his head against the grass and said, “Who knows, maybe you’ll lose your champion title tonight partner. Anything could happen.”

“Those be fighting words Sir,” Stelle claimed. “No one takes my championship title. On three, okay?”

He placed his teleslate beside him and focused on the sky. Free from Aquila’s grasp, the stars were visible in a way they’d never been before. Or maybe it was simply because the galaxy beyond wasn’t a simulated one and thus was more fleshed out and real. The reasons didn’t matter.

What mattered was that the sky shone.

The constellations, once depicting the titans, were now different. New stars, new galaxies. Eventually, the Grove would rewrite their star charts to depict the stars of Era Nova. Other people would leave this place and explore them. The choice was there for them. The galaxy was alive and able to do so.

“I bet you totally just blinked, didn’t you?”

“I haven’t,” Phainon said. “Are you saying that because you blinked?”

“Not at all.” Stelle said. And then, a few seconds later, “How about then. You absolutely blinked then didn’t you?”

The laugh caught in his throat. A small thing; A bud of contentment - not quite sprouting but getting there. Phainon hadn’t blinked but he said, “Sure, Partner. You caught me.”

“Hmph.” The trailblazer laughed. Loud and infectious. The kind of sound that made a person want to join in. “That’s what you get for trying to beat the Intergalactic Baseballer at a petty competition. I get to retain my title for another day.”

“You sure do,” Phainon agreed and smiled up at the stars.

chapters.title: Chapter 15
chapters.html:
Chapter Summary

a butterfly makes an appearance.

Chapter Notes

happy halloween!!

when thinking about how to react to the phrase 'trick or treat', i decided on 'treat'. so here's a little treat for you all! it's a little shorter than usual, but i think you'll see that where i stopped was a very natural pausing point. it's alright to have a chapter shorter than 2k every now and again. forgive me!

“—When even Boothill was turned into origami I was like, maaan, we’re definitely cooked. You know?”

A hum, half awake and only partly listening.

“And—” The speakers muffled slightly, as if Stelle had moved closer to her teleslate's microphone. She said, “Hey, partner, are you still listening?”

With heavy eyes, Phainon did his best to smother his yawn — only partially successful — and said, “Yeah. Keep going.”

“You’ve gone all quiet.”

“Just listening.” He said. Though he hadn’t been wholly listening to the words, focusing more on the tones of Stelle’s voice and the way her cadence rose and fell along with the tension of her anecdote, he’d processed enough that he had a general impression of the story. “Then the ghost turned your ranger friend into a bird, right? That's what happened?”

Though skeptical, Stelle said, “...That is correct. Mostly. Boothill’s not just a ranger but a galaxy ranger, but yeah that's pretty much the gist of it. Huh. Turns out you’re able to snooze and listen at the same time. Just make sure not to fall asleep completely, alright? There’s still more to the tale.”

Again, he hummed. Though he had long since closed his eyes, he could still see stars twinkling at the back of his eyelids. It was preferable to the empty void that had been the sky of evernight during the cycles.

“I’m not going to fall asleep,” Phainon said.

…He fell asleep.

Between one thought, he was listening to stories from the so-called land of dreams, and in the next, he was jolting at the gentle embrace of something warm.

His fingers brushed against it. Not as thick as a blanket though clearly it was the summer equivalent: not quite as thin as a sheet but somewhere in the middle.

Phainon opened bleary eyes and realised the stars were beginning to disappear. Not because reality was fading but because Okhema was preparing for dawn and they simply couldn’t be seen as easily in a sky that was a haze of orange and red.

There was purple too, though that wasn’t within the sky. It was in the curl of plaited hair, in the long brush of fabric covering hand to elbow and a lilac gaze.

He had not seen her since the day irontomb fell. Now, she stood only two paces from him with a woven basket in hand.

“Castorice…?”

She startled at the suddenness of his attention, stumbling back.

And yet, once she had regained her balance, everything about her seemed to soften. Her eyes, her smile. Even her voice, though that softness was also mixed with apology. “Ah, I’m sorry. Did I wake you?”

The blunt answer was yes.

Rubbing his eyes, Phainon scanned their immediate surroundings. Though few people were moving on the very outskirts of the plaza, the early hour kept it mostly vacant. Only he and Castorice existed at its centre. And if they were the only two then it must’ve been by Castorice’s hand that he was blanketed in further warmth.

He pulled his aching body up so he was sitting, and offered a half shrug. “It’s alright.”

If anything, it was probably for the best. He’d not intended to fall asleep while on his call with Stelle, no matter how inviting the stars had been for dreaming. Better to wake now, while everything was still quiet, than wake later to a plaza bustling with life and curious eyes.

“Ah, so I did…” Castorice’s smile shifted into something just as apologetic as her tone. “I thought you might sleep better with another blanket since it's always quite chilly at this time. I should’ve expected you would wake up instead....”

The sheet had pooled in his lap when he’d sat up. Phainon reached for it. It was a woven thing the colour of clay, uniform in most places but for fraying patches and worn edges.

“Did you make this?” He asked.

“Not this one, no,” Castorice said. “Though Lady Aglaea has promised to teach me how to weave one of my own when everything calms down.”

It was as good a conversation starter as any other and yet Phainon let it pass him by.

During the cycles he would’ve asked more. Would’ve asked after future projects, after current projects. He would have done anything to pull a warmer smile from his friend’s lips, to bring forth any signs of life.

It was just... he didn’t know whether he was allowed to ask those things anymore. Or maybe it simply felt wrong to do so, after everything.

So instead of asking any of those things, Phainon said, “It’s early. What are you doing out?”

Castorice’s cheeks grew gold at the question, gaze falling quickly onto that of the basket in her hands. It was a round wicker basket - if he squinted, it was possible to see multiple flashes of colourful fabric inside.

“Well,” her voice was not embarrassed, as her flush might have suggested, but rather contained a serene sort of excitement. “I’ve been volunteering at the newly opened Garden of Life with all the little chimeras. They’re early risers so I’ve been rising early too.”

Whirring cogs clashed at the back of his mind as he stared.

The words didn’t compute because he’d simply never heard them before. Not from Castorice. As much as she’d always coveted the chance at a normal life, the ability to be able to help plants blossom or animals thrive, she’d simply never been able to. As the Hand of Death, she was simply too deadly.

In fact, Phainon wasn’t sure he’d seen her interact with chimera very much at all. Full grown chimera had always been wary, as if they could sense her link to Thanatos. And the little cubs… those Castorice herself had always avoided. Cubs were far too impulsive and filled with curiosity, after all.

If she were volunteering then that meant—

“Your curse—”

The gentle smile from before bloomed into something he had never seen. Though Castorice had smiled in the past, it was never with as much radiance that bled from her now: Eyes crinkled under the weight of a beam, cheeks golden with sheer joy.

She had dimples. Phainon had never known because Castorice had simply never smiled with enough force for them to go noticed.

“It is gone,” she said with a practically breathless laugh.

“Gone…?”

It was only as Castorice nodded that Phainon realised how little distance there currently was between them. Even whenever she had known he’d had enough coreflames of his own to mitigate her curse with his own power, she had always made it a point to remain five paces away.

Now, at most, she was two.

“Yes. My touch— these hands… ” She glanced down to her hands and though all the cycles would suggest an oncoming frown, she continued to smile. “They are no longer made of ice.”

Castorice raised her gaze to meet Phainon’s stare, unflinching, radiating sheer and utter relief.

“There is warmth in them.”

Something in Phainon’s chest, glass and fragile, shattered.

And he continued to stare.

Stared as Castorice’s smile began to dim with concern. Stared as his fingers twitched by his sides. Stared as liquid began to pool in his eyes.

“Lord Phainon—?”

Then, all too quickly it was not enough to simply be staring anymore.

He scrambled to his feet, unthinking. Reached for her hand not with tact, or hesitation, but with a desperation that only millions of years of watching someone smile without said smile reaching their eyes could foster.

Castorice was right. Her hand was warm.

He could not feel the familiar chill of Thanatos’ embrace. Not the coreflame, not the lingering press of the Hand of Death’s curse. There was no need to fight against her curse with his own power because there was no sign of it having ever been there.

“Castorice,” Phainon said, and her name caught in his throat as he said it. He was choking, unable to express himself with anything but the tears that had broken free from his eyes and were now rolling down his cheeks. “It’s really gone. You can finally—?”

She didn’t say anything.

She didn’t need to.

Castorice simply dropped her basket onto the grass beside them and raised her arms, inviting him to step into her embrace. And though Phainon did not deserve such kindness, though he had been the cause of so much of her agony, he could not bring himself to turn her down.

Instead, he stepped into the fold and scooped her into his arms. Pressed his forehead against her shoulder and did his best to pretend that his own shoulders were not trembling. Unsure whether to hold his friend loosely, lest he hurt her, or hold her tightly so that he could be sure that the moment remained real, he wavered and ended up at a halfhearted middle ground of holding something easily breakable with tender care and firm grip.

It was not until she began to hug him back that it shifted into a more comfortable thing.

Castorice gave absolutely terrible hugs.

Her arms wrapped around his torso. Too tight for breath, it was less an embrace and more the cradle of a python readying to crush a man to death. Her fingers dug into flesh with too much force. Her hands were trembling.

And yet, terrible as it was, it was also perfect.

Phainon let out a laugh that was as wet as his eyes. His voice was thick with... with something, some emotion that he could not begin to name and thought he should have, he could not bring himself to lift his head from Castorice’s shoulder as he murmured, “I am so glad for you, Castorice. You deserve this.”

“Lord Phainon,” Castorice said, in much the same tone as his own. “If you keep crying, I don’t think I’ll be able to stop myself from crying as well.”

“I just—”

He trailed off. Finding the words was too difficult.

Instead, he just leaned into the warmth of the woman once cursed by Death and realised that with this warmth, she felt real.

Phainon was being held by the Castorice of the Era Nova. He was not being held by the ghost of her from the cycles. No copy of the Hand of Death had ever been this warm. At long last, he could finally hug his friend without the promise of death looming over them both, ready to drag him, unwilling, into the Sea of Souls.

“I think I understand,” Castorice said. Her own voice was cracking now, raw in a way that she usually did not show. “It has been a long wait for both of us, hasn’t it?”

“Yes,” he breathed.

“It might be too late to say it now,” she murmured and tilted her head so that her cheek pressed against his temples, “but I’ve been waiting to say it, so I will. Thank you for bringing us into the Era Nova, Lord Phainon. I pray this Era will be far kinder to you than the last.”

Chapter End Notes

how to make someone who has suffered so much over billions of years cry? oh well, how about offering him something that makes him so

inexplicitly relieved and happy, that he sobs tears of joy? yeah. that'll do it!

also - i have a lot of thoughts on this chapter in terms of phainon's characterisation, but maybe we'll get into that another day. if people want to hear my ramblings, ofc!

chapters.html:
Chapter Notes

thanks again to everyone for the lovely comments that you've left, i love and appreciate them all!

wanted to do a longer note but honestly guys, i'm tired. i'm just gonna go to bed instead haha. hope that you enjoy the chapter!

During the cycles, Phainon had only ever offered Castorice a hug one time.

It had been very early on. Before the coreflames had begun to burn away both his insides and his emotions, before the rage had claimed him as kindling. Before he’d donned the role of executioner, before he’d stopped caring whether his friends survived any set cycle and had still tried his best to work alongside the flamechase to buy them all a little extra time.

Back then, he’d had maybe… seventeen coreflames of Death nestled within his chest.

Enough that he could feel her curse like an ache in his bones and know that while it would try to drain his vitality, it would not do so with such speed to make it so he could not afford his dear friend an embrace she so desired.

Back then, Castorice had looked at him as if she might cry. Not with tears of joy but with a grief unlike any he had ever seen her display in the cycles following.

“Lord Khaslana,” she had murmured, fingers twitching as she held out the eighteenth cycles’ coreflame of Death in icy hands. “You know I couldn’t possibly accept such an offer. It would be selfish of me to take even a little bit of life from you for my own comfort when we all have such a long journey ahead of us.”

His face must’ve shown his disappointment because she’d added, “On the day that this is all over and we finally reach the true Era Nova, please embrace that Castorice instead. Until then, we shall both have to wait.”

He’d promised to wait until the end of their journey. And he’d held onto the promise, at least for a little while. Until it had faded, like most promises that he'd made within the cycles began to fade - not from lack of care but from the slow decay of memory. By the time the promise had unravelled from memory entirely, he had become Castorice’s executioner and there had been no place left in his chest for such attempts at kindness.

‘It has been a long wait for the both of us,’ Castorice said now, and Phainon knew it was not in reference to this promise, but it felt like that eighteenth iteration of Castorice was speaking through her regardless

…Of course she was. Every iteration of his friend was still Castorice, no matter whether she remembered or not.

Caught in this sudden reemergence of memory, Phainon didn’t track the moment that they both sank to their knees. It was only when morning dew began to leave his trousers damp and uncomfortable that he began to catch on. His body shuddered but whether it was from the damp or his own rising emotions was difficult to say.

Maybe it was both. Maybe neither.

Phainon didn’t know.

All he did know was that he probably should’ve let go of Castorice by now. Having someone who had sown more death than even she, the Hand of Thanatos, had witnessed continue to hold onto her like a lifeline must’ve been a harrowing experience. The issue was that he simply couldn’t bring himself to let go. Every time he tried to convince himself to unfold his arms, to lift his head, it was simply too much.

Instead, he kept his forehead pressed into the flat of Castorice’s collarbone and tried his best to settle his trembling shoulders. It should’ve been easy. He was relieved that her curse was gone, to finally be able to embrace her like they’d both always wanted, yes, but did he need to be so dramatic about it?

A few tears were understandable. This… This stubbornness of his tears demanding to be shed was a level of drama that was unnecessary.

And yet as much as he tried to stop himself he couldn’t.

Now that he had started Phainon wasn’t sure he knew how to stop.

It was as if in turning the faucet he had torn it free. Now the tears had started, he had little control over them. They poured out of him, grief catching in the curl of his ribs and squeezing his heart.

Even the sky had begun to weep alongside him. He didn’t need to look up to know that storm clouds had begun cradling Amphoreus because he could feel Aquila’s coreflames in his chest resonating with his tears. Rain began to fall alongside them and he could feel the pitter-patter of it falling in time with the drumbeat of his pulse.

“I’m sorry Cas,” he murmured, when she began rubbing a hand up and down his arm.

“Don’t apologise,” Castorice murmured, in much the same tone. Teary. Kind. With just a smidge of sadness in her voice. “I’ve got you, Lord Phainon. I hope my embrace grants you a little bit of peace.”

He hated to disappoint her but it was not peace that he found in her hold. His mind was roiling with previous memories and it was not until the rain began to shower in earnest, grief tearing itself free that he found anything somewhat close to peace.

As they remained holding one another, water running down his neck in channels, what he finally found in her hold was silence.

Not the typical silence that followed closely behind Death. As the torrent continued and the white noise began to wash away his thoughts, it became a silence no longer filled with melancholy, or grief, but rather the kind of silence that was offered by temporary reprieve and the temporary halt of somber memories.

It would be a lie to say that he felt better but there was a degree of comfort that came from her touch being the only warm thing he could feel.

Phainon wasn’t sure how to respond to her hope of peace. So, like with everything else, he moved them along and murmured, “You don’t need to call me Lord Phainon, Castorice. You never had to be so formal with me.”

Castorice’s laugh was a small thing. Not as light as genuine laughter but tickled nonetheless. Perhaps she simply found it absurd that he was here, crying in her arms, face hidden away in the crook of her neck and worrying about the fact they were being too formal with one another.

“I know I didn’t,” she said, softly. “Old habits are just hard to change, sometimes.”

Phainon swallowed back a sigh and finally, though he did not want to, pulled himself away.

As soon as he did, it was difficult not to feel guilty. The downpour had soaked them both. Castorice’s bangs clung to her forehead. Her clothes were so saturated they clung to her body as if unsure what else to do with themselves.

“Sorry,” he murmured again, gaze turning upwards to a sky coloured by multiple shades of grey. A shroud of heavy fog blocked the sky. Somewhere above, he could feel each cloud growing more swollen, pulling on the surrounding atmosphere’s humidity to help form more teardrops and rain.

“Don’t be,” Castorice said, gently, reaching for his hand. Still warm. Still so very kind. “It’s just a little bit of rain.”

For a moment, his mind struggled to place the meaning behind the words.

Then he realised that Castorice knew the rain was his fault.

It shouldn’t have surprised him, really. Okhema’s previous storm, the one that leaked free from Aedes Elysiae, had also been his fault. At least this time Okhema only had to deal with a little bit of rain.

Or a lot of it. Already the grass around them was slippery with mud.

…Phainon had to figure out how to stop crying before he flooded the city. It felt as if all of the coreflames of Sky beneath his skin had bound themselves to his grief, to his tears, and were just as uncontrollable.

“Why don’t we head inside?” Castorice suggested. “If we stay outside, we’ll be sure to catch a cold.”

Castorice’s quarters were not too far from Cyrene’s.

They were both in the building with blue bunting, on the ground floor, though Castorice’s rooms were in the adjacent corridor and sat at the opposite end of the building.

Phainon wasn’t entirely sure why he followed her back to her own rooms rather than disappearing back to Cyrene’s side and the comfort of rest that could be found within. It was possible he didn’t want to wake her.

Or maybe he just didn’t want to make her cry again.

And Cyrene would, he knew, if she saw that he had been crying. Was crying. Couldn’t stop crying.

Wasn’t the realisation that one was having a mental breakdown supposed to help? All Phainon had managed thus far was tears and an unnatural alteration to the weather that held the very literal risk of drowning half the city if he didn’t manage to get his own emotional state back under control.

The room Castorice brought him into could only be described as cosy. Bundles of black wool and sewing needles had been left in a large basket on the coffee table. Unfolded bundles of parchment had been left on the desk, beside an inkwell and an ornate feather quill.

As Castorice zipped past to collect towels for them both, Phainon’s focus remained on the pen.

The feather had been dyed with lavender - messily done, if the white streaks running along the vanes were anything to go by. He’d experienced enough colour theory sessions from Aglaea over the cycles to know that objectively, the pen nib would’ve looked better in silver rather than its deep gold colouring, and yet, to him, it was beautiful in its imperfection.

His attention had moved on to various crocheted animals on Castorice’s couch by the time she returned and pressed a bundle of fluffy towel and woolen clothing against his palms. Phainon lifted his gaze from a crocheted unicorn that resembled Little Ica to meet her eyes.

She’d taken the time to change out of her own soaked clothes. From deep lilac, she’d changed into a long indigo dress and a white cardigan. Her plaits were far messier from where she’d attempted to towel dry the strands to keep them from dripping water everywhere.

Castorice pointed towards the woolen fabric in his hands, her cheeks growing gold. “If you’d like, you can change into that and I’ll hang up your clothes so they can dry.”

“Alright,” Phainon murmured.

With a faint smile, she pointed him towards the bathroom and left him to change. First, he unpeeled his current clothes, shivering as water continued trickling down his neck. Then, after towelling himself down, he unfolded the black clothing Castorice had passed him.

It was a woollen jumper. Soft, with somewhat messy stitchwork around the sleeves and at the neckline. Handmade. Baggy and yet not too loose as to invite any chills. It must’ve swamped her whenever she wore it - though none of his memories included this particular jumper as being part of her wardrobe. Probably something she’d picked up within Era Nova then. It felt new, so that was probably it.

He wrung out his trousers as best he could, realised it was a losing task and decided he’d just have to deal with the dampness.

When he eventually left the bathroom behind, hair still clinging to his forehead, dripping water along the curve of his nose, Phainon was greeted with the scent of vanilla and warm milk. Castorice, standing by the stove in her little kitchen, turned to glance at him over her shoulder and said, “It fits you. Or, well, maybe a little big. I was worried I’d make it too small.”

For a moment, his mind was static.

Then, he said, “Did you make this for me?”

Castorice’s lips pulled up. “Of course I did.”

It was difficult to do anything but stare.

Part of him wanted to ask why, to ask what he’d done to deserve her care but really, he already knew the answer. They were friends. They always had been. Even when he’d thrust Dawnmaker through her ribs, or torn the coreflame of Death from her chest with clawed hands, they’d always been friends.

That was why he felt so damn guilty towards all of his fellow heirs. That was why he was such a monster, deep down.

Because despite all his affection for them, despite the love he held for his friends and dearest companions, it hadn’t ever been enough to make him hesitate before killing them.

“...Thank you,” he murmured and lifted his sleeve to wipe away the tears that continued to fall.

“I was going to wait until I'd finished everyone's gift,” Castorice continued, as he lowered his gaze, unable to keep looking at her. It felt like he was holding his breath until she finally turned back to the stove, at which point, the building pressure in his chest began to ease. “But I don’t mind letting you receive yours now. I hope you don’t mind that it’s black - there’s not a lot of colour variety in wool at the moment. I was lucky to be able to find this much in black.”

“I like it,” Phainon said, and pulled on his sleeves until they fit comfortably in his palms. Twisting the fabric was grounding. Helped keep him present and not trapped in the thoughts of the cycles. “I’ll treasure it forever.”

Castorice let out a small laugh. Equal parts relief and warm happiness.

“I’m glad,” she said. Then, with a low hum, “On rainy days like this, I always feel better with a cup of hot chocolate with a little vanilla and a sprinkling of cinnamon. It helps warm me up. Would you like some?”

“Oh, no you don’t need to—” Something like panic rose in his chest. “After everything… I don’t need to eat or drink anymore. You don’t need to waste it on me.”

A moment of silence.

Then, Castorice said, “I don’t think it’s wasted on you if you’ll enjoy it. If it’ll make you feel happy, even a little, then it could never be a waste.”

Phainon twisted the fabric of his sleeves even more, pressing his lips into a thin line.

Part of him wanted to explain that it wasn’t worth it. That he wasn’t worth it. That she should be out sharing hot chocolate with everyone else, or spending time with the chimeras at the Garden like she’d been planning on doing. He’d hurt everyone, whether they remembered it or not, whether they knew it or not.

Another part of him that sounded a lot like his inner hero, like Stelle or Cyrene, murmured that it was just hot chocolate and that accepting a little bit of kindness, whether he deserved it or not, wasn’t the end of the world.

“What do you think?” Castorice prompted, as he descended into silence and half-anxious thoughts.

Phainon wiped at his eyes again - they remained as wet as the rain outdoors - and offered a tiny nod. “If you don’t think it’ll be a waste.”

“Never,” she said, firmly. “Now come claim a mug for yourself. And help me reach the cinnamon, will you? Lady Cipher keeps hiding it on the top shelf whenever she visits and it's always impossible to reach without climbing onto the counter.”

Chapter End Notes

some ramblings on phainon's characterisation within ASU
