Chapter Notes

cocoa time!!! i've been kinda excited for this one - you'll see why.

Castorice had a whole collection of mugs hidden away in her kitchen cupboard.

Since none of them were plain, Phainon chose an old mug with painted chimeras that ran across its base and a chipped handle. It looked well used, well loved. Like an artefact in the life of the Maiden of Death that would require preservation within the new Era.

Part of him wanted to ask if these mugs had been collected within the one cycle he’d not been present for but Phainon couldn’t find the courage to ask. Instead, he reached up to the top shelf for the stashed powdered cinnamon that had been pushed as far back as it could possibly be—which was surprisingly far considering these were deep cupboards—and allowed Castorice to shoo him to the sofa.

Her pillows were just as soft as Cyrene’s were. Phainon sunk into couch cushions, leaned against the arm rest and rubbed at still wet eyes. It was starting to get ridiculous - biologically he should’ve stopped by now. And yet Phagousa’s coreflames, keeping him from dehydration, seemed to be actively working against his efforts to stop.

As he sat, awaiting both his friend and the hot chocolate she was making, Phainon brought his teleslate out of his pocket and opened his messages. His chat with Stelle was still open from the previous evening - at some point following the end of their call, she had sent a message boo-ing him for falling asleep halfway through such a riveting tale of origami and fruit matching. Then half a quint later, she’d sent a follow up message wishing him restful dreams.

Pressing out of her messages, he was met with the same unopened messages that he’d been avoiding since the beginning of the Era Nova. He kept promising himself that he would read them later but honestly, Phainon wasn’t sure when later would be. All he knew was that it continued to be not now.

The only message he opened was that of Cyrene’s when his teleslate buzzed with her incoming text.

Cyrene

Hey! Woke up and you weren’t here, is everything ok??

He could practically feel the worry oozing from the words. Which made sense - the last time she’d left him alone, not even a full twenty-four hours ago, reality had begun to unravel around him and he’d set about destroying his room until everything was stained in soot and coated in shattered glass. He was almost surprised she hadn’t called him immediately or demanded he share his location.

...Alright, maybe she wouldn't have demanded his location and he was simply exaggerating the extent of her worry but he was still surprised she hadn't called. Perhaps because it was still early and she hadn't wanted to risk waking him up? At this point, his natural state of being was asleep so she might've expected that he wouldn't be awake. Yeah, that seemed like the likeliest reason.

Phainon

I’m with Castorice.

She’s making hot chocolate.

Cyrene

Ah!!

Alright no worries then. I’ll get some chores done. If you need anything let me know and i’ll zoom on over!

Phainon

Will do.

Thank you, Cyrene.

Cyrene

Anytime!!

“Here you go.”

Phainon lowered his teleslate as Castorice’s shadow fell over him, gaze falling to the mug held in her outstretched hand. Wiping tears away with his sleeve one final time - really, why weren’t they stopping? - he reached out and took the mug, holding it between his hands. The warmth of the ceramic brushed against his fingertips and burned his palms. A pleasant burn, the kind that left the skin tingling.

“Thank you,” he murmured.

Castorice settled on the other side of the sofa, folding her legs up, leaning against the armrest. Her own mug— purple, with little ceramic butterfly wings for a handle— rested against her thigh.

In the absence of conversation, Phainon lifted his mug to his lips and inhaled the deep scent of cocoa. It was rich, accompanied by sweet vanilla and earthy cinnamon. He didn’t even need to drink in order to taste the sweet spice on his tongue, the aroma caught on his tongue and lingered as if he’d taken a large gulp of it.

“You’ll have to let me know if I put too much cinnamon in,” Castorice said lightly, as he continued to breathe in wisps of hot cocoa instead of actually drinking it. “Lady Cipher always says I’m too stingy with how much I add.”

“Cipher really likes cinnamon, is all,” he murmured. “You could put in a whole heaped spoonful and she’d probably ask for more.”

“She would not,” Castorice laughed. “That would be far too much.”

Phainon shrugged halfheartedly. He was pretty sure that Cipher had done that before, actually, in at least a few thousand cycles. The first time he’d seen it, he’d been horrified. Like with everything else however, it had not taken long for the emotion to fade into expectancy.

He was starting to think of the cycles again.

…Phainon was so tired of thinking about them. He didn’t want to think of anything.

So instead of thinking, he tilted his mug against his lips and took a sip in an attempt to focus on other things.

Cinnamon hit his tongue first - the subtlest smokiness in the spices paired with a faint hint of citrus. Citrusy as it was, it must’ve been Aidonian-grown. The cinnamon grown within their greenhouses always carried a hint of citrus. Not entirely sweet, but with a faint bitterness that had thawed into something softer.

Then, the silkiness of the drink itself. Warmed milk caught against his tongue - not scalding, luckily he still had enough control over his coreflames to avoid that - and blanketed it with a soft caress of cocoa and vanilla. Phainon rolled the taste around his tongue, let it warm him, let it linger.

And as it lingered, he found himself wondering if this was what home tasted like for Castorice. Rich cocoa and the lingering touch of cinnamon across the tongue.

He should’ve known, after everything, but he didn’t.

Had he ever asked?

No. He hadn’t. Why hadn’t he?

“What do you think?” Castorice asked.

“You didn’t put in too much,” he murmured, as it dawned on him that he couldn’t ask. That he never would because he didn’t deserve to. He took another sip; the cocoa clung to his tastebuds, earthy and sweet. “Cinnamon, I mean.”

“I’m glad,” Castorice said and her eyes crinkled against the weight of her smile.

They drank in silence.

Phainon knew he should’ve been saying something. This was his friend - the quiet wasn’t meant to be suspended for quite this long. And yet, every time he tried to find a topic that was safe, he came up short.

The world wasn’t glitching around him, not with Castorice’s warmth by his side acting as a grounding agent, but his mind was still electrified, still fuzzy every time he tried to think about what could be said. What was safe and what was not. What conversations they had once shared that Castorice remembered and which ones hadn’t happened in the cycle she remembered.

When he finished his hot chocolate, swallowing it alongside rising anxiety, he leaned forwards and placed it onto her coffee table with a dull thud. He ran a finger across the chip in the handle and sighed.

“I’m sorry, Castorice,” he murmured, at last.

From the corner of his eye, he watched Castorice’s brows furrow. She opened her mouth - as if, on instinct, she’d been ready to say he didn’t have anything to be sorry for - before forcefully pushing the words away. Though her hesitation was minute, it was an obvious thing.

She asked, “Why are you apologising?”

Well there was an entire list of things to apologise for but it was probably for the best not to get into all of that when he’d not prepared her for any of it. Apologising for killing her, or for lying to her, probably wasn’t best done when he was in her home. That was the sort of apology you gave when the other person had a means of escape.

“To have made you bring me here,” he said instead because that apology felt more pressing than the others. More appropriate for the situation. “I didn’t mean to steal you away from the chimeras or interrupt your time at the Garden.”

Castorice’s furrowed brows smoothed out.

“Oh,” she said, “you don’t need to worry about that. I can just go and see the chimeras tomorrow - right now, I’m very happy to have a cosy day inside with you.”

He probably should’ve felt reassured by that. In the past he would’ve been!

(In the past, he had not been… this. Broken. Cruel. Fighting against the destruction inside of him with every breath.)

“It feels like I haven’t seen you in a very long time,” Castorice continued. “And even if I had, I always have time for a friend.”

He wanted to say that he wasn’t just a friend but her enemy. That he was her executioner. That she was being too kind, too thoughtful, for someone like him. Phainon wasn’t sure whether telling her would be selfless or selfish, at this point. All he knew was that every time he tried to form the words they caught in his throat. The truth was too large to be spoken and the idea of breaching it even a little bit made him want to disappear from Amphoreus entirely.

Instead of saying any of this he simply shuffled closer on the sofa and, after double checking that she wasn’t overwhelmed by his closeness, leaned his head on her shoulder.

“Alright,” he said.

And then, bolstered by… he wasn’t sure what exactly, perhaps her warmth, or just her acceptance, Phainon asked, “What will you do with the chimeras tomorrow?”

Castorice physically brightened. He could feel it in the way her shoulders shifted, could see it in the animated way in which she began speaking with her hands. In how she was clearly excited over being able to share her latest venture, this new hobby that she’d never been able to take part in while cursed.

She took him through her daily routine. Mornings at the Garden weren’t exactly the busiest time - that was during the Parting hour, when chimeras returned to the garden with dusty coats of fur from a day of helping clear the rubble from Okhema, at which point bath time became a three-quint long process - but it was close. From preparing meals, to doing a daily check on each chimera to make sure they weren’t straining themselves and were in good health, things were in perpetual motion. There were so many chimeras, after all.

“We have a lot of people volunteering,” Castorice said, as he closed his eyes and focused on the calming lilt of her voice, “but even with everyone it’s difficult. We’re currently looking after all of the chimeras from the Grove’s equivalent Garden so it’s a little overcrowded.”

He hummed. “Is it possible to make the Garden bigger?”

“They’re considering it, but in terms of Okhema’s restoration, it’s not a high priority.” She paused. “I’ve been thinking of adopting a couple chimeras myself and bringing them home so they can have a little more room but I’m not too sure that I’m ready to do that just yet.”

Which made sense.

Even though she only held two cycles worth of memories that was enough for her to still have reservations. Her touch had brought death for so long that it wouldn’t have been strange if she thought the curse’s removal was only a temporary thing. And if it ever came back... well, she didn't need to say way she was hesitant.

…Maybe the Era Nova didn’t quite align in her head, either.

He let out a small sigh and said, “Keep thinking on it. Any chimera you would adopt would be lucky to have you.”

“Oh I don’t know about lucky,” Castorice said with a small laugh. “They might not feel that way when they realise I’ll be sewing lots of cute little outfits and hats for them to try on.”

He let out a half breath that was something close to amused but mostly sounded tired. “And sunglasses.”

“And sunglasses,” she agreed.

They continued like that. With Castorice, kind enough to carry the conversation, only requiring small comments and the occasional question to keep the room from falling back into silence.

It may not have been the perfect conversation but it was a start.

Topics flowed from chimera care, to the many crafting projects Castorice had begun - of the sweaters she was making for the heirs, she was currently working on three tinier sweaters for the Tribios triplets and was currently trying to figure out how to accommodate their wings into the pattern she was following.

Keeping things light, they danced through more topics. Castorice, alongside Cyrene and Hycaine, had made a pact to start a communal garden for all of the Chrysos Heirs to enjoy after Okhema's rebuilding efforts had been completed.

“We’re not sure whether it’ll be at the Grove or here in Okhema just yet,” Castorice admitted. “But Hyacine’s going to grow medicinal herbs while Cyrene and I focus on planting a vegetable garden.”

She looked so excited for this future that something in Phainon’s chest began to ache.

And past that, deeper down, just embers in his chest, he could feel something like excitement for her. Phainon smiled. Or rather, he grimaced, but that was close enough to a smile for him.

They were halfway into another ramble about a meal that Castorice had tried making with herbs that Cipher had found— see: probably stolen but Castorice clearly didn’t want to admit that bit— when they were interrupted by a series of knocks.

The raps weren’t particularly loud, though they echoed through Castorice’s living room regardless.

She jumped. Begrudgingly, Phainon lifted his head from where his cheek had remained pressed against her shoulder for the past quint.

“Expecting someone?” He asked.

“I wasn’t,” Castorice said, standing. “I’ll be right back.”

From where he remained on the couch, it was impossible to see the front door as Castorice opened it. Not that it mattered, really, who her guest was. If her visitor needed her urgently, then he’d go back to Cyrene’s rooms and fold himself up on the couch with outerworld music playing on a loop. If her attention wasn’t needed for longer than a few minutes, then he’d simply prompt Castorice on her return to the sofa to continue telling him about the Dromas curry she had been talking about.

Simple.

He didn’t care about who her guest was.

Castorice unlocked her door with a click of its latch just as Phainon retrieved his teleslate, intent on searching for the songs Cyrene had shown him the previous night.

Then she said, “Lord Mydei. Did something happen?”

Like electricity, Phainon jolted, fumbling with his teleslate. It slipped free from his fingers, landing on stone flooring with an almost deafening thud.

Well then.

Maybe he cared a little bit about who Castorice’s guest was.

“Just checking up on you,” came Mydei’s deep timbre. “You weren’t at the Garden this morning. I thought you might be sick.”

Phainon didn’t exactly register standing but one moment, he was trapped in cushions and a sofa that was cosy enough that it could swallow a person entirely, the next he was standing, craning his neck in an attempt to see the doorway.

Nothing from this angle.

At the edge of his hearing, the rain outside seemed to increase in its intensity. Heavier than before. Before it had been harsh but now it sounded downright torrential.

"Ah,” Castorice said. It was easy to hear the smile in her voice, the fondness she held for their fellow heirs. “You don’t need to worry. I’m not sick. I have a guest over today so I pushed back my visit to tomorrow.”

Phainon wasn’t sure whether she was going to invite Mydei in. He wasn’t sure whether he wanted her to. Whether he wanted to see Mydei or not.

—Ones and zeroes echoed in his mind’s eye and suddenly he was in the ruins of Aedes Elysiae again, holding a body that dissipated into broken fragments of code—

And it didn’t matter whether he wanted to see him or not because his feet were already moving. Because want did not matter - he needed to see Mydei and confirm that he was real. Even if he was only a fragment from the cycles, even—

He turned the corner and there he was.

Mydeimos, drenched by the rain and with the same crease in his right brow that he always got whenever concern had sunk into his physique with the heaviness of stone. He was holding a flask in his hand— no doubt he’d made Castorice soup the moment he’d thought she might be unwell. Like the last time Phainon had seen him, his gauntlets remained missing from calloused hands.

The room flashed, flooded by white-gold light.

And then, before any of them could react, a deafening crack of thunder split through the room, like a tear, ripping open a fissure of pure noise into Castorice's home, displacing the previous soothing ambience it held. It was as loud as a final breath was within silence.

Past Castorice’s shoulder, he met Mydei’s gaze, eyes widening as a second flash of lightning descended over Okhema.

Castorice turned with such speed she almost tripped over her own feet, concern present in the bite of her lip, “Phainon—”

Phainon couldn’t tear his attention away to focus on her. He was stuck, staring at Mydei, struggling to tell whether this copy of him was real or a piece of code readying to delete itself like the version in Aedes Elysiae had been.

Ripples of ones and zeroes pressed against the back of his eyelids as he blinked and it felt, almost, like he couldn’t breathe. He tried - once, then twice, until on the third try he managed to inhale a gulp of air that was entirely too dry.

“Lo—” Castorice moved towards him, pressing two sets of fingers into his palm. "Phainon."

She was still warm.

(Code didn’t emulate warmth like this, he reminded himself.)

Phainon blinked. Once and then a second time. And then, finally, he managed to tear his gaze away, across to Castorice’s hands holding his and to the look of deep concern she aimed towards him.

“Sorry,” he murmured. “I was just—”

He didn’t know how to explain himself so he simply folded his fingers with hers and offered another grimace-smile her way and repeated, "Sorry."

Then, because he was aware that there were two sets of eyes focused on him now, watching with caution— or maybe what he saw was worry? — he met Mydei’s gaze once more and murmured, “It’s been a while, Mydei.”

Chapter End Notes

Chapter Notes

i was very hype for this chapter. very excited. i've been very !!! while writing this one. hope you guys enjoy as much as i have!!

After the fight with Irontomb, after the Chrysos Heirs and their companions from beyond the stars had ushered in the Era Nova, it had been Mydei who pulled Phainon free from the scepter’s core.

Stelle had pried open loose sheets of metal with her lance, Cyrene and March 7th had cooled the molten, bubbling metal and fried circuitry within each breached layer and the Astral Express’s genius companions had stabilised the dying scepter’s core to keep it from imploding and sending out an invitation for another Aeon’s gaze upon Amphoreus.

Everyone had helped tear apart the remains of Irontomb to locate him but Mydei had been the one to breach the scepter’s core first.

It had been Mydei’s voice that murmured, ‘Found you’. It had been Mydei’s fingers, sharp and melting, that tore him free from the wires. Who had pulled Phainon, half-conscious, into his arms and carried him out of the wreck, one layer at a time, unyielding and strong despite the blood pouring from a gash in his forehead and the burns spread across shaking fingers.

The first voice Phainon had heard outside of Lygus’ and Irontomb’s in a thousand years had been that of his equal. A low cadence filled with exhausted, trembling relief.

He didn’t really remember much between waking and reaching the impromptu debrief on what had happened to bring them into the new Era. A thousand years of isolation and pain tended to make you groggy like that. But that had stuck: The tremble in Mydei’s voice. The force of fingers digging into flesh to ensure Phainon remained held in place and would not

disappear. The way his head had rested against warm skin as they escaped the scepter and ascended to the ruined land at Dawncloud’s peak.

Mydei had been the one to carry Phainon into the Era Nova.

And how had Phainon repaid him in the days following? He’d spent every waking moment trying his damned best to avoid him.

And when his attempts had been rendered impossible he had thrown the man into a block of frozen time so that he could flee without the risk of pursuit.

Fleeing had been necessary. Phainon knew that. The risk of doing something irreversible, something fatal, had been narrowly avoided. Staying would’ve been a prerequisite to disaster. Running, on this occasion, hadn’t been spurred by cowardice but by the knowledge that his anger was too hot for any other person to withstand.

Objectively, he knew this

And yet, looking at Mydei now - at the way his brows furrowed, the way concern danced behind his pupils as they locked eyes, no anger present, only worry, - it was hard to feel anything but guilt. All he could hear was ‘foundyoufoundyoufoundyou’ in that same tone, that same trembling exhaustion.

He didn’t want to think about how Mydei had said the words but there was an echo in his ears and he didn't know how to mute it. He wanted to. He wanted to stop it, to cut it out entirely, because that relief was the sort found only alongside affection. The sort of affection that came following the end of a timely wait.

…They had been equals.

Before.

During the cycles.

That had meant something. It had always meant something.

It hurt to linger on the reason why, though, so Phainon didn’t. Thinking about it would be too much of an admission. The weather was already out of control with his current thoughts, to delve into such ancient and fragile things…

Well. He didn’t want any other coreflames resonating with the emotions bubbling inside of his chest.

“Phainon,” Mydei said now, quietly. There was no relief in this word. Just concern. Just something bordering on… well, Phainon wasn’t too sure what it bordered on. He was more focused on the flare of lightning that spread through the room following the sound of his name from Mydei’s lips. “It has.”

Silence.

Phainon didn’t know what to say and it seemed, at this point, that neither Mydei nor Castorice knew what to say either. He probably should’ve said something, anything, should've convinced them all that he was alright. Maybe even blame the lightning and thunder on… actual weather fluctuations and not that of his own influence.

…Yeah, like they’d believe that.

They must've remained like that for at least half a minute, silent and unspeaking, before Mydei finally piped up once more. His attention shifted to Castorice as he said, “I just came to check you were alright. Since you are, I’ll let you both get back to your visit—”

A deafening roar of thunder flooded the room.

This time, Phainon didn’t catch the lightning coming in through the window. Instead, it spread across his vision as if his eyes were the source. Tinged with gold and flame, it was his vision - not the room - that was painted with light. Even after the initial flare, it remained, unwilling to fade from sight until he began physically shaking his head in an attempt to dislodge it.

When he lifted his head and looked between both his fellow heirs he found that they had returned to watching him.

Mydei’s gaze flicked from Phainon to the window. Quiet. Contemplative.

Hesitant, he said, “Or, I could come inside?”

Nothing. No thunder. No lightning. The room - and consequently Phainon’s vision - remained dimly lit.

Castorice squeezed his hand. She asked, “What would you prefer, Phainon?”

He wasn’t sure.

He wanted Mydei to stay while also wanting him to leave. His thoughts felt fuzzy from the thunder and the way light had caught in his eyes. It was difficult to tell what he wanted or what would be the best route to take - stay or go, what did it matter? He'd spent so long ignoring his own emotions that looking inwards was too difficult. Understanding his own emotions with any depth was impossible. It was already difficult enough figuring out the more superficial thoughts. Understanding his own wants? That was too much. He didn't know.

…Although maybe that was a lie. Maybe he did.

The storm had only worsened for one option, after all. And it hadn't been over the idea of Mydei staying.

Sighing, Phainon squeezed Castorice’s hand in return. The answer was clear, when taking the reactions of the weather into account. He asked, “Do you still have enough for hot chocolate?”

She nodded.

“Can you make enough for three?”

“Of course,” Castorice said. Her smile returned, as if her worry was just as temporary as the lightning outside had been and that there was no longer any need to fret. “Come in, Lord Mydei. We’re having cocoa - you’ll need to come and pick out a mug.”

Phainon didn’t want to make his friends worry more than they already were so while Castorice went to the kitchen to make another batch of hot chocolate and Mydei went to the bathroom to dry off (and hopefully stop looking like a drenched chimera), he returned to the sofa and proceeded to hug one of the pillows close to his chest.

Another message from Cyrene had found itself to his teleslate, checking in. It was no doubt in response to the worsening storm. The idea of typing anything left him tired and ill-eased so he simply sent a few stickers that hopefully explained the situation well enough to show that he was not in need of rescue.

Now that he’d invited Mydei in he wasn’t entirely sure what to do.

If things continued how they had previously with Castorice then they would settle into a conversation where Phainon didn’t need to be an overly active participant. Castorice could continue telling him about her daily life in the new Era and if Mydei joined in with that then it would be fine.

Probably.

...Who was he kidding? It wouldn’t be fine.

It’d be the awkwardest thing in existence.

If they settled into the same conversation as they had previously then Castorice's shared stories would begin to feel lesser. Not for lack of interest but because their intent would have changed. Instead of sharing for the sake of friendship, the stories would become padding used to cover the wound of everything unspoken between him and Mydei. Phainon didn't want her stories to feel less important because of awkwardness. Because they weren't. He didn’t want them to be offered in an attempt to rid the room of the lingering tension that his actions had brought.

Which meant that, really, what he needed to do before they settled into conversation as a trio was get rid of that tension. After that, he could go back to a more passive role.

Until that point however, that meant he had to talk.

To Mydei.

…

Phainon blinked away static and shoved his face into the pillow in his arms, letting out a long groan. Yeah. He would really rather do anything but open up, actually. The whole avoidance thing might not have been working wonders for his apparently poor mental health but at least it helped temporarily.

Okay. Maybe not temporarily. Momentarily. Same difference.

He didn’t want to talk.

And yet, hearing the door to Castorice’s bathroom click open, he knew that he was going to do it anyway.

Footsteps padded down the corridor and into the living space. Phainon could feel each step like a vibration against the soles of his feet— courtesy of Georios’ coreflames— and forced himself to look up from his pillow.

In the absence of Castorice’s warmth, without either Stelle or Cyrene around to soothe his mind with their presence, his surroundings were becoming distorted once more. Unreal. Less like reality and more like how videos on a teleslate feed tried to simulate reality.

Mydei glanced over momentarily before moving towards the kitchen. He said, “Cas—”

And then: A double-take. One moment he was mid-step and the next he had paused. He pivoted on his foot, turning back to Phainon. His brows furrowed, hair dripping rogue pieces of code onto the ground like water droplets. Footsteps changed trajectory as he approached the sofa.

“Are you crying?” Mydei asked as he stopped by the sofa’s arm. His voice was no louder than a whisper.

Phainon pressed his fingers to his cheeks and found that they were wet. Again. A quick look down showed that he’d left tear stains on the pillow in his arms. He set it down beside him and hoped it would dry soon. Honestly, he wasn’t sure what he was more surprised by: The fact his tears had returned or the knowledge that they had stopped for long enough that Mydei was only asking about them now.

He shrugged half-heartedly and said, “Yeah. I don’t really know how to make it stop.”

Mydei said, “I wouldn’t know.”

Ha. Asshole.

Despite himself, Phainon let out a wet laugh and wiped at his tears with the back of his hand. “Right. Princes don’t cry.”

“I didn’t mean it like that,” Mydei said and sat on the other end of the couch.

Yeah, Phainon knew that much. Knowing Mydei, the Kremnoan had simply meant that he didn’t stop himself from feeling things - that if he needed to cry then he would. Well, that was alright for him. He didn’t have 33 million cycles worth of hell rattling around in his head or have the need to disassociate to keep from drowning the entirety of Amphoreus.

“I know you didn’t,” Phainon sighed. It was easier to focus on the knitting needles sitting on Castorice’s table than to look Mydei in the eye, so he did, fingers curling in his lap. “I— I’ve been meaning to apologise. For that day. Eventually. I’ve just been…”

Doing bad? Sleeping the days away because the exhaustion had finally decided it wouldn't let him ignore it anymore?

He wasn't sure what to say.

“Apologise?”

Phainon chewed on his bottom lip. His fingers curled more until they were fists. “For… pausing you and the Professor and then leaving you both in that field.” He paused. Pressed his lips in a thin line. “And for what I said to you both.”

Well, alright, maybe mostly what he’d said to Mydei. He hadn’t actually done anything to deserve his ire. It was just… Phainon had been so angry. When Mydei hadn't taken his side over Anaxa's, he'd felt betrayed and then, when the prince had tried to calm he'd...

Well. He hadn’t wanted to stop.

And it had been easier to air his grievances, to take said anger out on the world and heirs around him, so he had. It probably made him a terrible person but considering all the murder and destruction that wasn’t exactly anything new.

“I didn’t…” He sighed again. The sound caught in his throat alongside a breathlessness brought on by his own guilty admission. “Well… I did mean to. But it wasn’t fair of me.”

“The fault is with us. Anaxagoras shouldn’t have been so forceful and I should’ve stepped in sooner than I did.” Mydei said. His voice sounded like syrup. Not in tone but in how the words stuck together as Phainon tried to process them. Difficult to parse. Even more difficult to swallow. “And on that account I am sorry.”

Nope. This wasn’t how it was supposed to go.

He forced his gaze up, meeting gold with blue. His eyes were wide, imploring. Perhaps desperate too, as emotion crashed against the insides of his stomach with enough force to leave him nauseous. He said, “I trapped you both in time. For days.”

“Yes.”

“And I was cruel,” he continued. “What I said to you both—”

“Was not as cruel as you think it was,” Mydei interrupted. Phainon let out a noise of indignation and Mydei fixed him with a long stare. “Phainon, you called my immortality fake and then called me pathetic for dying. We have said harsher things to one another during spars.”

…Alright. Good to know that he had some sort of a filter even as the flames of his rage turned everything to dust.

Had he really not said anything more? There had been a lot of roiling thoughts and ranting in his head at the time. Phainon had been certain what he’d said was much worse than just that a few comments on immortality and death.

“Your actions did not come across as cruel,” Mydei continued. “Just cornered. And we were the ones who cornered you. That wasn’t fair of us.”

Phainon opened his mouth. Tasted blood on his tongue. Closed it again.

A quick glance down was enough to see that reality was fragmenting further around him. Though Mydei wasn’t actually bleeding out before him from the gaping wound in his chest - (he hoped so anyway) - Phainon sure could see gore and viscera as if it were truly present.

“Right,” he said and swallowed thickly.

(Titans, he was stupid for letting Mydei come in.

…How long did it take Castorice to make hot chocolate, again? Surely not this long. It felt like it’d been a quint. What was taking her so long?)

“And for what it’s worth,” Mydei continued, into the silence, after a brief - not nearly long enough - hesitation. “I’m sorry for dying. Even if it was prophesied I did not want to leave you to bear everything alone.”

‘Don’t be sorry’, Phainon thought, guiltily and exhausted, fists digging into the flesh of his thighs with enough force to bruise. ‘I’m the one who killed you.’

A pause.

Mydei’s lips parted in surprise and though his eyes did not widen, his pupils shook. Startled. Mydei was startled by something and staring at him like—

—like—

…Oh no.

No.

No. No— Titans, he didn’t just say that out loud, did he?

“I—” Phainon jumped back, hip catching against the arm of the sofa with such power that it tore a hiss from his throat. A nervous laugh followed, bursting from trembling lips. As unwelcome as the words he’d apparently spoken aloud. No. Of all the things to actually admit to why this. Why murder? Why the Flame Reaver? “I mean—”

He was on his feet before he could think about moving. Lightning caught in his eyes and remained there. Phainon wasn’t sure if the thunder in his ears was that of his pulse or the skies outside.

“I didn’t say anything—” He gasped. “That was— I’m just— It wasn’t—”

A hand caught his wrist like a brand. Phainon tried to yank it away but the hold was firm. As firm as the way Mydei said his name.

“Phainon,” Mydei repeated, ignoring the way he was trying to take back words that should not have been said. “Phainon, look at me.”

No, he couldn’t do that.

Anything but that.

“Phainon,” Mydei repeated. “Nikador above, listen to me would you? Phainon, I know already. I knew. I always knew. You don’t— Stop panicking. I already knew.”

The truth dawned on him all at once.

Harsh and irrefutable, accompanied by a chill worse than that found in the Hyperborean snow plains, Phainon came to the realisation that he was well and truly fucked.

Avoidance wasn’t going to help him now. It couldn’t. Because Mydei knew.

He knew that Phainon had been his murderer. That he was the one who had cleaved through flesh with a sword as decayed as the rest of him, shattering his tenth thoracic vertebrae and leaving him in a pool of his own blood to die, slow and pained, choking on his final breath.

How?

And how much did he know?

How far did Mydei’s knowledge go? Did he know only of his death within the 33,550,336th cycle, the one he could remember, or did he know about all of them? Had he counted each betrayal in every fragment of shattered bone, seen each death by Phainon’s hand? Was he horrified by the sheer number of them, these countless ends that Phainon had issued him?

When Mydei looked at him, could he see how much blood had died into the cracks of his skin?

Phainon had tried to scrub himself free of the memories but these deeds could never be washed clean. Was it obvious? When the Kremnoan looked could he tell how even the hottest of his flames could not permanently burn away the memories?

It felt like he was drowning.

Not in water but in spiralling thoughts. In uncertainty.

Phainon tried to breathe and barely managed a gasp.

“No,” he said, a strangled sound of distortion and static. His ears were ringing. A whine rose in his throat, rippling with desperation and pleas.

Not this.

He’d tell them how many cycles he’d passed through. He’d give them details about everything else he had suffered. About Lygus and his experiments. About Nanook and his swordsman and the war he had waged at the end of Amphoreus’ code. Anything they wanted to know he would tell them.

Anything but this.

Mydei’s fingers were still holding his wrist, pressing into the skin with an intensity of a bruise to prove how unwilling he was to let go. And Phainon knew he deserved it, deserved this show of hatred, of unmoving anger, yet he tried to yank free from the prince’s hold regardless, vision burning, thoughts melting—

“No,” he rasped again, voice trembling.

He hadn’t meant to say it out loud. The thought hadn’t been one he wanted to share, so why had he? The why didn’t matter, he just needed to find a way to take them back, to undo it.

But how could he? Time didn’t work like that, he couldn’t—

Ice slithered down his spine and as the cold spread through him, so too did clarity.

Who was he to say that he couldn’t?

The people of Amphoreus, with the help of Orynyx’s power, could reverse the flow in time of broken objects. With a single coreflame you could - even in this new Amphoreus where time had linked itself to the rest of the observable universe - quicken or slow the rate of growth in plants. With thousands, he had managed to suspend time within a fragment of space.

…And that was only with thousands.

If he used more coreflames… if he used them all… would he be able to undo this? Would he be able to take back the words that had slipped from his lips? Take back the admission that had led Mydei to know the truth?

Phainon didn’t have the finesse of someone born to inherit Time’s coreflame, nor the skill to do so with the same ease and understanding, but that didn’t need to mean anything. Who needed finesse when one had brute power?

33 million coreflames of Time remained in his body. If he tried using them then maybe he could rewrite how it had gone. Instead of his instinctive refusal of Mydei’s apology, he could accept it. He could pretend things were fine between them, that he wasn’t a monster, that they wouldn’t all hate him after every monstrous act he had committed.

Ticking echoed in his ears.

“Phainon,” Mydei’s voice, around the moving clock in his ears. “Phainon. Listen to me, I promise—”

A laugh burst from his throat, drowning Mydei’s words out before they could register. He must’ve sounded crazed, like the stress of admission was too much but that was fine. Mydei wouldn’t remember. He’d redo this interaction and then he wouldn’t need to lose him. He wouldn’t have to lose any of them.

He looked up at Mydei, to his worry and dismay, and yanked his arm free.

“It’s okay,” he murmured. His voice sounded distant to his ears. “It’s fine.”

“Yes,” Mydei repeated, desperate. “It’s—”

“I just won’t say it next time.”

Mydei’s eyes widened. “What—”

Phainon took hold of thirty-three million coreflames of Time, took hold of the cosmic clock of existence and began pulling the hands backwards.

It was nothing like trying to control water. To pull at Time was nothing like dragging at a rippling tide, or picking away at loose threads of space. It was a slow drag, heavy in the way singular atoms were heavy - not in truth but in relativity. Seconds passed in reverse. Words flowed backwards.

The coreflames burning through his body flared. They pulsed. Dizzying with their intensity, they melded into one, into something limitless, power expanding doublefold, tenfold, over and over. And yet, the more he pushed anticlockwise on Time’s passage, the more his power intensified, the more it began to feel wrong.

Amphoreus strained against him. No, not just Amphoreus - the galaxy. The whole goddamned universe.

A burn settled in his chest. His heart was beating in reverse. Blood boiled in his veins as it moved in the wrong direction and as the world spun back on its axis, Phainon found himself unable to breathe.

Power cycled through him in a way antithetical to comprehensible existence.

His vision, rippling with gold, wasn’t able to track the backwards flow of time. His pulse heavy in his ears, wrong and distorted, couldn’t hear the world reversing itself. The only thing proving that things were going back was the reverse of sensation.

A hand shackled around him once more as if he’d never yanked himself free. Because he hadn’t.

Then, fingers lifted from his wrist entirely.

It was difficult to know how long his focus remained on the backwards flow. Could’ve been a second or a year - Time didn’t make sense when it was being physically altered. It stretched and expanded while simultaneously squishing together.

All Phainon knew for sure was that one moment he was pushing everything back and the next he had to let go of time entirely so that he could resume breathing.

Time settled back into motion as if it had never been altered. It did not burst, or run, it simply continued moving in tandem with its natural course. A steady walk towards tomorrow.

Phainon gasped. He swallowed down air like a man starved of it. Legs trembling, he barely managed to keep himself upright. Wavering, the world blurred around him as the burn continued to settle in his bones and electrified each nerve.

A hand caught his wrist like a brand.

It helped steady him, though Phainon knew that was not its intended purpose. He blinked away light and surprise and tried to yank his arm free from the hold. Again, it was firm. Just as firm as Mydei’s voice when he said his name.

Heaving in more air, he stilled.

“Phainon,” Mydei repeated. It hadn’t been possible to hear the concern last time, considering how messy his own thoughts had become, but hearing things a second time made it easier to pick out. It was low. Not quite frantic but definitely tinged with a worry that bordered on the edge of panic. “Phainon, look at me.”

…He hadn’t gone back far enough.

Phainon tore his gaze from the floor to his hands. Despite the burn of his body, the golden sheen to his vision, his flesh was still intact. No outward signs of any burn. His fingertips weren’t flaking away into ash and embers.

There wasn’t even any numbness that typically came from housing the coreflames. From using them.

(Something snarling in the back of his mind remembered being remade under Nanook’s gaze. The Aeon had done something to him. Made it so that his body could withstand the burn. What had They turned him into?)

“Phainon,” Mydei repeated. “Nikador above, listen to me would you? Phainon, I know already. I knew. I always knew. You don’t— Stop panicking. I already knew.”

The same phrase as before.

He hadn’t gone back far enough but that was alright. Phainon had proven that it could be done. Who truly expected things to work on the first try? They rarely did. That was what trying again was for. If at first you don’t succeed and all of that nonsense.

He could withstand a second attempt. His vision was bathed in gold but the flames hadn’t taken the sense entirely. His body wasn’t fuel for the flames, they had become fuel for him. This body, whatever it had been turned into, was clearly capable of withstanding the power usage - it might be uncomfortable but he was clearly capable of surviving it.

“Try again,” Phainon murmured and took a deep breath.

Time began to unfurl.

Mydei’s fingers lifted from his wrist.

His blood had reached a temperature where it no longer boiled but burned. His lungs were cracking under the weight of the pressure, of the vacuum created within the gaps of time.

Clearly, the universe did not enjoy being handled with such heavy hands.

…And yet, Phainon couldn’t bring himself to care. Existence could deal with a little bit of clumsy handling.

The more he dragged time back, the more it began to dig its heels into the cosmos and resist. A gasp caught in his throat that was unable to develop in fruition. The pressure upon his shoulders, the weight of reality, was immense. Phainon’s pulse thundered against his eardrums with an intensity near bursting.

The next time he let go of the coreflames, everything was ringing.

When time began to flow once more, Phainon’s legs crumpled.

His heart caught against his ribs like a vice. The muscle squeezed. It whimpered. The only reason he remained standing was because a hand wrapped around his wrist and held him in place.

“Phainon,” Mydei said. Repeated. Phainon hadn’t done anything more than bring them back to this same point in time. Seconds. Millions of coreflames and he could only manage a few seconds? No. He was better than that. If he boosted the coreflames with the power of the others… “Phainon, look at me.”

It was worth a try.

Phainon’s teeth gnashed, molars grinding.

“I can do better,” he gasped and tried again.

On his third attempt, Mydei did not catch him by the wrist but with both arms as his legs gave way beneath him entirely.

That was fine. He didn’t need to be able to stand. He just needed to go back far enough.

“Phainon—”

He just had to try again. If he powered himself with more coreflames then maybe it would work this time.

“Phainon, what—”

Something sharp dug into his head. A lance through the brain. The universe had grown teeth in response to his meddling and had begun biting back, pushing against him with each attempt.

Ha, what a joke. Clearly, the universe should’ve known better. He was used to a little pain. This was nothing.

“Phainon, is that—”

This time, Mydei’s voice was louder. Loud enough that Castorice, in the other room, could hear. Phainon heard footsteps padding into the room but it didn’t matter. He didn’t want to hear her worry.

He went back.

“Phainon, what are—”

Not good enough. He’d use more coreflames. All he needed to do was drag time back - he was not its prisoner anymore. Right now he was the one imprisoning it.

“Wait—”

Go back.

“—Is that—”

Try again.

“—Are you—”

He had to take the words back.

“—bleeding?”

Huh?

Phainon lifted a hand to his nose and sure enough, he was. Golden blood trickled from his nostrils, a smear of it across his lips, dripping from his chin.

“I’m fine,” he said, pushing weakly at hands that settled on his shoulders, supporting his body. “I can just—”

He reached for—

Agony sprang through his body. It wasn’t simply pain but something beyond that. Pain was physical. This was something beyond physicality, something beyond the bundle of nerves that begged for him to stop.

Intrinsic understanding flooded through him. It was not a consequence of using the coreflames themselves. The power he was using sat comfortably within his body but the ricochet of the world around him as he influenced it with their use had begun to tear at him in a way that not even this body could handle.

His jaw slammed shut. Too late to catch the cry that tore itself free.

On instinct, he dropped hold of the world around him.

Fingers caught hold of his chin and yanked his head up.

“Phainon,” Mydei said, voice harsh and frantic. His face was pale, pupils trembling as he met Phainon’s eyes. It wasn’t an expression that Phainon had seen him wear often. Usually, Mydei held himself with more calm. He didn’t panic.

…Why was Mydei panicking?

“Whatever you’re doing,” Mydei said. “Stop it. You’re hurting yourself. You don’t need to, it’s alright.”

“It’s not alright,” Phainon gasped. Tears had begun to mix with his blood. “You were never supposed to know. I can’t undo it.”

“I always knew,” Mydei said, roughly. “I realised as I was dying. I’ll always know.”

“You can’t.” Phainon pulled himself back.

“Why not?”

They deserved to know. Realistically, he knew that. This wasn’t something centered just around him, it wasn’t wholly his own truth. They deserved to know who had killed them. The identity of the Flame Reaver. Denying them was cruel.

…But Phainon was cruel.

He’d hurt them so much and they deserved to know that. But if they knew then they wouldn’t stay by his side. And as much as he hated them for what they’d placed on his shoulders, as much as he couldn’t always look at them, as much as he didn’t deserve to remain beside them, he loved them so dearly that he didn't care. This cruelty was inconsequential if it meant that he didn't have to bear their hatred.

He wanted to remain by their side so badly and he couldn’t do that if they knew.

“Because you’ll hate me for all of it,” Phainon shouted. “I killed you. I killed all of you. So many times. I don’t— You’ll—”

One final time. He could try one final time. Irrelevant of the pain, irrelevant of everything. He’d use everything. Every coreflame. Every flicker of power to make everything go away. To undo it all.

Mydei stared.

Something caught in his expression. Past the panic. Past the worry and all of the concern.

Sadness.

Deep, unending.

“Hate you?” Mydei said. “Never. Phainon, you know that I l—”

Coreflames rose within him. Every single one.

He tore into time and ripped it open. Threw it into reverse and lashed out at every piece of pressure that existence threw at him. Undo it. He had to undo it, every word. Every admission.

It couldn’t happen.

No. Phainon couldn’t accept this. He could manage more than a few seconds. He could. He just needed to hold onto his breath a little longer. He just needed to deal with the agony, the pain, the suffering. He’d dealt with similar pain over billions of years so why couldn’t he do this—

He held on until he needed to breathe and then, after that, he held on even longer. Held on until the suffering was too much, until his lungs deflated entirely, until there was no thought of being able to continue for even a moment more.

Time ricocheted.

The universe growled and crashed back into motion. Teeth bared. Daring him to try again for even a second longer. Exhaustion flooded through him with such force that his entire body sagged.

The coreflames, flickering in his body, wavered. Drained and unwilling to respond to the urge of his bones for more power.

Phainon opened his eyes and Mydei was staring.

His eyes were sad. Filled with a sorrow that ran deeper than any other than Phainon had seen him display in the past.

“Hate you?” He said, and something in Phainon’s eyes shuttered. There was no undoing this, was there? “Never. Phainon, you know that I—”

He stopped but this time it was not the backwards drag of time that cut him off.

It was coughing.

Phainon’s coughing. Wet and sickly, into trembling hands.

“Stop,” Mydei said, and pulled Phainon into his arms. Briefly, he could hear Castorice’s voice but her words weren’t sinking in. She must’ve been summoned by his shouting. Or maybe it had been before that, when the pain had torn a cry from his lips. “Stop using the coreflames. I don’t hate you. I could never. I told you my weakness for a reason. I always knew it would be you.”

…He must’ve been lying. He had to be.

The sins that he’d accumulated. They couldn’t be forgiven. He was a monster. If he couldn’t undo it then he’d never… They wouldn’t—

“You can’t know,” Phainon repeated. His voice was no louder than a whisper, depleted of all its strength. “If you know then you'll all leave and I’ll be left alone.” Something in him cracked. His voice. His mind. “I can’t go back to that again. I can’t.”

Silence.

Thickly, Mydei tightened his hold on him and said, “You won’t.”

Around him, a second set of arms wrapped around him. Warmth where previously there hadn’t been. It made the promise feel a little more real.

“Never,” Castorice agreed.

Phainon buried his head into Mydei’s shoulder, leaned into Castorice’s warmth and did not fight the sobs that tore free from the depths of his being.

Chapter Notes

after writing this chapter, and being asked on twt whether this fic has a happy ending, i have indeed updated my tags to claim that it does.

this fic is all about healing and while there's definitely a lot of angst going on rn, it's not all pain for pains sake. we will reach a happy end eventually, i promise!! place your trust in me and the process. i'll get us there <3

Phainon was still sobbing when the pounding at Castorice’s door began.

It was a heavy sound. Not just in the way the sound reverberated through Castorice’s home but in the way it displaced the warmth and allowed the cold of reality to trickle down his spine. As his friend pulled away, he was left to Mydei’s embrace, coughing up coagulated blood from where it had set in his lungs.

“You’re okay,” Mydei murmured as Castorice’s footsteps padded away from them. One of his hands cradled the back of Phainon’s skull, keeping him close. Not that Phainon had the energy to pull away even if he’d wanted to. “I’ve got you.”

His tears had dried but his blood had not.

The flow had slowed from his nostrils but beads of gold still dripped sluggishly from his chin. Each cough brought up a spray of it. It was difficult to know what exactly he’d done to his body. His pain was absent - not in actuality, (Phainon knew it hadn’t simply disappeared), but because a lifetime of agony simply rendered him incapable of identifying anything that wasn’t pure agony.

“Hyacine’s gonna be mad at me,” he muttered.

Mydei didn’t lie to him. He simply agreed and said, “Yes. A little bit. But mostly she’ll be worried.”

Worried.

Titans, he didn’t want them to be worried.

He wanted to say that she didn’t need to be worried, that none of them needed to be worried, but he didn’t get the chance because as Castorice unlatched the door he heard Cyrene’s voice, loud and frantic, echoing from the outside corridor, “Is he still here?”

Phainon didn’t hear Castorice’s reply but he heard her general tone. Concern attempting to give way to calm.

“I’m coming in,” Cyrene said, footsteps thundering into the room. Something like a gasp caught in her throat as her cold followed her into the room, catching sight of him. While he didn’t want to lift his head from Mydei’s shoulder, Phainon did so anyway.

Her expression was nothing short of thunderous. She stalked closer, ice forming in patches on her skin, frost catching in the gaps beneath fingernails. Every breath came out foggy.

Cyrene took a split moment to assess the state that he was in - the blood, his tears, the weakness that had entered trembling bones - before dropping to her knees before him and placing both hands on his cheeks.

They burned with the force of a shiver. Phainon hissed from the discomfort and tried to pull back but she simply followed after him and did not let go. Instead of freeing him, she lifted his chin until there was no choice but to meet her gaze.

Lips trembling, voice high and shrill, Cyrene said, “Do you have any idea what you’ve just done? What you could’ve done?”

He frowned.

Because no he didn’t.

He didn’t even know what she was talking about.

“You could’ve torn the universe to pieces,” she continued. Ice spread in a patch across his cheek. It was so cold that even his own blood, hotter than could ever be described as ‘natural’, froze as well. Mydei’s hold of his body tightened. “Time isn’t meant to go backwards like that. It’s not a wheel; It’s like paper - if you so much as touch it in the wrong way it tears open and everything falls apart!”

“You felt that?” Phainon murmured.

“Of course I felt that!” She snapped. The force of her voice made him flinch back into Mydei’s chest. “You can’t undo time for Amphoreus like that. One wrong move and you desync us all from the rest of the universe. Amphoreus won’t survive that. It won’t.”

The cold was too much. He began attempting to peel Cyrene’s hands away, nails digging into icy fingers and trying to rip them away before the freeze settled into frostbite and he stopped being capable of breaking free at all.

“I wouldn’t have done that,” he said, roughly.

“Not intentionally,” Cyrene agreed, “but you almost did. You could’ve.”

“No,” Phainon repeated. His voice cracked in defense of himself. “I couldn’t. I kept it synced. It wouldn’t have. I’m not an idiot, Cyrene. I know — I know enough to understand that breaking a clock is stupid—”

“—Somehow I doubt that—”

“—I moved it all back together!” He could feel his frustration rising alongside his defensiveness. “But it doesn’t matter anyway because it didn’t work. I couldn’t do it. I didn’t manage to—Nothing came of it, okay? I’m not strong enough to— to break things like that.”

Cyrene dropped her hands from his cheeks. The sting of cold remained but at least now there was a chance for his skin to thaw.

Then, slowly, she said, “What do you mean you ‘moved it all back together?’”

“I didn’t isolate time or anything,” he said. “I just moved all of it back. Nothing would have unsynced itself, I didn’t—” His gaze flicked from her, to where Castorice stood behind them both, picking at her nails in an attempt to keep her panic from showing, to Mydei’s sad eyes and thin pressed lips. “—didn’t do anything that would hurt Amphoreus.”

“Only something that would hurt yourself,” Mydei muttered.

Phainon flinched away from that comment as well.

Because that hadn’t been the intention. It wasn’t like he’d known that trying to reverse everything would leave him coughing up blood, body weak and unresponsive. Getting hurt hadn’t been intentional. It had just been the consequence of trying.

“Phainon,” Cyrene said, brows threading together. “Did you just turn back time, multiple times, for the entirety of the cosmos?”

“It didn’t work,” he bit out. “I couldn’t do it. I got— the most I ever managed was a minute. It didn’t work. They still know.”

“Know what?” Cyrene asked.

Mydei’s voice was a quiet thing in his ear. “About the Flame Reaver.”

For a moment there was nothing but silence. Cyrene continued staring. Castorice tried to look at him - clearly found it too hard - and proceeded to stare at the floor instead.

Then, disbelief began to trickle into Cyrene’s eyes.

“All of this—” She waved her hands up and down Phainon’s body, voice shaking, “—because you wanted to avoid having a conversation?”

“That’s not what this was.” He said, though it was obvious to everyone present that he was lying.

“No, it absolutely is,” Cyrene continued. Her exasperation leaked free, like the beginning trickles in a broken dam, the calm before the flood. “Do you even know how many things out there would’ve noticed you breaking the laws of time? The universe is already looking at Amphoreus enough and you’re adding more eyes onto us because you can’t handle talking to your friends?”

The words sliced into him like a knife.

“That’s not fair—”

“—It’s the truth!” Cyrene cried. “All of these secrets are killing you and you’re letting them. Because you, what? You don’t trust that they’d cope with the truth of what happened? This isn’t healthy, Phainon. Can’t you see that?”

Of course he could see.

It wasn’t like he was blind to it. He’d said it before to the trailblazer, hadn’t he? He wasn’t doing well - he’d confirmed that with Stelle. Yesterday. He knew. How couldn’t he know?

The fact was just that he didn’t want to talk about it. He didn’t want to tear things open and suffer more pain when the world already hurt enough. Hurting his friends more wasn’t going to help. It was going to leave him isolated and alone and he couldn’t handle that.

It wasn’t about being able to handle a conversation, it was about being unable to survive the aftermath.

They might not currently hate him for the truth of the Flame Reaver but that was just right now. Their deaths probably hadn’t sunk in yet. That was all. When it did, when the truth settled in…

“Look,” Cyrene continued, when his silence had stretched for too long. “I understand, alright. It’s hard. It’s—”

Frustration bubbled into anger. Into that same rage that had flooded him before in the field with the professor and Mydei. Into the same fury that had led to the destruction of Aedes Elysiae.

“No, Cyrene,” he snapped, trying to pry Mydei’s hands from his waist so that he could stand. “You don’t understand.”

It was such an easy shift in emotion - her ice had carved the warmth from him and now all he felt was cold.

“You only had to watch,” he continued. He batted at Mydei’s arms, unable to loosen them but the man wasn’t letting go. The grip didn’t tighten but it wasn’t easing either. “You think that reading about everything that happened equates to understanding how it felt? I had to live through everything you read. Every summary. Every scene. Every chapter. Over and over and over and over and over. How could you ever understand that?”

Cyrene reared back as if his words were a slap. He could see her frustration give way to something deeper: To ripples of pain rising from beneath the surface.

She said, “That’s not fair. It wasn’t easy for me either, you know. I didn’t have a choice—”

“I wish I hadn’t had a choice!” Phainon’s voice broke into a dry laugh. Or perhaps it was another sob. Whatever it was, it was accompanied with a spray of blood. “You didn’t have a choice on whether to keep going but I did. You didn’t have to choose but I did. Keep suffering, Phainon. Forgo rest for another cycle, Deliverer. It’s only a little pain, Khaslana! Every single time I breathed I had to keep consciously making the same choice. And you think you could ever understand that?”

“Well, not entirely but—”

“You told me that it would be a romantic story, Cyrene.” He spat. “But it wasn’t. You lied. Where was the romance in all of this? It only ever hurt. As you were reading about the cycles, I had to suffer them. It wasn’t romantic, it was a fucking tragedy and it was your idea that put me into them.”

Cyrene no longer looked like she’d been slapped.

She looked like he’d stabbed right into her chest with Dawnmaker. Eyes blown wide, pain trembling through her body accompanied with the kind of twitch that came from a heavy bleed.

Phainon wanted to feel bad about it but he didn’t. He would, later. But currently all he felt was a thrum of satisfaction that came with hurting someone as deeply as he hurt.

“You chose it too, you know.” Cyrene said. Her voice came out small. “There was no other way.”

“And?” He snapped, and tried once more to struggle free from Mydei’s hold. Still, nothing. He was utterly trapped. “That’s supposed to make me feel better? There was no other way so it doesn’t matter?”

“That’s not what I mean! You’re twisting my words!”

He was.

He just didn’t care.

Rational thought wasn’t part of his thinking process anymore. Rationality didn’t matter. He just wanted her to leave him alone. He wanted her to stop pushing. He’d been perfectly happy when they’d scarcely talked about everything he'd experienced, when she’d been on his side.

“I don’t care what you mean.”

Cyrene wiped tears from her eyes, expression growing as frigid as his own. Her brows furrowed and he watched, in real time, as she steeled herself. Pushed her shoulders back and prepared to bite back.

“No,” she said, with growing realisation. “You don’t care, do you? You know, Khaslana, you were always awful to me whenever you got angry.

Always have been. And yet you never learn from it! Taking things out on me isn’t going to make you feel better - I’m just trying to help.”

His voice settled into a snarl. “I don’t want your help.”

He felt wild. Rabid. Like something trapped in a cage, trying to lash out and break free. She’d pushed him into a corner under the guise of help and now she was trying to make him back down?

Phainon hated her. He truly did.

(It wasn’t fair how deeply he could love someone while also despising them. He wanted to carve that care out of his chest but he couldn’t. Even after 33 million cycles it still clung to him. He couldn’t stop caring. That was the problem).

“No, of course not,” Cyrene said, coldly. “You don’t want anyone’s help! You’d rather run yourself into the ground! Pretend everything’s fine as if you’re not consistently questioning reality or destroying everything around you!”

A snarl caught in his throat. No words. Just pure, animalistic rage. It flashed across his vision - a deep burn of gold that settled in his eyes and remained there.

And yet, unflinching, Cyrene continued. “What comes next Khaslana? Going to demolish another building because you’re a little angry? Going to freeze me in time because I’m pushing you a little too much?”

His jaw clenched. Eyes narrowed into a sharp glare.

“Oh, you thought we didn’t know about that one?” She asked, “About the fact you tore a building in two because of some argument you were having with absolutely no one?”

Heat was flaring in his chest; The increased temperature made Mydei hiss and loosen his arms.

Phainon took the opening, wrestled free and stood to face her eye to eye.

Or at least, he tried to.

He’d barely managed to rise when his legs collapsed beneath him. His breath rattled in his lungs with such intensity that he wouldn’t have been surprised if all his blood had collected inside of them. The room was beginning to grow a light shade of grey, blurring at the edges. The world was spinning.

“Shut up,” he snarled.

“Or, you know what? How about you just set off to some other farming village and spend days destroying it. Why don’t you do that?” Cyrene snapped. “It’s such a normal thing for people who are completely fine to do!”

“Shut up!”

“You know, I should’ve listened to Stelle when she told me it was stupid trying to entertain you with all of this!” Frost prowled the floorboards around her, stalking, circling around Phainon as if he were something to be preyed upon. A clash of fire and ice. “I should’ve never agreed to keep everything about the cycles secret. This whole time I’ve just been reinforcing your avoidance. The delusion that things will just work out eventually. I’m not doing it anymore.”

Phainon’s glower burned even brighter. He said, “What?”

Cyrene didn’t answer. She’d already turned her attention from him to the others in the room. With her chin lifted, she now focused on Castorice, on Mydei. She said, “Do you want to know how many cycles it really was?”

Neither Castorice nor Mydei said a word.

“Don’t you dare.”

She didn’t pay him any mind.

Cyrene simply opened her mouth—

(Phainon tried to gather all of the coreflames in an attempt to— to do something, anything. To freeze her, to open an infinity gate and throw her elsewhere, to figure out a way to make her stop— but each one was exhausted. Each flame was an ember of what it usually was, worn from the push against time and the universe.)

—turned her gaze back on to him—

“Don’t,” he pleaded, wild and yet so, so desperate.

—and said, “Thirty-three million, five hundred and fifty thousand, three hundred and thirty-six.”

For a moment: Nothing.

Just a buzzing in his ears as her voice echoed against his ear drums. As the world spun. As everything blurred, monochrome and lifeless, around him.

Then the words registered and Phainon choked on the bitter taste of his own anger.

Somehow, he managed to push himself up to his feet.

His body didn’t feel like it was truly his. It was moving but it didn’t feel like he was the one puppeteering it. When he howled with fury everything felt like it was bordering on distortion.

The only real thing was the wrath that ran through him. The fire running through his chest, that monstrous thing living beneath his skin, the destruction singing in his veins.

It didn’t feel real when he lunged at Cyrene.

It didn’t feel real when Mydei caught him around the waist and pulled him back. Or when Castorice tried to usher Cyrene from the room.

It didn’t feel real as he fought to break free from Mydei’s hold. When his energy began waning once more and his body sagged in place, unable to keep fighting.

The world began to grow more and more grey, everything began spinning like a kaleidoscope, and all Phainon could feel as unconsciousness greeted him was rage.

End: Act 1
